domain.title: The Command Line
domain.tag: bash · text processing · signals · the tools that compound
domain.why: The command line looks intimidating and is actually one of the highest-leverage things you'll learn — once it's comfortable, it makes every other kind of work faster, from finding a bug to automating something boring. It's also easy to use badly: a lot of real damage to real systems has been caused by someone typing a command-line instruction they didn't fully understand. This domain makes sure you're the person who does understand it.

people.name: Chet Ramey
people.role: Maintainer of GNU bash and GNU readline since 1990
people.contribution: Has maintained bash for over three decades, including the POSIX-conformance work, the `[[ ]]` and `(( ))` compound commands, arrays, associative arrays and `${var@Q}`. The Bash Reference Manual and the CHANGES file are his; they are the only authoritative statement of what bash does.
people.note: No public X account found. Design decisions are argued out on the bug-bash and austin-group mailing lists.

people.name: Brian Kernighan
people.role: Co-author of awk and of the original Unix documentation
people.contribution: The K in awk (with Alfred Aho and Peter Weinberger, 1977) and still the maintainer of onetrue-awk. Also wrote The Unix Programming Environment with Rob Pike, which is where the compose-small-tools-with-pipes argument was first written down properly.
people.note: No social media presence. The 2024 second edition of The AWK Programming Language is the current reference.

people.name: Greg Wooledge
people.role: Author of BashFAQ, Bash Pitfalls and the Bash Guide
people.contribution: Wrote and still maintains mywiki.wooledge.org, which contains the definitive write-ups of the word-splitting, `for f in $(ls)`, `while read` subshell and quoting failures. BashPitfalls is the fastest cure for the bugs in this domain.
people.note: Reachable on the #bash IRC channel on Libera.Chat rather than any social platform.

people.name: Stephane Chazelas
people.contribution: Found CVE-2014-6271 (Shellshock), the bash function-export parser bug that let exported environment variables execute code. Also the author of thousands of Unix Stack Exchange answers that are the practical reference for what differs between bash, dash, ksh and zsh.
people.note: Writes on Stack Exchange rather than social media.

people.name: Julia Evans
people.role: Writer of Wizard Zines; explainer of systems tooling
people.contribution: Wrote Bite Size Command Line, Bite Size Linux, How Git Works and the strace/perf/tcpdump zines. Her method - take one tool, find the ten facts that actually unlock it, draw them - is the reason many people got past copy-pasting shell commands.
people.note: Primarily on Mastodon (social.jvns.ca/@b0rk) and Bluesky (b0rk.jvns.ca) now; her site lists no X account.

people.name: Andrew Gallant
people.role: Author of ripgrep and the Rust regex crate
people.contribution: Wrote ripgrep, which combines a finite-automata regex engine (no backtracking, linear time), parallel directory traversal and gitignore filtering. His 'ripgrep is faster than...' post is the best public writeup of how grep-class tools actually spend their time.
people.note: His site and GitHub list no X account; he posts on Mastodon.

people.name: Vidar Holen
people.contribution: Wrote ShellCheck, the static analyser that turns the folklore in BashPitfalls into machine-checkable diagnostics with stable SC codes. Every SC number has a wiki page explaining the bug class, which makes it a curriculum as much as a linter.
people.note: GitHub profile (koalaman) lists no X account.

people.name: Daniel Stenberg
people.role: Author and maintainer of curl and libcurl since 1998
people.contribution: Wrote curl, which is now in essentially every operating system, car and games console. The `-w` write-out variables that turn curl into a per-request latency profiler are his design, as is the everything-curl book.
people.note: Now on Mastodon (@bagder@mastodon.social) and Bluesky (daniel.haxx.se); his GitHub profile no longer lists X.

people.name: Stephen Dolan
people.contribution: Designed jq as a small typed functional language over JSON rather than a text filter, which is why `select`, `map`, `group_by` and `to_entries` compose instead of needing an escape to a real language. The streaming filter model is the reason jq handles inputs larger than memory.
people.note: jq is now community-maintained at jqlang.github.io/jq; no X account listed on his profiles.

people.name: Andrew Tridgell
people.contribution: Invented the rsync algorithm (rolling checksum plus strong hash) in his PhD thesis, which is why rsync can synchronise a large file over a slow link by sending only the changed blocks. Also wrote the reverse-engineered BitKeeper client whose fallout led directly to git.
people.note: Now works on ArduPilot; no X account listed on his GitHub profile.

people.name: Nicholas Marriott
people.contribution: Wrote tmux, whose client/server split is the mechanism that lets a session outlive the terminal that started it. The pane, window and session model plus copy-mode search is what makes long-running remote work survive a dropped connection.

people.name: Anish Athalye
people.role: Co-creator of MIT's The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
people.contribution: Built and taught the Missing Semester course (with Jon Gjengset and Jose Javier Gonzalez Ortiz), whose shell, shell-tools, data-wrangling and command-line-environment lectures are the best free structured path into this domain.

people.role: Author of Ghostty; previously created Vagrant and Terraform

people.name: Dan Luu
people.role: Systems engineer; empirical writer on tooling and latency
people.contribution: Measured terminal-emulator input latency across real terminals and published the numbers, and wrote 'Files are hard' on how badly filesystem error handling is done. Both are correctives to the assumption that console tooling is a solved, uninteresting layer.

sections.note: expansion order is the whole game

L0.body:
# bash rewrites every word in this fixed order, then runs it:
#  1 brace  2 tilde  3 parameter/variable  4 command substitution
#  5 arithmetic  6 word splitting  7 pathname (glob)  8 quote removal

n=3
echo {1..$n}        # {1..3}      brace ran BEFORE $n was expanded
echo $((1+2)){a,b}   # 3a 3b       brace ran before arithmetic too

v='*'
echo $v              # a.txt b.txt glob ran AFTER $v expanded
echo "$v"            # *           quotes cancel steps 6 and 7
L0.cloze:
n=3
echo {1..$n}        # prints {{c1::{1..3}}} — brace expansion runs before parameter expansion
v='*'
echo $v              # prints {{c2::the matching filenames}} — globbing runs after parameter expansion
echo "$v"            # prints {{c3::*}} — quoting suppresses word splitting and globbing

concepts.L1: Brace expansion, tilde, parameter and variable, command substitution, arithmetic, word splitting, pathname (glob) expansion, then quote removal. In that order, every time.
concepts.L2: Word splitting happens *after* variable expansion. That single ordering fact explains nearly every bash bug involving spaces in filenames, and being able to recite the sequence is a legitimate signal of shell literacy.
concepts.L3: Read the order left to right and every result follows. `{1..$n}` cannot expand: brace expansion is step 1, `$n` is not substituted until step 3, so braces see literal text, not a range, and pass it on unchanged - with n=3 the line finally printed is `{1..3}`, braces intact but the variable substituted. Nesting is a separate mechanism: `$(( 1 + $(echo 2) ))` works because arithmetic expansion expands its own operand text first - parameter expansion, command substitution, quote removal - and only then evaluates it. The decisive rule: expansion never rewinds, so what step 3 produces is offered to steps 6 and 7 but never back to step 1. Hence `b='{a,b}.txt'; echo $b` prints the braces literally, while `g='*.txt'; echo $g` globs. Quotes suppress steps 6 and 7 and are removed at step 8; `eval` is a deliberate second run of the whole sequence. Step 6 is developed in Word splitting and IFS.

L4.prompt_tpl:
In an empty directory, a bash script contains:
  `n={n}`
  `echo {{1..$n}}`
What is printed?
L4.explanation: Brace expansion is step 1, parameter expansion is step 3. When braces are considered the word still contains a dollar sign, which is not a valid numeric or character range, so brace expansion leaves that word untouched. Parameter expansion then runs on it anyway, so n IS substituted: the printed line is the braces and dots literally, with the value in place. For a variable range use seq, a C-style for loop, or eval.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory contains exactly the files a.txt and b.txt. A script runs:
  `v='{star}'`
  `echo $v`
  `echo "$v"`
What are the two output lines?
L4.answer: Line 1: a.txt b.txt   Line 2: *
L4.explanation: Unquoted, the expansion of v happens at step 3 and produces a bare asterisk, which is then still present when pathname expansion runs at step 7, so it matches both files. Quoted, steps 6 and 7 are suppressed for that word, so the asterisk survives to output.

L4.prompt_tpl: Recite the eight expansion steps bash applies to a word, in order.
L4.answer: brace expansion; tilde expansion; parameter and variable expansion; command substitution; arithmetic expansion; word splitting; pathname (glob) expansion; quote removal.
L4.explanation: Parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion are performed left to right in a single pass, which is why they are sometimes counted as one step. The load-bearing facts are that brace expansion is first and that word splitting and globbing come after variable expansion.

L4.prompt_tpl:
In an empty directory, bash runs:
  `set -- {lb}1..{n}{rb}`
  `first=$#`
  `r='{lb}1..{n}{rb}'`
  `set -- $r`
  `second=$#`
  `echo $((first + second))`
What single number is printed?
L4.answer: n plus 1. For n=4 first is 4 and second is 1, so 5 is printed; n=6 gives 7; n=9 gives 10.
L4.explanation: Brace expansion is step 1, so the literal word becomes n separate words and first is n. The value of r only arrives at step 3, one step after brace expansion has already gone past, and expansion never rewinds, so its braces are never read as a range; word splitting at step 6 finds no spaces, so second is 1. The sum is n plus 1. Only eval, a deliberate second run of the whole sequence, gets brace expansion out of a variable.

L4.prompt_tpl:
In an empty directory on bash 5, a script runs:
  `b='{blist}.txt'`
  `echo $b`
What exactly is printed? Answer with the single output line.
L4.answer: {a,b}.txt
L4.explanation: Brace expansion is step 1, and at that moment the word is `echo $b`, which contains no braces at all. Parameter expansion at step 3 inserts the text, but expansion never rewinds to an earlier step, so the braces are never read as a list. Pathname expansion at step 7 is still ahead, which is why an asterisk in a variable does glob. To get a list from a variable, use an array or eval.

L4.prompt_tpl:
The user's home directory is /home/kumar. A bash script runs:
  `d='{tilde}/logs'`
  `echo $d`
What exactly is printed? Answer with the single output line.
L4.answer: ~/logs
L4.explanation: Tilde expansion is step 2: it rewrites only an unquoted tilde already present in the word. Here the tilde is inside single quotes at assignment time and only reaches the word at step 3, one step too late, so nothing ever expands it and ls or cd on that value fails. Write `"$HOME/logs"` instead. Note the contrast: d=~/logs without quotes does expand, because assignment words get tilde expansion.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory contains exactly a.txt and b.txt. A bash script runs:
  `b='{blist}.txt'`
  `g='{star}.txt'`
  `echo $b`
  `echo $g`
Give the two output lines, then state the single rule about the expansion order that decides why the two variables behave differently.
L4.answer: Line 1 is {a,b}.txt and line 2 is a.txt b.txt. Both values arrive at step 3. Brace expansion is step 1, already behind, and expansion never restarts, so the braces stay literal. Pathname expansion is step 7, still ahead, so the asterisk in the substituted text is globbed. The rule: text produced by an expansion is subject only to the steps that come after it.
L4.explanation: That one rule is the whole predictive content of the ordering: steps before a substitution can never see its output, steps after it always do. It also explains why an unquoted expansion is word-split at step 6 but never brace-expanded, and why eval - a deliberate second run of the entire sequence over the already-expanded text - is the only way to get brace expansion out of a variable. See Word splitting and IFS.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory contains exactly {n} files, named note1.txt, note2.txt and so on up to note{n}.txt, and nothing else. Bash options are at their defaults, so a pattern that matches nothing is left in place unexpanded. The script runs:
  `set -- {lb}note,memo{rb}*.txt`
  `echo $#`
How many positional parameters are there? Answer with the number.
L4.answer: n plus 1. For n=3 the parameters are note1.txt note2.txt note3.txt memo*.txt, so 4; n=5 gives 6; n=8 gives 9.
L4.explanation: Step 1 turns the single word into two words, note*.txt and memo*.txt - brace expansion is textual and never consults the filesystem. Step 7 then globs each of them separately: note*.txt yields its n matches, memo*.txt matches nothing and is left in place. So the count is n plus 1 and one argument names a file that does not exist - the classic reason a loop over a glob runs once too often. See Globbing, and what happens when nothing matches.

resources.title: POSIX.1-2017, Shell Command Language (Chapter 2)
resources.why: Section 2.6 gives the four-stage order every POSIX shell must obey, so you can see which parts of the bash sequence are portable and which - brace expansion, process substitution - are bash extensions that will not survive dash or a strict sh.

L0.body:
v='a b'
files='*.txt'

echo $v          # two words: a and b
echo "$v"        # one word: a b
echo '$v'        # the literal two characters $v

printf '[%s]' $v ; echo    # [a][b]
printf '[%s]' "$v"; echo  # [a b]

set -- a 'b c' d
printf '<%s>' "$@"; echo  # <a><b c><d>   correct
printf '<%s>' "$*"; echo  # <a b c d>     joined into one word
printf '<%s>' $*  ; echo  # <a><b><c><d>  split apart
# default: quote every expansion, including "$@" — exceptions are deliberate

concepts.L1: Double quotes prevent word splitting and globbing but allow expansion. Single quotes prevent everything. Unquoted is almost always a bug.
concepts.L2: Quote every variable expansion by default: `"$var"`, `"$@"`, `"${arr[@]}"`. The exceptions are rare and deliberate. `$@` unquoted and `$*` quoted are both usually wrong — `"$@"` is the one you want.
concepts.L3: Quoting is lexical: it applies to the word as typed, so double quotes skip brace expansion, tilde expansion, word splitting and pathname expansion, while parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic still run; quote removal (step 8) strips the quotes. Only splitting and globbing reach an expansion's value, since brace and tilde run first; hence the two-step rule. Inside double quotes a backslash is special only before `$`, backtick, `"`, backslash and newline. Single quotes disable everything, backslash included, so one cannot appear inside; close, escape, reopen: `'it'\''s'`. `"$@"` is special-cased to one word per positional parameter - with none, zero words, where `"$*"` gives one empty word; in a larger quoted word its first parameter absorbs the text before, its last the text after. `"$*"` joins on the first character of IFS; `"${arr[@]}"` in Arrays generalises it.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`set -- a 'b c' d`
  `printf '<%s>' "$@"; echo`
  `printf '<%s>' "$*"; echo`
  `printf '<%s>' $*; echo`
With IFS at its default value, what are the three output lines?
L4.answer:
<a><b c><d>
<a b c d>
<a><b><c><d>
L4.explanation: "`$@`" expands to one word per parameter, preserving the space inside 'b c'. "`$*`" concatenates all parameters separated by the first character of IFS (a space) into a single word. Unquoted `$*` is joined the same way and then word-split again, which destroys the grouping.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A backup script does:
  `src={src}`
  `cp $src /backup/`
It has worked for a year. A user creates a directory named 'My Documents'. What breaks, at which expansion step, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: Word splitting (step 6) runs after parameter expansion (step 3), so the unquoted `$src` becomes two arguments, 'My' and 'Documents'. cp then tries to copy two nonexistent paths. The fix is cp "`$src`" /backup/ — quoting suppresses word splitting for that word.
L4.explanation: An expansion on the right-hand side of an assignment is not word-split, so `src=$v` needs no quotes; a literal space is different - it ends the assignment word at parse time, so the quotes shown in the `src=` line are required. It is the later unquoted use that breaks. This is the single most common shell bug and ShellCheck flags it as SC2086.

L4.prompt_tpl:
IFS is at its default and the current directory is empty. A bash variable v holds a single string of exactly {n} space-separated words, none of which contains a glob character. A script then runs:
  `count() ( echo $# )`
  `count $v`
  `count "$v"`
Answer with the sum of the two numbers printed.
L4.answer: Unquoted, `$v` is word-split into n arguments; quoted, `"$v"` is exactly one argument whatever it contains. Sum = n + 1. Worked draws: n=2 gives 2+1=3, n=3 gives 4, n=5 gives 6, n=8 gives 9.
L4.explanation: Word splitting runs after parameter expansion and only on unquoted expansions, so the shell hands `count` one argument per word. The double quotes suppress that step for that word alone, which is why a quoted expansion is always exactly one argument - the property every filename with a space depends on.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script contains:
  `n={n}`
  `echo "n=$n and the word is $(echo today)"`
  `echo 'n=$n and the word is $(echo today)'`
Give the two output lines, in order.
L4.answer:
n={n} and the word is today
n=$n and the word is $(echo today)
L4.explanation: Double quotes keep parameter expansion and command substitution alive, so both `$n` and the substitution run. Single quotes remove the special meaning of every character with no exception, so the second line is the literal text, dollar signs and parentheses included. Nothing inside single quotes is ever expanded.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script is invoked with exactly {n} arguments, none of which contains whitespace or a glob character. Its body is:
  `count() ( echo $# )`
  `count "$@"`
  `count "$*"`
  `count $*`
Answer with the sum of the three numbers printed.
L4.answer: `"$@"` gives n; `"$*"` gives 1 always, because a quoted expansion is one word even when it is empty; unquoted `$*` gives n again, since no argument contains whitespace. Sum = 2n + 1. Worked draws: n=0 gives 0+1+0=1, n=1 gives 3, n=3 gives 7, n=5 gives 11.
L4.explanation: The trap is n=0. "$@" is special-cased to expand to nothing at all, so a wrapper written as cmd "$@" runs cmd with no arguments; "$*" is an ordinary quoted expansion and yields one empty argument, so cmd "$*" runs cmd with a single empty string. That difference is why for x in "$@" is safe on an empty list and for x in "$*" is not.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script contains:
  `w={w}`
  `echo "$w\$w b\\c d\e"`
  `echo '$w \$w'`
  `echo 'it'\''s '"$w"`
Give the three output lines, in order.
L4.explanation: Inside double quotes a backslash is special only before a dollar sign, a backtick, a double quote, another backslash or a newline: so backslash-dollar gives one dollar sign, two backslashes give one, and backslash-e is left alone as two characters. Single quotes protect every character, backslash included, so line 2 is literal. Line 3 is the only way to get a single quote in: close, escape it, reopen.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script is invoked as `./s.sh {a} {b} {c}` - three arguments, none containing whitespace. Its body is the single line:
  `printf '<%s>' "pre$@post"; echo`
What is printed?
L4.answer: <pre{a}><{b}><{c}post>
L4.explanation: L3 states the rule: inside a larger double-quoted word, the first positional parameter absorbs the text before "$@" and the last absorbs the text after, while the parameters between stay separate words. Apply it and the three fields fall out. It is why "--flag=$@" is almost always a bug: only the first argument gets the prefix.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A log scanner is run in a directory that holds several files ending in .log:
  `dir={dir}`
  `pat=alpha`
  `grep -c "$pat" "$dir/*.log"`
It prints `grep: {dir}/*.log: No such file or directory` and exits non-zero, though the files are there. Say which expansion step the quotes suppressed, why the quotes around `$pat` are nonetheless right, and give the corrected command.
L4.answer: The quotes round the whole path suppressed pathname expansion, step 7, for that word, so the asterisk survived to grep as a literal character and grep looked for one file whose name ends in *.log. `$pat` is a different case: it is the value of an expansion, which must not be split or globbed, so its quotes are correct and must stay. The fix quotes only the variable and leaves the glob outside the quotes: grep -c "$pat" "$dir"/*.log
L4.explanation: Quoting is per word and all-or-nothing for the steps it cancels, so a quote drawn round a whole path kills the glob inside it too. The standard answer is a word with a quoted part and an unquoted part: `"$dir"/*.log` is one word to the parser, the expansion is protected, and the asterisk is still unquoted when pathname expansion runs. ShellCheck SC2086 calls this the composite-argument case.

L0.body:
p=/var/log/nginx/access.log.1

echo "${p##*/}"    # access.log.1   longest prefix match  -> basename
echo "${p%/*}"     # /var/log/nginx  shortest suffix match -> dirname
echo "${p%.*}"     # /var/log/nginx/access.log
echo "${p%%.*}"    # /var/log/nginx/access
echo "${p//\//:}"  # :var:log:nginx:access.log.1
echo "${#p}"       # 27
echo "${p:5:3}"    # log

echo "${u:-default}"   # value if u is unset OR empty
echo "${u-default}"    # value only if u is UNSET
echo "${u:?must be set}" # print to stderr and exit if unset/empty

concepts.L1: `${v:-default}`, `${v:=assign}`, `${v:?error}`, `${v#prefix}`, `${v%suffix}`, `${v//find/replace}`, `${v:offset:len}`, `${#v}`, `${v^^}` upper, `${v,,}` lower.
concepts.L2: These replace most calls to sed, cut, basename and dirname, and they're pure builtins — no fork, no exec. In a loop over ten thousand items that's the difference between instant and a minute.
concepts.L3: One `#` or `%` strips the shortest match, two strip the longest; `#` works from the front, `%` from the back. Remember it by keyboard position: `#` is left of `%` on a US layout, and it operates on the left of the string. The colon in `${u:-x}` is the difference between 'unset or empty' and 'unset only': with a colon, an empty string counts as absent. `${u:=x}` also assigns; `${u:?msg}` writes `msg` to stderr and exits a non-interactive shell. `${p//a/b}` replaces every occurrence, `${p/a/b}` only the first, and the pattern is a glob pattern, not a regex.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`p={p}`
  `echo "${{p##*/}}"`
  `echo "${{p%.*}}"`
  `echo "${{p%%.*}}"`
What are the three lines?
L4.answer: For /var/log/nginx/access.log.1: access.log.1 / /var/log/nginx/access.log / /var/log/nginx/access. For /etc/ssl/certs/ca.pem.bak: ca.pem.bak / /etc/ssl/certs/ca.pem / /etc/ssl/certs/ca.
L4.explanation: ##*/ strips the longest prefix ending in a slash, giving the basename. %.* strips the shortest suffix starting with a dot, removing only the last extension. %%.* strips the longest such suffix, removing every extension at once.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script needs a port number: use the value of PORT if the caller set it to something non-empty, otherwise {d}. Which of the three forms is right?
L4.answer: port=`${PORT:-{d}}`
L4.explanation: The colon form substitutes the default when PORT is unset OR set to the empty string, which is exactly what an unset key in a container spec or a `PORT=` line in an env file looks like. `${PORT-{d}}` substitutes only when PORT is entirely unset, so PORT="" would leave the port empty. `${PORT:={d}}` also assigns back into PORT, a side effect you rarely want on a read, and it fails outright on a positional parameter.
options: port=`${PORT:-{d}}`
port=`${PORT-{d}}`
port=`${PORT:={d}}`

L4.prompt_tpl:
A non-interactive script contains:
  `unset NAME`
  `echo "${{NAME:?{msg}}}"`
  `echo REACHED`
What appears on stdout?
L4.answer: Nothing. The :? form writes 'script: line N: NAME: <msg>' to stderr and the shell exits immediately, so REACHED is never printed and stdout is empty.
L4.explanation: This is the cheapest possible argument validation: it fails at the point of use with a message naming the variable, and it needs no if statement. The exact exit status differs between invocation modes (1 from a script file), so test for the failure, not for a specific code.

L4.prompt_tpl: In bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux, `s={s}`. Give the output of each of these three expansions, each echoed inside double quotes, in this order: `{e1}`, then `{e2}`, then `{e3}`.
L4.answer: For s=parameterexpansion: 18, then ram, then PARAMETEREXPANSION. For s=commandline: 11, then mma, then COMMANDLINE.
L4.explanation: `${#s}` is the length of the value in characters. `${s:offset:length}` is zero-based, so offset 2 is the third character, and the third field is a LENGTH, not an end index: three characters starting at index 2. `${s^^}` upper-cases every character; a single caret, `${s^}`, would upper-case only the first. All three are done by the shell itself, with no fork and no exec.

L4.prompt_tpl: In bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux, NAME is unset and `v={v}`. A script runs these four echo lines in order, each echoing the expansion inside double quotes: `{e1}`, then `{e2}`, then `{e3}`, then `{e4}`. Give the four output lines.
L4.answer: none, then none, then --out=Report.TXT, then report.txt. On the other draw: none, none, --out=BUILD_Log, build_log. The second line is the point: `${NAME:=none}` does not only substitute, it assigns, so the bare `$NAME` afterwards is no longer unset.
L4.explanation: `${NAME:=none}` is the assign-default form: it expands to the default AND writes it back into the variable, which is why the next line prints none; `${NAME:-none}` would have left NAME unset. `${v:+alt}` is the mirror image, expanding to alt only when v is set and non-empty, which is how an optional flag is built with no if statement. `${v,,}` lower-cases every character, `${v^^}` upper-cases.

L4.prompt_tpl: In bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux, one variable holds the single string `t={t}`. Give the output of each of these, in order, each echoed inside double quotes: `{e1}`, then `{e2}`, then `{e3}`.
L4.answer: For t=foo bar oops: f0o bar oops, then f00 bar 00ps, then Foo bar oops. For t=hello world of shells: hell0 world of shells, then hell0 w0rld 0f shells, then hello world of shells, unchanged, because `/#` anchors the pattern to the start of the string and this string does not begin with f.
L4.explanation: One slash replaces the first match only; two slashes replace every match. A slash followed by `#` anchors the pattern to the beginning of the value and a slash followed by `%` anchors it to the end, so an anchored form that does not match leaves the value untouched rather than erroring. The pattern is a glob, not a regex, so o means the literal character.

L4.prompt_tpl: In bash 5.2, `s={s}`. A script writes `{bad}` intending the last three characters, and it does not do what the author meant. Give two things: what `{bad}` actually evaluates to here, and the expansion that really yields the last three characters.
L4.answer: `${s:-3}` evaluates to abcdefgh, the whole string: with the minus touching the colon this parses as the use-default form, meaning 'expand to s, or to 3 if s is unset or empty', and s is neither. The substring form needs the minus separated from the colon: `${s: -3}` with a space, or `${s:(-3)}`, which yields fgh.
L4.explanation: The colon is shared by two unrelated forms, and the tokenizer resolves the ambiguity in favour of use-default. The tell is what happens on an empty s: `${s:-3}` then returns 3, while `${s: -3}` returns the empty string. A negative LENGTH is different again and needs no space: `${s:2:-2}` keeps everything from index 2 up to two characters from the end, which for abcdefgh is cdef.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script computes a directory as `{dex}` and a base name as `{bex}`, claiming these are a pure-bash dirname and basename. For p={p}, say what each of the two expansions actually produces and what the dirname and basename utilities print for the same p. Then design the fix: name every case in which these two expansions disagree with the utilities, and say what a correct pure-bash dirname must substitute in each.
L4.answer: For p=report.txt: `${p%/*}` gives report.txt and `${p##*/}` gives report.txt; dirname prints . and basename prints report.txt. For p=/usr/bin/: `${p%/*}` gives /usr/bin and `${p##*/}` gives the empty string; dirname prints /usr and basename prints bin. For p=/foo: `${p%/*}` gives the empty string and `${p##*/}` gives foo; dirname prints / and basename prints foo. Three disagreements: no slash at all, where dirname must substitute a dot; the only slash leading, where the empty result must become a single slash; and a trailing slash, which must be stripped before either expansion runs.
L4.explanation: Pattern removal that matches nothing is a silent no-op, so a path with no slash comes back unchanged where dirname says dot. A path whose only slash is the leading one leaves nothing in front of it, so the expansion gives the empty string where dirname says /. And the expansions know nothing about a trailing slash, so /usr/bin/ has an empty basename. Three special cases, which is why POSIX specifies the two utilities separately.

L4.prompt_tpl: IFS is at its default and `p={p}`. A script runs the command `{cmd}`, with the expansion left unquoted. Say how many arguments mkdir receives and what they are, name the expansion step that runs on the result of parameter expansion and causes this, and give the fix.
L4.answer: mkdir receives 4 arguments: -p, my, documents/2026 and reports, so it creates three unrelated paths instead of one, and four directories once -p makes the intermediate documents/2026 under documents. The step is word splitting: the shell splits the RESULT of the unquoted expansion on the characters of IFS, which defaults to space, tab and newline. The fix is one pair of quotes, `mkdir -p "$p"`, since word splitting is skipped inside double quotes.
L4.explanation: Parameter expansion produces a string; the expansion sequence then applies word splitting and pathname expansion to that string unless it was quoted. The splitting happens on the value, never on the literal text you typed, which is why a variable holding spaces breaks a command that looked fine in the editor. See Word splitting and IFS, and The expansion sequence, for the ordering this depends on.

L0.body:
v='a b'

[ $v = 'a b' ]      # bash: [: too many arguments — [ is a COMMAND
[ "$v" = 'a b' ]    # fine
[[ $v = 'a b' ]]    # fine unquoted: [[ ]] is SYNTAX, no word splitting

f=report.tar.gz
[[ $f == *.tar.gz ]]              # glob match, unquoted RHS
[[ $f == "*.tar.gz" ]]            # false: quoted RHS is a literal
[[ $f =~ ^([a-z]+)\.tar\.gz$ ]] && echo "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"   # report

[[ 10 > 9 ]]        # FALSE — string compare, "10" sorts before "9"
[ 10 -gt 9 ]        # true — numeric
(( 10 > 9 ))        # true — arithmetic context

concepts.L1: `[` is a command with argument parsing. `[[ ]]` is shell syntax with no word splitting, pattern matching via `==`, and regex via `=~`. `(( ))` for arithmetic.
concepts.L2: Inside `[[ ]]` you don't need to quote variables against word splitting, and `<` compares strings rather than redirecting. Use `[[ ]]` in bash always; `[` exists for POSIX sh portability only.
concepts.L3: `[` is an ordinary command -- a builtin, and `/usr/bin/[` -- so the shell expands and word-splits its arguments before it runs. With `v='a b'`, `[ $v = x ]` gets four words before the `]`; bash prints `[: too many arguments` and exits 2, a usage error, not a syntax error, that `if` reads as false. `[[ ]]` is a compound command the parser knows, so operands are never split or globbed -- though the right-hand side of `==` is a glob pattern unless quoted. Parsing also frees `<` and `>` from redirection: they compare strings by locale collation, so `[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is false; for numbers use `-gt`/`-lt`, or `(( ))`. Also: `-eq` inside `[[ ]]` evaluates both sides as arithmetic, running command substitution in the text, while `[` refuses a non-integer; and `(( ))` inverts value to status, so `(( count++ ))` on a zero counter returns 1 and kills a script under `set -e` (The safety preamble).

L4.prompt_tpl:
`x={x}`
  `y={y}`
  `[[ $x > $y ]] && echo A || echo B`
  `(( x > y )) && echo C || echo D`
What two lines are printed? Answer in the form `X then Y`.
L4.answer: B then C
L4.explanation: `[[ $x > $y ]]` compares its operands as STRINGS by the locale's collation, and 10, 100 and 20 each begin with a character that sorts before the 9 or 3 on the right, so the test is false: B. `(( x > y ))` evaluates them as integers, where the left value really is larger: C. Inside `[[ ]]`, `>` and `<` are lexical comparisons, not numeric ones; use `(( ))` or `-gt`/`-lt` whenever the operands are numbers.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`file='{f}'`
  `if [ $file = '{f}' ]; then echo match; fi`
The file genuinely is named that. The script prints an error instead of 'match'. Why, and give two fixes.
L4.answer: `[` is an ordinary command, so its arguments go through word splitting before it runs: unquoted `$file` becomes the two words of `{f}`, so `[` receives those two words, then `=`, then `{f}` -- four words where it expects three. Bash prints `[: too many arguments` and returns 2, so the `if` takes the else path. Fix 1: quote it, `[ "$file" = '{f}' ]`. Fix 2: use `[[ $file = '{f}' ]]`, where the parser suppresses word splitting on the operands.
L4.explanation: The distinction is parsing, not politeness. [[ ]] is recognised by the parser before expansion happens, so it can suppress splitting on its operands; [ cannot, because by the time it runs the words are already separate arguments. Note that the assignment needs quoting too.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5 on Linux. The variable holds a single string that contains a space:
  `v='{v}'`
  `[ $v = '{v}' ] && echo A || echo B`
  `[ "$v" = '{v}' ] && echo C || echo D`
  `[[ $v = '{v}' ]] && echo E || echo F`
Which three letters reach stdout? Answer in the form `X then Y then Z`.
L4.answer: B then C then E
L4.explanation: Line 1 is unquoted, so `$v` splits into two words and `[` gets four arguments before the `]`: bash writes `[: too many arguments` to stderr and returns 2, which the shell reads as false, so B. Line 2 quotes the expansion, so `[` gets exactly the three arguments it expects: C. Line 3 is `[[ ]]`, a compound command whose operands the parser exempts from word splitting, so the unquoted form is already safe: E.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5 on Linux. The variable is set to the empty string:
  `{setv}`
  `[ -n $v ] && echo A || echo B`
  `[ -z $v ] && echo C || echo D`
  `[ -n "$v" ] && echo E || echo F`
What three letters are printed, in order? Answer in the form `X then Y then Z`.
L4.answer: A then C then F
L4.explanation: Unquoted `$v` expands to an empty word that is then removed, so the shell really runs `[ -n ]` and `[ -z ]`. POSIX fixes test by argument COUNT: with exactly one argument the result is true when that argument is a non-empty string -- and `-n` and `-z` are themselves non-empty strings, so both lines are true: A, then C. Only the quoted third line passes the empty string through as a real argument, so it is false: F. Always quote, or use `[[ ]]`, where an empty expansion still counts as one operand.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5 on Linux:
  `x={x}`
  `pat='*o'`
  `[[ $x == $pat ]] && echo A || echo B`
  `[[ $x == "$pat" ]] && echo C || echo D`
What two lines are printed? Answer in the form `X then Y`.
L4.answer: A then D
L4.explanation: On the right of `==` inside `[[ ]]` an unquoted expansion is a glob PATTERN, so `*o` matches any string ending in o -- hello, cargo and tempo all do: A. Quoting the right-hand side turns it into the literal two-character string `*o`, which no value here equals: D. The left-hand side is never a pattern. That is why `[[ $x == $y ]]` is not string equality when `$y` holds user data containing a star or a question mark; quote the right-hand side for literal equality.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5 on Linux:
  `f='{f}'`
  `re='^[a-z]+'`
  `[[ $f =~ $re ]] && echo A || echo B`
  `[[ $f =~ "$re" ]] && echo C || echo D`
What two lines are printed? Answer in the form `X then Y`.
L4.answer: A then D
L4.explanation: Unquoted, `$re` is an extended regular expression and `^[a-z]+` matches the leading lowercase letters of both filenames: A. Quoted, bash 3.2 and later treat the right-hand side of `=~` as a LITERAL string, so the test asks whether the filename contains the seven characters `^[a-z]+`, which it does not: D. Quoting a regex disables it, which is why the idiom is to put the pattern in a variable and use it unquoted.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A script begins `#!/bin/sh` and runs on Debian, where /bin/sh is dash. It contains:
  `a={a}`
  `b={a}`
  `[ "$a" == "$b" ] && echo same`
It works when the author runs `bash script.sh` but not in production. What does dash print, what is the exit status of `[`, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: dash prints something like `script.sh: 4: [: {a}: unexpected operator` and `[` exits 2, so `same` is never printed. `==` is a bash (and ksh/zsh) extension to `[`; POSIX test defines only `=` for string equality, and dash implements exactly POSIX, so it reads the third word as an unknown operator. Fix: write `[ "$a" = "$b" ]`, which works in every shell, bash included. Run and checked on dash 0.5.12.
L4.explanation: A shebang of /bin/sh is a promise to use only POSIX features; bash-only spellings (`==` in `[`, [[ ]], arrays, `local`) then fail only in production. Either write POSIX sh, or change the shebang to /usr/bin/env bash and mean it. ShellCheck flags exactly this class of bashism when it sees an sh shebang.

L4.prompt_tpl:
This script, run with bash 5 on Linux, prints nothing and exits with status 1:
  `set -euo pipefail`
  `count={start}`
  `(( count++ ))`
  `echo "total is $count"`
Change the second line to `count={other}` and it prints normally. Explain the mechanism, and give two fixes that keep `set -e`.
L4.answer: `(( expr ))` reports the VALUE as an exit status, inverted: a non-zero value gives status 0, a value of 0 gives status 1. `count++` is post-increment, so the expression's value is the OLD count. Starting at 0 that value is 0, `(( ))` returns 1, and `set -e` exits the script before echo -- the variable is still incremented, nobody sees it. Starting at {other} the old value is truthy, status 0, and the script prints `total is` followed by one more than {other}. Fixes: `(( ++count ))` (pre-increment yields the new, non-zero value), `(( count++ )) || true`, or `count=$(( count + 1 ))`, an assignment whose status is 0 regardless. All three starts were run.
L4.explanation: Arithmetic truth is C truth (non-zero is true) while shell truth is 0 for success, so (( )) has to invert, and that inversion collides with set -e. The same trap bites `(( flag = 0 ))` and `(( i-- ))` at 1. Under The safety preamble, treat a bare (( )) as a command that can fail.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash 5 web handler on x86-64 Linux does:
  `n=$1        # comes straight from the query string`
  `if [[ $n -eq {k} ]]; then grant_access; fi`
The author argues that `-eq` is a numeric comparison, so non-numeric input can only make the test false. Say what an attacker can actually achieve, why `[ "$n" -eq {k} ]` behaves differently, and give the fix.
L4.answer: `-eq` inside `[[ ]]` runs both operands through arithmetic evaluation, and bash arithmetic re-evaluates the CONTENTS of a variable as an expression and performs command substitution inside an array subscript. So an argument of `a[$(id>&2)]` executes `id` -- arbitrary command execution before any comparison happens (the test itself then returns 1). Run on bash 5.2.21: the command runs and its output appears. `[ "$n" -eq {k} ]` uses the plain builtin, which demands a decimal integer: it prints `integer expression expected` and exits 2, with no evaluation. Fix: validate before comparing -- `[[ $n =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || exit 1` -- and keep untrusted text out of `(( ))`, `-eq` and array subscripts entirely.
L4.explanation: Arithmetic evaluation is a second interpreter hiding inside the test constructs. Anywhere bash evaluates arithmetic -- (( )), `$(( ))`, -eq and friends inside [[ ]], array subscripts, `let` -- variable contents are treated as code and can reach command substitution. Whitelist the input with a regex first; never read `-eq` as a type check.

L0.body:
false | true | grep -q zzz
echo "$?"                 # 1   (status of grep, the LAST command)
echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"   # 0   WRONG — the echo above already reset it

false | true | grep -q zzz
st=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")     # capture FIRST, before anything else runs
echo "${st[@]}"           # 1 0 1

set -o pipefail
false | true; echo "$?"     # 1  — pipefail returns the last NON-ZERO status
# $? is the LAST stage only; PIPESTATUS holds every stage
L0.cloze:
false | true | grep -q zzz
st=({{c1::"${PIPESTATUS[@]}"}})   # must be captured before any other command runs
echo "${st[@]}"                 # {{c2::1 0 1}}
set -o {{c3::pipefail}}                # make the pipeline fail if ANY stage failed

concepts.L1: A pipeline's exit status is that of the *last* command by default. `${PIPESTATUS[@]}` holds all of them.
concepts.L2: `grep foo file | head` succeeds even if grep fails. This is why `set -o pipefail` exists, and why `curl ... | bash` can silently run a truncated script — a real and exploited failure mode.
concepts.L3: Each stage is a separate process: the shell forks them all, wires the pipes, then waits for each, so it knows every status. POSIX says a pipeline's status is the last command's, so bash keeps the rest in `PIPESTATUS`, a bash array with no POSIX equivalent. Bash rewrites it after the next command of any kind - even a bare assignment or `[[ ... ]]` - which is why the naive `echo $?; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"` prints `0`; `st=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")` works because the expansion precedes the assignment. `set -o pipefail` (POSIX only since Issue 8, 2024) makes the status the rightmost non-zero one - what catches curl in `curl -sS ... | bash`, where the last stage cannot tell a truncated body from a whole one. It is not free: `yes | head -n 1` leaves `141 0` - head closes the pipe, yes dies of SIGPIPE, $128+13=141$ - so pipefail can fail a script that is working. The 128+N encoding is Exit codes.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`false | true | grep -q {pat}`
  `echo "$?"`
  `echo "${{PIPESTATUS[@]}}"`
The pattern matches nothing. Give the two numbers printed, in order, in the form `3 then 8`.
L4.answer: 1 then 0
L4.explanation: The second number is the surprise. PIPESTATUS reflects the most recently executed foreground pipeline, and a simple command counts as a one-stage pipeline, so the successful `echo "$?"` on the line before already overwrote it; the 0 describes that echo, not the pipeline. To use it, assign it to your own array as the first thing after the pipeline: st=("`${PIPESTATUS[@]}`").

L4.prompt_tpl:
A deploy step runs:
  curl -s https://{host}/install.sh | bash
The connection is cut after {n} KB. Describe the failure and the two shell-level mitigations.
L4.answer: curl exits non-zero but the pipeline's status is bash's, which is 0, so the caller believes the install succeeded — while bash has already executed the truncated prefix of the script, possibly a half-finished rm or an unbalanced conditional. Mitigations: set -o pipefail so the pipeline reports curl's failure, and download to a file first, verify a checksum, then execute it.
L4.explanation: The deeper problem is that piping to a shell executes each line as it arrives, so partial execution has already happened by the time you learn about the error. pipefail turns a silent success into a loud failure; downloading first removes the partial-execution window entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux, pipefail off. A script contains exactly these two lines, one after the other:
  bash -c 'exit {a}' | bash -c 'exit {b}' | bash -c 'exit {c}'
  `echo $((PIPESTATUS[0] + PIPESTATUS[1] + PIPESTATUS[2]))`
Answer with the number the second line prints.
L4.answer: PIPESTATUS holds one status per stage, left to right, so the sum is a+b+c. Verified draws: a=7,b=0,c=4 prints 11; a=2,b=3,c=5 prints 10; a=9,b=3,c=0 prints 12; a=2,b=0,c=0 prints 2.
L4.explanation: `$?` would give only the last stage, c. PIPESTATUS is the whole vector. It survives here only because the arithmetic is expanded while the echo line is being prepared, before that echo becomes the most recent command and overwrites the array. Put any other command - even a bare assignment - between the two lines and you read 0 instead.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux. A script contains:
  set -o pipefail
  bash -c 'exit {a}' | true | true
  echo $?
  set +o pipefail
  bash -c 'exit {a}' | true | true
  echo $?
Give the two numbers printed, in order, in the form `3 then 8`.
L4.answer: {a} then 0
L4.explanation: With pipefail the pipeline's status is the rightmost NON-ZERO stage status, so a failure in the first stage is still reported. Without it the status is the last stage's, and `true` succeeded. Rightmost non-zero is not the same as the first failure or the largest: with stages exiting 3 then 4, pipefail reports 4; with 4 then 3 it reports 3.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux with GNU coreutils. A script contains:
  set -o pipefail
  yes | head -n {n} > /dev/null
  `echo $?`
head does exactly what it was asked to do and nothing goes wrong. What single number is printed?
L4.explanation: head prints its n lines, exits 0 and closes its end of the pipe; yes keeps writing, gets SIGPIPE (signal 13) and dies, so that stage's status is $128+13=141$ and PIPESTATUS is `141 0`. pipefail promotes 141 to the whole pipeline. This is why `set -euo pipefail` plus a pipe into head or grep -q can kill a script that is working perfectly.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux. A script is exactly:
  set -e
  bash -c 'exit {a}' | cat
  `echo "line 1: $?"`
  set -o pipefail
  bash -c 'exit {a}' | cat
  echo 'line 2'
Its entire stdout is the one line `line 1: 0`. Answer with the script's exit status.
L4.answer: The first pipeline's status is cat's, which is 0, so set -e sees success and line 1 prints `line 1: 0`. With pipefail on, the second pipeline's status is a, set -e aborts, `line 2` is never printed and the script exits a. Verified: a=9 exits 9, a=3 exits 3.
L4.explanation: set -e acts on the pipeline's status, which by default is the last stage's - so a failing producer feeding a filter that succeeds is invisible to it. pipefail is what extends set -e over the whole pipeline. Note also that set -e never fires for a command in an `if` condition or on the left of `&&`, which is why a preamble is not a substitute for checking statuses.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A release script starts with `set -eu` and does NOT set pipefail. It contains:
  `ver=$(curl -sS https://{host}/latest.txt | tr -d '[:space:]')`
  `rm -rf /opt/app/versions/$ver`
  `install_release "$ver"`
The host is unreachable: curl writes nothing to stdout and exits {code}. Say exactly what the script does, why neither set -e nor set -u stops it, and give two one-line changes that would.
L4.answer: curl exits {code}, tr reads an empty stream and exits 0, and a command substitution takes the status of the pipeline inside it - so the assignment succeeds and ver is the empty string. set -e sees status 0; set -u tests whether a variable is SET, and ver is set, just empty. `rm -rf /opt/app/versions/$ver` then expands to `rm -rf /opt/app/versions/` and deletes every release. Fixes: `set -o pipefail` so the substitution carries curl's {code} and set -e aborts the assignment; and a value check, `[ -n "$ver" ] || exit 1`, with the expansion quoted.
L4.explanation: Two independent facts combine. A command substitution's status is the status of the pipeline inside it, which without pipefail is the last stage's - and a filter like tr, wc or sed almost never fails. And set -u catches unset, not empty. A fetch failure plus a filter that cannot fail is all it takes to turn a version string into an rm -rf of a directory root.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must run `{a} | {b} | {c}` and, when it fails, report WHICH stage failed and with what status. Design the idiom: give the exact bash lines, and justify each one - why the capture must be the very next command after the pipeline, why calling a function as that next command is nevertheless safe, and why `set -o pipefail` alone cannot answer the question.
L4.answer: Run the pipeline, then on the very next line copy the array: `st=("${{PIPESTATUS[@]}}")`, then loop - `for i in "${{!st[@]}}"; do [ "${{st[i]}}" -ne 0 ] && printf 'stage %d failed with status %d\n' "$i" "${{st[i]}}" && break; done`. The capture must be first because bash rewrites PIPESTATUS after the next command of any kind, including a bare assignment or a test. A function call is safe as the next command because the reset happens when that command completes, so the function's own first line still sees the pipeline's array - a `report` function whose body starts with `local st=("${{PIPESTATUS[@]}}")` works, verified. pipefail cannot answer it: it collapses the vector to one number, the rightmost non-zero status, which tells you a stage failed but not which - and if two stages fail you only ever see the right-hand one.
L4.explanation: The design point is that PIPESTATUS is the only place the per-stage information exists, and it lives for exactly one command. Everything else follows: copy it into your own array first (Arrays), index it, and treat pipefail as a summary rather than a diagnostic. A stage status of 128+N means that stage was killed by signal N rather than exiting - Signals and Exit codes.

L0.body:
s='  a   b  '
printf '[%s]' $s   ; echo   # [a][b]      runs collapse, edges trimmed
printf '[%s]' "$s" ; echo   # [  a   b  ]  no splitting at all

IFS=:
p='a::b:'
printf '[%s]' $p ; echo      # [a][][b]   empty field KEPT in the middle

unset IFS                    # back to the default $' \t\n'
IFS=: read -r u x rest <<< 'root:0:/root:/bin/sh'
echo "$u $x $rest"           # root 0 /root:/bin/sh   last var takes the remainder
# IFS also picks the character that "${arr[*]}" joins on

concepts.L1: IFS is the list of characters the shell splits unquoted expansions on. Its default is space, tab and newline. It also chooses the joining character for "`$*`", and it is the field separator `read` uses.
concepts.L2: Whitespace characters in IFS behave differently from other characters: runs of them collapse into one delimiter and leading and trailing ones are ignored, while a non-whitespace delimiter like `:` marks every field, so empty fields are preserved.
concepts.L3: The special case is written into POSIX: an IFS whitespace character is treated as a delimiter that may repeat, so `'  a   b  '` yields exactly two fields. A non-whitespace IFS character delimits exactly one field boundary each, so `'a::b'` yields three fields, the middle one empty, and `read` with `IFS=:` on `/etc/passwd` correctly produces empty strings for empty columns. This is why `IFS=$'\n\t'` in a safety preamble is only a partial fix: it stops splitting on spaces but still collapses runs of tabs and newlines. And because `read` assigns the unsplit remainder to its last variable, `IFS=: read -r u x rest` is a complete field parser in one line with no fork.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 on Linux. Run:
  `IFS={sep}`
  `s='a{sep}{sep}b'`
  `printf '[%s]' $s; echo`
What is printed? And what is printed if the last line becomes `printf '[%s]' "$s"; echo` ?
L4.answer: Unquoted: `[a][][b]` for every separator. Quoted: one field only, printed as `[a::b]`, `[a,,b]` or `[a||b]`. A non-whitespace IFS character marks exactly one field boundary each, so the two adjacent separators bracket an empty field that survives; double quotes suppress word splitting altogether, so `"$s"` stays a single word whatever IFS holds.
L4.explanation: Two rules at once. Word splitting applies only to unquoted expansions, and a non-whitespace IFS delimiter is never allowed to collapse. That asymmetry is why `cut -d:` on /etc/passwd handles an empty password column correctly while a space-splitting loop silently merges columns.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`IFS=: read -r a b c <<< '{line}'`
  `echo "c=$c"`
What is printed?
L4.answer: For 'w:x:y:z': c=y:z. For 'one:two:three:four:five': c=three:four:five. read assigns the entire unsplit remainder of the line to its final variable.
L4.explanation: This is deliberate and useful: it means read never silently drops data when there are more fields than variables. It also means you must supply enough variables, or use an array with read -ra, if you want every field separated.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 on Linux with IFS left at its default (space, tab, newline). Run:
  `v='{val}'`
  `set -- $v`
  `echo $#`
What number is printed?
L4.answer: For `v='  a   b  '`: 2. For `v='a b c'`: 3. For `v='  x  '`: 1. Leading and trailing IFS whitespace is discarded, and each run of IFS whitespace counts as a single delimiter, so the field count is the number of runs of non-blank text, never the number of spaces.
L4.explanation: IFS whitespace is the forgiving case: runs collapse and the edges are trimmed. That is why an unquoted expansion of a raggedly spaced value still yields clean fields, and equally why it destroys a filename that contains a space. `set --` reassigns the positional parameters, so `$#` is exactly the number of fields produced.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 on Linux. Run:
  `IFS={sep}`
  `set -- one two three`
  `printf '%s\n' "$*"`
  `printf '%s\n' "$@"`
What does each of the two printf lines print?
L4.answer: The first prints one line, the three words joined by the separator: `one-two-three` (or `one:two:three`, `one+two+three`). The second prints three lines: one, two, three. `"$*"` joins the positional parameters with the FIRST character of IFS; `"$@"` produces one word per parameter and ignores IFS entirely.
L4.explanation: IFS has two jobs and only one of them is splitting. As a joiner it is used by `"$*"` and by the star form of an array expansion, and only its first character is used. `"$@"` is the form you almost always want, because it is unaffected by IFS and hands on every argument exactly as it stands.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 on Linux. A script keeps IFS at the default space, tab, newline as a safety measure, then tries to print each colon-separated field of a record in its own brackets, empty fields included:
  `rec='{rec}'`
  `for f in $rec; do printf '[%s]' "$f"; done; echo`
What does the loop actually print, and what is the one-line fix?
L4.answer: It prints the whole record as one field: `[root::0:0]` (or `[a::b]`, `[x::y:z]`). The record contains no space, tab or newline, so with the default IFS there is nothing to split on and the expansion yields a single word. The fix is to set the delimiter the data actually uses before the loop: `IFS=:`, which makes every colon a field boundary and keeps the empty field.
L4.explanation: A safe IFS is not a universal IFS. Restricting IFS to whitespace protects filenames that contain spaces, but it makes structured records unparseable, because splitting only ever happens on characters that are actually in IFS. Choose IFS to match the data being split, and restore it afterwards.

L4.prompt_tpl: GNU bash 5.2 on Linux, IFS at its default, and `v='{val}'`. In exactly one of these three lines does the shell split the value of v into more than one word. Which line?
L4.answer: `set -- $v`
L4.explanation: Word splitting happens to unquoted expansions in a context where the shell is building a list of words: command arguments, a for list, `set --`. The right-hand side of an assignment is a single-word context, and the inside of the double-bracket construct is not split either, which is why `[[ ]]` is safe with an unquoted variable while `[ ]` is not.
options: `set -- $v`
`if [[ $v == a* ]]; then :; fi`

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 on Linux, IFS at its default, in a directory whose only files are aa, ab and ba. Run:
  `v='{pat} a'`
  `printf '[%s]' $v; echo`
What is printed, and where in the expansion sequence does each step happen?
L4.answer: For `*`: `[aa][ab][ba][a]`. For `a*`: `[aa][ab][a]`. For `?a`: `[aa][ba][a]`. Parameter expansion produces the raw text first, word splitting then cuts it into the two words (the pattern, and `a`), and only afterwards is each of those words matched against filenames. The second word matches no file, so bash leaves it alone.
L4.explanation: Word splitting runs before pathname expansion, so a glob character that arrives inside a variable is still expanded, and it is expanded once per field. That is the ordering taught in The expansion sequence, and the untouched second word is the default behaviour described in Globbing, and what happens when nothing matches. Quoting `"$v"` stops both steps.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 on Linux. A privileged backup script reads one line from a config file that unprivileged users can edit, then runs:
  `opts=$(cat /etc/backup.opts)`
  `tar -czf /backup/out.tgz $opts /srv`
The config file contains exactly this line:
  {evil}
How many arguments does tar receive, what is the consequence, and why is putting double quotes round the expansion not the fix?
L4.answer: Five arguments for the first two config lines and six for the third: word splitting turns one expansion into one argument per field, so the attacker injects genuine tar options, and GNU tar's --checkpoint-action=exec runs their command as the privileged user. Quoting is not the fix: it makes the whole line a single argument, which breaks every legitimate multi-option config while the data stays attacker-controlled. The fix is an array the script itself fills, expanded as `"${opts[@]}"`, with the config file restricted to a whitelist of values rather than raw option text.
L4.explanation: Splitting an untrusted string into argv is command injection by another name: the attacker needs no semicolon, only a flag. Two lessons follow. Quoting is a correctness fix, not an authorisation fix. And when a command genuinely needs a variable number of arguments, the shell's answer is an array, never an unquoted string.

L0.body:
echo {a,b}{1,2}          # a1 a2 b1 b2   cartesian product
echo {1..5}              # 1 2 3 4 5
echo {1..10..3}          # 1 4 7 10      step
echo {01..03}            # 01 02 03      zero padding preserved
echo file{,.bak}         # file file.bak
mv access.log{,.1}       # mv access.log access.log.1

n=3
echo {1..$n}             # {1..3}  — LITERAL: braces expand before $n exists
echo nope{1,2}.txt       # nope1.txt nope2.txt  — even though neither file exists
echo nope*.txt           # nope*.txt            — a glob with no match stays literal

concepts.L1: Brace expansion generates text. It is step 1 of the expansion sequence, it is purely textual, and unlike globbing it does not consult the filesystem at all: `{a,b}` produces two words whether or not files named a and b exist.
concepts.L2: Because it runs before parameter expansion, a variable can never appear inside a range: `{1..$n}` is emitted literally. People assume braces are a kind of glob and are then surprised both by that and by the fact that brace output is not filtered against real files.
concepts.L3: The ordering is the whole lesson. Bash brace-expands the raw token before any dollar sign has meaning, so `{1..$n}` is not a range: the word is left unchanged, and parameter expansion then turns it into a literal `{1..3}` that becomes a filename or argument. Use `seq 1 "$n"` or a C-style `for` loop; the everyday idiom is the empty alternative, `mv path/file{,.bak}`. A brace expression is only well formed with unquoted braces plus a comma or a valid sequence, so `{a}` and `{1..}` pass through untouched. Braces generate, globs filter: `echo nope{1,2}.txt` prints two names that do not exist, while `echo nope*.txt` prints the pattern unchanged - and because braces run first, their output is still globbed, so `{a,b}*.txt` can leave one word expanded and one literal. It is also a bashism: dash makes `app/{bin,lib}` one literal directory. See Globbing, and what happens when nothing matches.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`n={n}`
  `echo {{1..$n}}`
  `echo {{1..{n}}}`
What are the two lines?
L4.answer: For n=4: line 1 prints {1..4}, line 2 prints 1 2 3 4. For n=6: line 1 prints {1..6}, line 2 prints 1 2 3 4 5 6. The braces stay literal on line 1 because brace expansion saw a dollar sign where it needed a number; the variable itself is still expanded later.
L4.explanation: Brace expansion is step 1 and parameter expansion is step 3. On line 1 the range is malformed at step 1, so bash leaves the word alone - but it does not stop expanding it: step 3 still substitutes n, so what you see is a literal pair of braces around the value. Line 2 contains a real integer range and expands to separate words. Verified with bash 5.2.21.

L4.prompt_tpl:
In a directory containing no files at all:
  echo miss{{1,2}}.log
  echo miss{star}.log
What are the two lines?
L4.answer:
miss1.log miss2.log
miss*.log
L4.explanation: Brace expansion is textual generation and never checks the filesystem, so it happily produces names for files that do not exist. Pathname expansion is filtering, and by default a pattern that matches nothing is left in place unquoted rather than removed - the behaviour shopt -s nullglob changes.

L4.answer: 3*n words, the cartesian product of the three letters and the n numbers. Verified with bash 5.2.21: n=2 gives 6 words (a1 a2 b1 b2 c1 c2), n=4 gives 12, n=5 gives 15.
L4.explanation: Adjacent brace groups in one word combine as a cartesian product, not as a concatenation of the two lists: each alternative of the first group is paired with every alternative of the second, so the count is the product and not the sum. Nothing is filtered afterwards, because brace expansion never looks at the filesystem.

The sequence starts at the start value and adds the increment until it would pass the end value, so the end is included only when it is reached exactly. Counting the steps that fit gives floor of (end minus start) over increment, plus one for the start itself. Bash never overshoots the end, and a negative increment is treated as its magnitude.

Three sequence expressions, all textual. A leading zero on either endpoint pads every generated number to the width of the widest endpoint, so you get 08 09 10 11 and not 8 9 10 11. A descending range is legal and counts down. Character ranges take an increment too, so a to e by 2 is a c e. Verified with bash 5.2.21.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU bash 5.2 with default options (no nullglob, no failglob). The current directory contains exactly one file, named a.txt. What does this print?

    {cmd}
L4.answer: a.txt b*.txt
L4.explanation: Brace expansion runs first and is purely textual, turning the word into a*.txt and b*.txt. Pathname expansion then runs on each of those separately: a*.txt matches the real file, b*.txt matches nothing and, with nullglob off, an unmatched pattern is left in place. Running first does not mean running last - brace output is still fed to every later expansion. Verified with bash 5.2.21.

L4.prompt_tpl: In {shell}, an incorrectly formed brace expansion is left unchanged. Exactly one of these three commands prints its argument exactly as typed. Which one?
L4.answer: echo x{1..}y
L4.explanation: A correctly formed brace expansion needs unquoted braces and either an unquoted comma or a valid sequence expression. x{1..3}y is a valid sequence and gives x1y x2y x3y. x{,}y has a comma, so it is valid: both alternatives are empty and it gives xy xy. x{1..}y has neither a comma nor a complete range, so bash prints it verbatim. Verified with bash 5.2.21.
options: echo x{1..3}y
echo x{,}y
echo x{1..}y

L4.answer: app/{bin,lib}
L4.explanation: The bug is not in mkdir, it is in the assumption that a bash feature is shell syntax. POSIX lists tilde, parameter, command and arithmetic expansion, field splitting, pathname expansion and quote removal - no braces - so dash hands the word to mkdir unchanged and mkdir -p creates a directory whose name is the literal nine-character text {bin,lib} (plus app itself). Fix the shebang to /bin/bash, or write the two paths out. The failure is silent: mkdir exits 0.

L4.answer: /cache /tmp
L4.explanation: Brace expansion runs before parameter expansion, so the one word first becomes two words and only then is the unset variable substituted into each. Quotes stop word splitting and globbing, not the ordering: every quoting habit here is correct and the script still deletes two top-level directories. The defence is a guard before the command - set -u, or a parameter expansion that aborts on an unset variable (`${prefix:?config missing}`), or an explicit test that prefix names a non-empty directory. See The safety preamble.

concepts.t: Globbing, and what happens when nothing matches

L0.body:
# in a directory holding a.txt b.txt c.md
echo *          # a.txt b.txt c.md
echo *.txt      # a.txt b.txt
echo [ab].txt   # a.txt b.txt
echo z*         # z*   <-- NO MATCH: the pattern is passed through unchanged

shopt -s nullglob ; echo z*   # (prints an empty line)
shopt -s failglob ; echo z*   # bash: no match: z*
shopt -s dotglob  ; echo *    # .hidden a.txt b.txt c.md
shopt -s globstar ; echo **/*.txt   # recurses into subdirectories
shopt -s extglob        # on its OWN line: bash parses a whole line before
echo !(a).txt           # running it; !( ) on the same line is a syntax error
L0.cloze:
echo z*                 # no match -> bash prints {{c1::z*}}, the pattern itself
shopt -s {{c2::nullglob}}       # ...so that a non-matching pattern expands to nothing instead
shopt -s {{c3::globstar}}       # ...so that **/ recurses into subdirectories
shopt -s dotglob        # ...so that * also matches {{c4::dotfiles}}

concepts.L1: Pathname expansion replaces a word containing an unquoted `*`, `?` or `[...]` with the sorted list of matching filenames. It is a filter over what exists on disk, and it is done by the shell, not by the command you are calling.
concepts.L2: The default when nothing matches is to leave the pattern alone, so `rm z*` in an empty directory calls rm with the literal argument `z*` instead of calling it with no arguments. Loops over globs therefore need a guard, or nullglob.
concepts.L3: `for f in *.log; do rm "$f"; done` in a directory with no logs runs exactly once, with `f` set to the five characters `*.log`, and rm then reports no such file. That is the classic one-iteration-too-many bug: `shopt -s nullglob` makes the loop run zero times, `failglob` makes the shell refuse the command. Globs are also not regexes - `*` matches any string including the empty one, `.` is an ordinary character, and a leading dot must be matched explicitly, which is why `mv * /dest` silently leaves dotfiles behind. And because the shell builds the whole expanded list and hands it to execve, `rm *` in a huge directory dies with `Argument list too long`: that is E2BIG from the kernel, not a fault in rm and not a limit bash imposes - the builtin `echo *` prints the same list happily. Working around it is what `find . -print0 | xargs -0` exists for.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory contains no file matching the pattern, and nullglob is not set. A script runs:
  `for f in {pat}; do echo "[$f]"; done`
The body runs exactly once. Answer with the exact single line it prints, brackets included.
L4.answer: [{pat}]
L4.explanation: An unmatched glob is left unexpanded by default, so the loop body runs once with f set to the literal pattern - the one-iteration-too-many bug. shopt -s nullglob makes the loop run zero times; failglob makes bash refuse the command outright. Otherwise guard the body, for example with a leading test that skips f when no such file exists.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want to iterate safely over every file in a directory, including names containing spaces and newlines, in a script that must also do nothing when the directory is empty. Which construct?
L4.answer: shopt -s nullglob; for f in ./*; do ... done
L4.explanation: The glob emits one word per filename whatever characters the name contains, and ./ also stops a name beginning with a dash being read as an option; nullglob only fixes the empty case. `for f in $(ls)` is broken by any space in a filename because command substitution is word-split. find | while read is broken by newlines in filenames unless it is null-delimited.
options: shopt -s nullglob; for f in ./*; do ... done
for f in $(ls); do ... done
find . -maxdepth 1 | while read f; do ... done

L4.answer: a.txt b.txt
L4.explanation: A question mark matches exactly one character, so ab.txt is out; a bracket list or range matches one character drawn from the set. The leading dot of .hidden must be matched explicitly, and c.md fails the .txt suffix. Bash returns the matches sorted by the current locale collation, so a.txt comes before b.txt.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory holds {v} files whose names do not begin with a dot and {h} files whose names do begin with a dot, and nothing else. dotglob is off, as it is by default. A script runs: cp * /backup/
How many files land in /backup? Answer with the number of files.
L4.answer: {v}. The {h} dotfiles are not matched by a bare star, so they are silently left behind.
L4.explanation: Pathname expansion never matches a leading dot unless shopt -s dotglob is set, so a bare star copies only the visible files and a backup written this way loses .gitignore, .env and every other dotfile. A bare star never matches the entries . and .. whatever dotglob says; a dot-leading pattern such as .* did match them until bash 5.2 made globskipdots the default.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory holds {n} files ending in .log, {m} files ending in .txt, and no other files. nullglob is not set. A script runs:
  `for f in *.log *.txt *.csv ; do count=$((count+1)) ; done`
How many times does the loop body run? Answer with the number of iterations.
L4.answer: {n} plus {m} plus 1. The two matching patterns contribute one word per file; *.csv matches nothing and survives as a single literal word, so the body runs once more with f set to the five characters *.csv. Worked draw: 3 .log files and 4 .txt files give 8 iterations, verified by running it.
L4.explanation: A for list is built by expanding every word in it, and an unmatched pattern is not dropped - it stays as itself. With shopt -s nullglob the count falls to the number of real files; with failglob bash aborts the command instead. This is why a loop over several globs needs nullglob or a per-iteration existence test.

L4.prompt_tpl: A nightly cleanup script runs `rm *` in a spool directory that an untrusted upload process can write to. The attacker plants a file named {fn} there. Work out what rm does with that word, then answer with the corrected command that keeps the glob but makes such a name impossible to read as an option, using a path prefix rather than an end-of-options marker.
L4.answer: rm ./*
L4.explanation: The shell expands the glob into ordinary arguments, and rm parses a word beginning with a dash as an option wherever it appears in the list: -i turns the run interactive so nothing is deleted, -f suppresses the errors that would have alerted you, -r makes it recursive. Writing the glob as ./* forces every word to start with a dot and a slash, so it can only be a path. rm -- * also works, and is the end-of-options form the question excluded.

L4.prompt_tpl:
The current directory is completely empty. On x86-64 Linux, GNU bash 5.2 runs:
  f={f}
  if [[ $f == *.txt ]]; then echo A; fi
  if [[ $f == "*.txt" ]]; then echo B; fi
Answer with exactly what is printed, or the word NOTHING if there is no output.
L4.answer: A
L4.explanation: Inside double brackets the right-hand side of == is a pattern matched against the string, and no pathname expansion happens at all, which is why the test still works in an empty directory. Quoting that side turns the pattern into a literal, so B would need f to be the five characters *.txt. Contrast single brackets: `[ $f = *.txt ]` is an ordinary command whose words are glob-expanded, and with two .txt files present it fails with 'too many arguments'. That contrast is already covered in the earlier concept Test constructs.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux, execve refuses an argument list whose total size exceeds {limit} bytes, and the kernel copies each argument into that space as a C string, one after another with nothing else in between. A directory holds files whose names are each {len} characters long. Ignoring the environment and the array of pointers, derive roughly how many such names `rm *` can carry before the exec fails with Argument list too long. Answer with the number of files.
L4.answer: floor of {limit} divided by ({len} + 1): a C string of {len} characters occupies {len} + 1 bytes, because of its terminating NUL. For a 2097152-byte limit and 24-character names that is 83886 files; for 262144 and 40-character names it is 6393.
L4.explanation: Each argument is copied as a NUL-terminated C string, so a name of n characters costs n + 1 bytes; dropping the terminator over-counts by enough that the naive limit/len answer misses. The ceiling is the kernel's, not rm's - the same list printed by the echo builtin never fails - and the real figure is lower still, since the environment and an 8-byte pointer per argument count too. The escape is find -print0 piped into xargs -0, the subject of 'find and xargs as an execution engine'.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory holds {n} files ending in .log, {m} files ending in .txt, and no other files. nullglob is not set. A script runs:
  `for f in *.log *.txt *.csv ; do count=$((count+1)) ; done`
How many times does the loop body run? Answer with the number of iterations.
L4.answer: {n} plus {m} plus 1. The two matching patterns contribute one word per file; *.csv matches nothing and survives as a single literal word, so the body runs once more with f set to the five characters *.csv. Worked draw: 3 .log files and 4 .txt files give 8 iterations, verified by running it.
L4.explanation: A for list is built by expanding every word in it, and an unmatched pattern is not dropped - it stays as itself. With shopt -s nullglob the count falls to the number of real files; with failglob bash aborts the command instead. This is why a loop over several globs needs nullglob or a per-iteration existence test.
