resources.title: POSIX Shell Command Language (trap, special built-ins)
resources.why: What is portable rather than bash-specific: condition EXIT is spelled 0, ERR and RETURN are bash extensions, and a script that must run under dash should use only what this page defines.

resources.title: GNU coreutils manual: mktemp invocation
resources.why: The other half of the idiom: why `mktemp -d` rather than a guessed /tmp path, what -p and -t do, and the fact that it can fail, which is what makes an unchecked cleanup path dangerous.

concepts.L1: `local` for all variables inside functions — bash defaults to global, so an unlocalized loop variable silently clobbers the caller's.
concepts.L2: `local` on the same line as a command substitution masks its exit status: `local x=$(false)` returns 0. Declare and assign on separate lines when the status matters.
concepts.L3: Bash has no block or function scope: an assignment inside a function writes the global, so an unlocalised loop counter in a helper silently clobbers the caller's. `local` creates a dynamically scoped binding visible to the function and everything it calls; a name resolves at run time by walking outward through the callers, so a callee assigning without `local` writes the nearest live binding, not necessarily the global. Masking follows from `local` being a command: `local out=$(false)` is one command whose status is `local`'s, and `local` succeeds. Split into `local out` then `out=$(false)`, the assignment is its own command, so `set -e` and an explicit check both see it fail. `declare`, `export` and `readonly` mask identically. A function returns a status, never a value: results leave through stdout and a command substitution - a subshell, see Subshells versus the current shell.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`set -e`
  `h() {{ local out=$({fail}); echo "h saw $?"; }}`
  `g() {{ local out; out=$({fail}); echo "g saw $?"; }}`
  `h`
  `g`
  `echo done`
What does this script print? Answer with the single output line.
L4.answer: h saw 0
L4.explanation: `local` is a command with its own exit status, so it swallows the failure of anything on its right-hand side: h prints 0. g declares first and assigns second, so the assignment is its own command with status 1 - and under set -e that kills the script before its echo runs, so neither 'g saw 1' nor 'done' is ever printed. Declaring and assigning on separate lines is the only way to make the status observable; it is what ShellCheck SC2155 tells you to do.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`process_all() {{ for i in {a} {b}; do :; done; }}`
  `for i in x y z; do process_all; echo "outer i=$i"; done`
Three identical lines are printed. Answer with that one line.
L4.answer: outer i={b}
L4.explanation: Dynamic scoping means a callee clobbers the caller's variables by name alone, and a bare loop counter is the easiest way to do it: process_all leaves the global i at the last word of its own list. The outer loop still runs three times, because bash keeps its own copy of the word list x y z, but `$i` no longer reports where that loop is. When the outer loop is a while whose condition tests `$i`, the same clobbering makes it exit early or never end. `local i` inside process_all fixes it.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script runs:
  `count_up() {lb} local i; for i in $(seq 1 {k}); do total=$((total+i)); done; {rb}`
  `total=0`
  `count_up`
  `echo "$total"`
What number is printed? Answer with the number.
L4.answer: The sum 1 through {k}, that is {k}({k}+1)/2. k=4 prints 10, k=5 prints 15, k=10 prints 55.
L4.explanation: Only `i` was localised. `total` was never declared with local, so the assignment inside the function writes the caller's global - that is the default, not an accident - and the accumulated sum survives the return. This is the one case where the default helps you: a bash function has no return value, so writing a global is a usual way to hand a number back. Had `total` been declared local inside count_up, the script would print 0.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script runs:
  `v={gv}`
  `show() {lb} echo "$v"; {rb}`
  `run() {lb} local v={lv}; show; {rb}`
  `run`
  `show`
What two lines are printed, in order? Answer with the two words separated by a space.
L4.answer: {lv} {gv}
L4.explanation: `local` is not private to the function that declares it: the binding is visible to every function called while run is still on the stack, so show prints run's value the first time. When run returns, bash restores the previous binding, so the second call to show prints the global again. That is dynamic scoping - what you see depends on who called you, not on where the code was written.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script runs under bash 5.2 with default shell options:
  `v={gv}`
  `clear_it() {lb} unset v; echo "clear_it sees $v"; {rb}`
  `holder() {lb} local v={lv}; clear_it; echo "holder sees $v"; {rb}`
  `holder`
Answer with two words separated by a space: the value the clear_it line prints, then the value the holder line prints.
L4.answer: {gv} {gv}
L4.explanation: `unset` does not restore a shadowed name, it removes the binding it finds - here holder's local - so the global underneath becomes visible again, and stays visible for the rest of holder. That is why both lines print the global value and neither prints the local one. `shopt -s localvar_unset` changes this to mark the local unset instead; it is off by default. The lesson is which binding a name reaches, not what a status carries.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A file named logfile does NOT contain the text {pat}. A bash script runs:
  `is_ready() {lb} grep -q {pat} logfile; echo "checked"; {rb}`
  `is_ready`
  `echo "$?"`
What number does the last line print? Answer with the number.
L4.answer: 0, on every draw. grep exits 1 because it matched nothing, but the function's status is the status of its LAST command, and the echo succeeded.
L4.explanation: A function with no explicit `return` exits with the status of the last command it ran. The trailing echo - a log line, a progress message, anything - overwrites the status you meant to report, so `if is_ready; then` is always true and the check is dead code. Fix it by ending with the test itself, or by capturing the status first and returning it explicitly.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script runs:
  `name={g}`
  `setname() {lb} name={s}; {rb}`
  `wrap() {lb} local name={l}; setname; echo "wrap sees $name"; {rb}`
  `wrap`
  `echo "global is $name"`
Answer with two words separated by a space: the value wrap sees, then the value of the global afterwards.
L4.explanation: setname contains no `local`, so it writes the nearest live binding of that name - and while wrap is on the stack that binding is wrap's local, not the global. The global is never touched. This is what dynamic scoping means: a name is resolved at run time by walking outward through the callers, not by where the code sits. So a helper you did not write can be captured by any caller that declares the same name local, which is why shared globals in bash are given prefixed names.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bash script runs:
  `walk() {lb} local d=$1; if [ "$d" -gt 0 ]; then walk $((d-1)); fi; echo "$d"; {rb}`
  `walk {n}`
It prints one number per line. Answer with the SUM of all the numbers printed.
L4.answer: n(n+1)/2. n=3 prints 0,1,2,3 and sums to 6; n=4 sums to 10; n=5 sums to 15. Each frame recovers its own d as the recursion unwinds.
L4.explanation: Every call of walk executes its own `local d`, so bash pushes a fresh binding and restores the previous one on return. The recursion descends to 0 and the echoes fire on the way out, so the lines are 0,1,...,n and the sum is n(n+1)/2. Delete the word local and every frame shares one cell: the innermost call sets it to 0, all n+1 lines print 0, and the sum is 0. That is the difference between a stack of bindings and a single global.

L0.body:
$ shellcheck deploy.sh

In deploy.sh line 4:
cp $src /backup/
   ^-- SC2086: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

In deploy.sh line 9:
local out=$(build)
      ^-- SC2155: Declare and assign separately to avoid masking return values.

In deploy.sh line 12:
cd "$dir"
^-- SC2164: Use 'cd ... || exit' in case cd fails.

# disable one deliberately, with a reason:
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # word splitting is intended here
L0.cloze:
$ {{c1::shellcheck}} deploy.sh
SC{{c2::2086}}  unquoted variable expansion — word splitting and globbing
SC{{c3::2155}}  local/declare masks the assignment's exit status
# {{c4::shellcheck disable=SC2086}}   suppress one check on the next line, with a comment saying why

concepts.L1: A static analyzer for shell scripts. Catches quoting bugs, subshell scope issues, useless use of cat, and most of the above automatically.
concepts.L2: Run it in CI. It finds real bugs in almost every non-trivial script written by someone who hasn't been running it, and the fix rate is high because the diagnostics are specific.
concepts.L3: ShellCheck parses a script into a syntax tree rather than grepping it, so it knows each expansion's context: `cp $src /backup/` raises SC2086, the same `$x` inside `[[ ]]` does not, since nothing there is split or globbed - the bug there is SC2053: an unquoted right-hand side of `==` is a glob. Every finding has a stable number and a wiki page with failing input and fix: SC2086 quoting, SC2155 masked exit status, SC2164 unchecked cd, SC2162 read without -r, SC2046 unquoted command substitution. It cannot see runtime: a path built at run time is unreadable to it (SC1090/SC1091), and a clean report proves nothing about logic. It exits 0 clean, 1 with findings, 2-4 when it could not run, so a gate must separate them; xargs flattens all to 123 (find and xargs as an execution engine). Pair every `# shellcheck disable=SCxxxx` with a reason; a bare disable is how a linter stops being trusted.

L4.prompt_tpl: Name the ShellCheck codes for these four bug classes and state the fix for each: unquoted variable expansion; `local x=$(cmd)`; `cd` whose failure is unchecked; `read` without -r.
L4.answer: SC2086 - quote the expansion. SC2155 - declare and assign on separate lines. SC2164 - use `cd ... || exit`, or `set -e` plus a check. SC2162 - use `read -r`.
L4.explanation: These four account for a large share of the findings in a script written by someone who has not run the tool, and all four are silent-wrong-answer bugs rather than crashes, which is why static analysis pays here more than in most languages.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CI job runs shellcheck on {n} scripts and 40 warnings appear. What is the correct first move?
L4.answer: Fix the SC2086 and SC2155 findings first, then gate the build at zero
L4.explanation: The mcq answer must be the exact option text or the grader marks every correct pick wrong. Triage by bug class: SC2086 is silent data corruption and SC2155 is a silently swallowed exit status, while style findings can wait. Blanket-disabling loses the signal permanently, and a warning-only step is a blanket disable with extra steps.
options: Fix the SC2086 and SC2155 findings first, then gate the build at zero
Add `# shellcheck disable=all` at the top of each script and move on
Turn the CI step to warning-only and revisit next quarter

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux, at the top level of a script (not inside a function):

export v=$(exit {code})
echo $?
w=$(exit {code})
echo $?

This is the SC2155 case. Answer with the two numbers the script prints, first echo then second, separated by a space.
L4.answer: 0 {code}
L4.explanation: export, local, readonly and declare are commands. In `export v=$(cmd)` the status `$?` reports is export's own, which is 0, and the substitution's status is thrown away; the plain assignment `w=$(cmd)` reports the command's, here {code}. Split the line - `export v` then `v=$(cmd)` - and `$?` is the command's again. That is SC2155, 'Declare and assign separately to avoid masking return values', and it is why a failing build step inside such an assignment passes unnoticed. Verified on bash 5.2.21 for all three draws.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A CI step runs: shellcheck {script}

The file exists, is readable, and parses. ShellCheck prints {n} warnings at or above the severity threshold in use. What exit status does shellcheck return? Answer with the number.
L4.explanation: ShellCheck's documented return values: 0 all files scanned with no issues, 1 all files scanned with some issues, 2 some files could not be processed, 3 bad command-line syntax, 4 bad options. The count of findings never reaches the status: {n} findings and ninety both give 1. The useful split is 1 (the script has problems) against 2, 3 and 4 (shellcheck itself could not do its job - missing file, unknown flag, unknown formatter). A gate that only tests for non-zero cannot tell those apart, and --severity=error makes lower findings invisible and the status 0.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux:

x={word}
if [[ $x == f* ]]; then echo MATCH; else echo NOMATCH; fi

ShellCheck reports no SC2086 for the unquoted $x on that line. What does the script print?
L4.answer: MATCH
L4.explanation: Inside `[[ ]]` no word splitting or globbing is done on expansions, so SC2086 genuinely does not apply - ShellCheck knows this because it parsed the construct rather than matching `$x` in text. Verified on bash 5.2.21: foo, food and foobar all match. The right-hand side of `==` is different: it IS a pattern. Write `[[ $x == $y ]]` with y=f* and the same glob happens through a variable, which is SC2053; quote it, `[[ $x == "$y" ]]`, for a string comparison.

L4.prompt_tpl:
This script passes shellcheck with zero findings (bash 5.2, x86-64 Linux):

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
count=$(grep -c {pattern} {logfile})
echo "count: $count"
echo done

It works for months and then silently stops producing output. Say what happens on a day when {logfile} contains no {pattern} line, what the script's exit status is, and why a clean shellcheck report could never have caught it.
L4.answer: grep -c prints 0 and exits 1 when nothing matches. In `count=$(...)` the assignment's status is the substitution's status, so under set -e the shell exits right there: neither echo runs and the script exits 1, printing nothing at all. Verified on bash 5.2.21 - with a matching line it prints 'count: 1' then 'done' and exits 0; with none it prints nothing and exits 1. ShellCheck cannot see it: the script is quoted correctly and syntactically clean, and grep's exit contract is runtime behaviour, not syntax. Fix: `count=$(grep -c {pattern} {logfile} || true)` - verified to give count 0 and status 0 - or `if ! count=$(grep -c {pattern} {logfile}); then count=0; fi`.
L4.explanation: A linter checks the shapes it can prove wrong; it does not know that grep returns 1 on no match, that diff returns 1 on difference, or what your own commands mean. Shellcheck-clean is a floor, not a proof. The interaction here is with the safety preamble: set -e makes a legitimate 'nothing found' status fatal, which is why || true (or an if) belongs on commands whose non-zero status is information.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A CI gate is written as:

`find {dir} -name '*.sh' -print0 | xargs -0 -r shellcheck -S {sev}
rc=$?
if test "$rc" -eq 1; then echo findings; exit 1; fi
if test "$rc" -ne 0; then echo tool error; exit 2; fi
echo clean`

GNU findutils, GNU xargs. Name the independent ways this gate reports the wrong thing - there are at least three - and give the exit status xargs actually returns when shellcheck finds problems in one file.
L4.answer: xargs returns 123. (1) xargs does not pass a child's status through: if any invocation exits 1-125 xargs exits 123 (verified: `printf 'a\nb\n' | xargs -n1 sh -c 'exit 1' _` gives 123). So rc is never 1, the findings branch is dead, and every real finding is announced as 'tool error' with exit 2; shellcheck's 2, 3 and 4 are flattened to the same 123, so a file it could not read looks exactly like a finding. (2) With -r, when find matches nothing - scripts with no .sh suffix, a renamed directory, a wrong starting path - xargs never runs, rc is 0, and the gate prints 'clean' having checked no files. (3) -S {sev} sets the MINIMUM severity reported: SC2086 is info-level and SC2155 is warning-level, so -S warning already hides every SC2086 and -S error hides both, and a script full of unquoted expansions produces no findings, exit 0, 'clean'. Fix: drive the loop yourself, `while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do shellcheck -S info -- "$f" || rc=$?; n=$((n+1)); done < <(find DIR -name '*.sh' -print0)`, branch on shellcheck's own status, and fail if n is 0.
L4.explanation: Exit status is plumbing and xargs is a lossy junction: 123 for any child exiting 1-125, 124 for a child exiting 255, 125 if a child is killed by a signal, 126 or 127 if the command could not be run or not found. Those numbers exist because one status cannot carry many children's. A gate needs three outcomes - clean, findings, tool broken - so it must read the tool's own status, set a severity floor low enough to see the bug classes it cares about, and prove it looked at something.

L0.body:
x=1
( x=2 )        ; echo "$x"   # 1  — ( ) forks a subshell
{ x=2; }       ; echo "$x"   # 2  — { } is just grouping, same shell
y=$(x=3; echo) ; echo "$x"   # 2  — $( ) is a subshell

cd /; ( cd /etc ); echo "$PWD"   # /   — cd in a subshell does not escape

# every one of these forks:
#   ( ... )      $( ... )      `...`      cmd1 | cmd2   (each stage)
#   cmd &        <( ... )      >( ... )
# these do NOT fork:
#   { ...; }     while/for/if bodies     function calls     source file
# to get a value OUT of a subshell, capture its stdout:  v=$(subshell)
L0.cloze:
x=1
{{c1::( x=2 )}}   ; echo "$x"   # 1 — this form forks
{{c2::{ x=2; }}}  ; echo "$x"   # 2 — this form does not
# a pipeline runs {{c3::each stage}} in its own process
# `cd` inside ( ) is a deliberate use: it {{c4::cannot leak to the caller}}

concepts.L1: A subshell is a forked copy of the shell: it inherits variables, functions, the working directory and open file descriptors, and nothing it changes propagates back to the parent. Braces group commands without forking, so assignments inside them persist.
concepts.L2: The distinction is invisible in the syntax unless you know it, and the failure mode is a silently unchanged variable rather than an error. Counting inside a piped `while` is the famous case, but `$( )`, `&` and `( )` have exactly the same property.
concepts.L3: The rule is mechanical: if bash must run something concurrently or in isolation it calls fork, and a forked process cannot write to its parent's memory. That makes `( cd "$dir" && make )` a good idiom - the directory change is scoped and cannot leak - and makes `count=$((count+1))` inside a pipeline stage useless. To get a value out of a subshell you must send it through a file descriptor: capture stdout with `$( )`, or write to a temp file. To keep a loop in the current shell, redirect with `< file` or `< <(cmd)`. A subshell also gets its own trap set, so an EXIT trap inside `( )` fires when the subshell ends.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`x={n}`
  `( x=99 )`
  `echo "a=$x"`
  `{{ x=99; }}`
  `echo "b=$x"`
What are the two lines?
L4.answer: a= the original value (1, 5 or 7), then b=99.
L4.explanation: Parentheses fork a subshell, so the assignment happens in a child process whose memory is discarded on exit. Braces are pure grouping with no fork, so the assignment writes the current shell's variable. The only visible difference in the source is the bracket character.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script must run `make` inside {d} and then continue working in its original directory, and must be correct even if make fails. Which construction?
L4.answer: ( cd build/ && make ) — the cd happens in a subshell, so the parent's working directory is untouched no matter how the subshell ends, and the && ensures make is not run if the cd failed.
L4.explanation: `cd build/; make; cd ..` is wrong twice: the final cd is skipped if make aborts under set -e, and `cd ..` is not the inverse of cd if build/ was a symlink. pushd/popd works but leaks on an early exit unless trapped.
options: ( cd build/ && make )
cd build/; make; cd ..
pushd build/; make; popd

L4.prompt_tpl: At the top level of a script, `echo $$` and `echo $BASHPID` print the same PID, say {pid}. Bash then forks a real child process to run `( echo $$; echo $BASHPID )`. Which statement is correct?
L4.answer: Inside the subshell, $$ still prints {pid} (the top-level shell's PID); $BASHPID prints the subshell's own new PID.
L4.explanation: The bash manual documents $$ as expanding to the invoking shell's PID even inside a () subshell - a Bourne-shell compatibility quirk, computed once and never updated. $BASHPID is a bash-only addition that always calls getpid() fresh, so it changes on every fork, subshells included.
options: Inside the subshell, $$ still prints {pid} (the top-level shell's PID); $BASHPID prints the subshell's own new PID.
Inside the subshell, $$ prints the subshell's new PID; $BASHPID prints {pid}, unchanged.
Both $$ and $BASHPID print {pid} inside the subshell, because a subshell shares its parent's process ID.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`count={c}; ( count=$((count+1)) ); ( count=$((count+1)) ); echo $count`
What number does this print?
L4.answer: It prints {c} unchanged: c=3 prints 3, c=8 prints 8, c=21 prints 21 - running the subshell twice does not accumulate anything.
L4.explanation: Each `( )` forks a fresh process; the assignment inside happens only in that process's own copy of memory and is discarded when it exits. Doing this fork-and-discard twice in a row changes nothing about the parent's count - isolation does not partially leak or build up over repeated forks, it simply never happens for the parent shell.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`x={n}`
  `( x=$((x+1)); ( x=$((x+1)); echo "innermost=$x" ); echo "middle=$x" )`
  `echo "top=$x"`
What are the three numbers printed, top to bottom?
L4.answer: Each level only ever moves one step up from its own fork point: innermost=n+2, middle=n+1, top=n, printed in that order. n=10: innermost=12, middle=11, top=10. n=20: innermost=22, middle=21, top=20. n=100: innermost=102, middle=101, top=100.
L4.explanation: Each pair of parentheses forks from whatever value its own parent process currently holds, and nothing a child does reaches back up even one level: the inner subshell's increment never reaches the middle one, and the middle one's increment never reaches the top. Isolation does not accumulate or leak sideways - every level sees only its own fork point.

L4.prompt_tpl: A deploy script starts with `set -e`. Partway through: `if ( {cmd} ); then echo ok; fi` - the author's intent is that the whole script aborts immediately if {cmd} fails inside the subshell. It does not abort; the script just continues past the `if` with nothing printed. Explain why, and give a fix that still runs {cmd} in a subshell but aborts the script on its failure.
L4.answer: set -e exempts any command used as an if/while/until test (and anything negated with !, or not the last element of a && or || list) - a subshell used as that test is no exception, so ( {cmd} ) failing there is read as an ordinary false test, not a failure to abort on. Fix: don't use it as a condition - run ( {cmd} ) || exit 1 as a statement instead, or drop the if and let the bare ( {cmd} ) trigger -e directly.
L4.explanation: set -e's own exemption list applies to whatever command sits in the exempted position, including a parenthesized subshell - wrapping a check in ( ) does not restore abort-on-failure. Putting the subshell as the left side of an explicit || exit 1 does restore it, because that position is not exempt.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script sets one cleanup handler, `trap cleanup EXIT`, at the top, then later runs `( step_that_might_fail )` as an ordinary subshell partway through, with more script after it. Running `trap` with no arguments *inside* that subshell still lists the `cleanup EXIT` entry as active. Does `cleanup` actually run when this subshell finishes, and when does it run instead? Justify from what a subshell inherits.
L4.answer: No - cleanup does not run when the subshell finishes, even though `trap` lists it as set there. It runs exactly once, when the original top-level shell that installed it - the one whose `$$` / `$BASHPID` the trap was registered under - actually exits. The listing you see inside the subshell is inherited bookkeeping, not a promise that it fires on that subshell's own exit.
L4.explanation: Bash's Command Execution Environment section documents that a subshell duplicates the parent's trap table, which is why `trap` inside it still shows the entry; but the EXIT pseudo-trap only fires for the shell instance that owns it when that instance itself terminates, not for every nested subshell that merely inherited the listing. Relying on it as a per-subshell cleanup hook is the bug - see Traps and cleanup for the trap that does run on demand instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to run {n} independent, slow shell computations in parallel and then collect all {n} of their results into the current shell. A backgrounded subshell (`cmd &`) cannot write to the parent's variables. Give a construction that gets all {n} results back correctly attributed, name the bash command that waits for one specific background job and reports its own exit status, and say what becomes of a variable a backgrounded subshell sets.
L4.answer: Send each job's output to its own file (or named pipe) instead of a variable: for i in 1..{n}, run `job_i > out_i.txt &` and record `pids[i]=$!`. Then for each i, `wait "${{pids[i]}}"` blocks until exactly that job finishes and sets `$?` to its exit status, after which `out_i.txt` can be read safely. A variable set inside `cmd &` (e.g. `result=$(cmd) &`) is set only in that forked copy's memory and is gone the instant it exits - only what the background job writes to a file descriptor, file, or pipe survives; see wait, `$!` and parallelism in bash.
L4.explanation: `cmd &` forks exactly like `( cmd )` - the memory barrier is identical - so the only channel out of a parallel job is something written outside its own process. Recording each job's own PID with `$!` and calling `wait` on that specific PID (rather than a bare `wait`) is what lets the script know which job finished and whether it succeeded, rather than only that all of them eventually did.

prog > out.txt 2>&1     # stdout to the file, then stderr to WHERE STDOUT NOW IS
prog 2>&1 > out.txt     # stderr to the terminal, stdout to the file — order matters
prog &> out.txt         # bash shorthand for the first form

prog 2>/dev/null        # discard stderr only
prog >/dev/null 2>&1    # discard both
prog >> log.txt         # append instead of truncate

exec 3> report.txt      # open fd 3 for the rest of the script
echo hi >&3
exec 3>&-              # close it

diff <(sort a) <(sort b)   # process substitution supplies a /dev/fd path
L0.cloze:
prog {{c1::> out.txt 2>&1}}   # both streams to the file
prog 2>&1 > out.txt   # stderr goes to {{c2::the original stdout (the terminal)}}
prog {{c3::2>/dev/null}}      # discard stderr, keep stdout
exec {{c4::3>}} report.txt     # open fd 3 for the remainder of the script

concepts.L1: A redirection assigns a file descriptor number to an open file. `2>&1` means 'make fd 2 a duplicate of whatever fd 1 currently is', so it copies the destination at the moment it is processed, and redirections are processed strictly left to right.
concepts.L2: `2>&1 > file` looks like it should send both streams to the file and does the opposite: stderr is pointed at the terminal (stdout's value at that instant) and only stdout is redirected. `> file 2>&1` is the order that works.
concepts.L3: Think of the fd table as an array of pointers. `> out.txt` sets slot 1 to the file. `2>&1` sets slot 2 to a copy of slot 1's current pointer. Reverse the order and slot 2 is copied while slot 1 still points at the terminal, after which slot 1 is repointed and slot 2 is left behind. That also explains why `cmd > file 2>&1` and `cmd &> file` are the same, and why `cmd 2>&1 | less` works while `cmd | less 2>&1` does not. `exec 3> file` redirects the shell itself rather than one command, which is how a log file stays open across a script; `exec 3>&-` closes it.

L4.answer: A: both OUT and ERR. B: only OUT (ERR goes to the terminal).
L4.explanation: Redirections are applied left to right and 2>&1 duplicates fd 1's current target, not its future one. In B, fd 2 is aimed at the terminal before fd 1 is moved to the file, so the two streams end up in different places.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A cron entry is written as:
  {n} * * * * /opt/job.sh 2>&1 >> /var/log/job.log
Errors still land in cron's mail instead of the log. Fix it and say why.
L4.answer: The order is reversed: 2>&1 duplicates fd 1 while fd 1 is still cron's pipe, so stderr keeps going there, and only stdout is appended to the log. Correct form: /opt/job.sh >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1.
L4.explanation: The mnemonic that survives: put the file redirection first, then duplicate onto it. Reading it as 'send stderr to where stdout goes' is what makes people write it backwards; read it as 'copy fd 1's current value into fd 2' instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script runs `exec > {f} 2>&1` near the top (no command name, so it redirects the shell itself), and nothing after that line redirects fd 1 or fd 2 again. Later the script does `some_cmd` and then, further down, a plain `echo starting stage two >&2`. Where does 'starting stage two' end up?
L4.answer: In the file (f), appended after whatever some_cmd already wrote there.
L4.explanation: exec with no command name does not run a program; it changes the shell's own file descriptors. exec > f 2>&1 opens f on fd 1 and duplicates fd 2 onto it for the shell process itself, so every command the script runs afterward - including a bare echo >&2 - inherits those already-redirected descriptors until something redirects them again. A per-command redirection like `some_cmd > f 2>&1` would NOT have this effect: it is scoped to that one command, and a later echo >&2 in the same script would still go to the script's original stderr, not the file.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file already holds {a} bytes. A command then appends {b} more bytes to it with >> (which opens the file with O_APPEND and therefore never truncates). How many bytes does the file hold afterward?
L4.answer: a+b bytes: the existing content survives and the new bytes land after it, unlike > which truncates the file to zero length before the first write.
L4.explanation: The kernel opens an O_APPEND file descriptor so that every write() happens at the current end of file regardless of where the process last wrote, so prior content is never overwritten. > instead opens with O_TRUNC, which discards existing content immediately, before the command writes a single byte.

L4.prompt_tpl: prog writes OUT to stdout and ERR to stderr. Is the resulting file the same after `prog &> {f}` as after `prog > {f} 2>&1`? Give the file's contents in both cases.
L4.answer: The same in both cases: the file contains OUT and ERR (interleaved in whatever order the program wrote them).
L4.explanation: &>word is bash's own shorthand and is defined to be exactly equivalent to >word 2>&1: it opens the file for fd 1 and then duplicates fd 2 onto it, in that order, so the left-to-right ordering trap does not apply to this form.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script runs `echo status: {s} >&3`, but the script never executed `exec 3> file` or any other redirection that opens fd 3 beforehand. What happens when this line runs, and why?
L4.answer: bash reports '3: Bad file descriptor' and the echo command fails with a nonzero exit status; nothing is written anywhere.
L4.explanation: N>&M duplicates an existing descriptor onto another one; it never creates a descriptor. There is nothing to duplicate until something, usually exec N> file, has already opened fd N, so referencing an unopened descriptor fails immediately instead of silently doing nothing or opening one implicitly.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script must send both stdout and stderr to log.txt, but only stdout should also appear on the terminal; stderr must stay silent to the user watching the terminal. Which single command line achieves this?
L4.answer: cmd 2>>log.txt > >(tee -a log.txt)
L4.explanation: 2>>log.txt sends stderr straight to the file, silent to the terminal. Routing stdout into >(tee -a log.txt), a process substitution, makes stdout go to both the terminal and the file. > log.txt 2>&1 sends everything to the file and nothing to the terminal; 2>&1 | tee log.txt merges stderr into stdout, so errors show on the terminal too.
options: cmd 2>>log.txt > >(tee -a log.txt)
cmd > log.txt 2>&1
cmd 2>&1 | tee log.txt

printf '1\n2\n3\n' | tee >(wc -l > count.txt) > /dev/null  # write side

ls -l <(echo hi)
# lr-x------ 1 u u 64 ... /dev/fd/63 -> pipe:[13847]

concepts.L1: Process substitution turns a command into a filename. `<(cmd)` runs cmd with its stdout on a pipe and substitutes the path `/dev/fd/N` for that pipe, so any program that takes a filename can read a command's output directly.
concepts.L2: It is not a subshell you are inside - it is a separate background process, and the substitution's own exit status is not reported anywhere. `< <(cmd)` is two tokens: a redirection followed by a path, and the space between them is required.
concepts.L3: Two things it buys you. First, tools with a two-file interface - `diff`, `comm`, `join`, `paste` - become usable on pipelines with no temp files and no cleanup. Second, `while ... done < <(cmd)` fixes the piped-loop scope bug, because the loop is the parent reading from a file rather than the last stage of a pipeline. The cost is the status: `while read ... done < <(false)` succeeds, so a failing producer is invisible - write to a temp file with a trap when that matters. And `/dev/fd/N` is a pipe, so it cannot be seeked: a consumer that rewinds or stats its input for a size fails where it would work on a real file.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`n=0`
  `printf '{a}\n{b}\n' | while read -r l; do n=$((n+1)); done`
  `echo "pipe=$n"`
  `m=0`
  `while read -r l; do m=$((m+1)); done < <(printf '{a}\n{b}\n')`

What are the two lines?

L4.explanation: In the pipeline the loop is the final stage and therefore a forked child, so its increments die with it. With process substitution the loop is not part of a pipeline at all - it is the current shell reading from a /dev/fd path - so the variable persists.

L4.prompt_tpl: `ls -l <(echo hi)` prints a symlink to `pipe:[...]` rather than a regular file. Name two practical consequences.
L4.answer: First, the substitution's exit status is unavailable: the producing command runs in the background and nothing reports whether it failed, so `cmd < <(might_fail)` succeeds regardless. Second, the path is not seekable, so any consumer that rewinds, reads its input twice, or stats it for a size will misbehave where it would work on a real file.
L4.explanation: A third, occasionally biting: /dev/fd only exists on systems that provide it, and the pipe is closed when the consumer exits, so a consumer that opens the path lazily or twice may find it gone. When any of these matter, write to a temp file with an EXIT trap.

L4.prompt_tpl: `wc -l < <(seq 1 {n})` reads through a process substitution instead of a real file. What number does it print?
L4.answer: {n} - seq 1 {n} writes exactly {n} lines to the pipe, and wc -l just counts input lines; it cannot tell the /dev/fd path from a real file, so the count is unchanged.
L4.explanation: seq 1 n always emits exactly n lines, one per number. The <(...) only changes where wc -l's input comes from - a pipe named by a /dev/fd path instead of a disk file - not how many lines arrive, so wc -l reports n either way.

L4.prompt_tpl: Neither missing1.txt nor missing2.txt exists. What is $? after `diff <(sort missing1.txt) <(sort missing2.txt)`, and why?

options: 0, because both failed sort processes produce empty streams and diff finds two empty inputs identical
1, because diff always reports a mismatch when either input command errors
diff hangs forever because the failed process substitutions never close their pipes

L4.prompt_tpl: `diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)` returns 0 whenever both files are unreadable, because two empty streams count as identical - a real sort failure stays invisible. Using a trap-based cleanup (see 'Traps and cleanup'), design a comparison that fails loudly when either sort fails, and state what you give up to get it.
L4.answer: Write each side to its own temp file and check each sort's exit status before diffing: ta=$(mktemp); tb=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$ta" "$tb"' EXIT; sort a.txt > "$ta" || exit 1; sort b.txt > "$tb" || exit 1; diff "$ta" "$tb". You give up process substitution's whole advantage - no temp files, no cleanup - and now need the EXIT trap to guarantee the temp files are removed on every exit path, including the early ones.
L4.explanation: This is the direct trade the L3 names: process substitution hides a producer's exit status, so recovering it costs the very thing <(...) buys you. The trap is what makes the temp-file version safe to use in a script that might exit early.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Trace this nested construct: `comm -12 <(sort <(printf 'banana
apple
cherry
')) <(sort <(printf 'cherry
date
apple
'))`. Each inner `<(printf ...)` becomes a /dev/fd path that the outer `sort` reads as an ordinary input file; each `sort`'s own stdout becomes a further /dev/fd path that `comm` reads. What does it print, in order?
L4.answer: apple then cherry, one per line - comm -12 keeps only the lines common to both sorted inputs, and comm's output is alphabetical because its inputs are sorted.
L4.explanation: Nothing about nesting is special: a /dev/fd path is just a filename, so sort accepts the inner substitution as its input file exactly as it would a real file, and comm accepts the outer one the same way. The common lines between {banana, apple, cherry} and {cherry, date, apple} are apple and cherry, listed alphabetically.

Process substitution deliberately hides the producer's status because the parent never treats it as a job; an explicit `cmd & pid=$!` does treat it as a job, and `wait $pid` is the shell's own mechanism for recovering a background job's exit status, so the redesign buys back exactly what `>(...)` gave up.

L0.body:
cat <<'EOF'          # QUOTED delimiter: no expansion at all
hello $name `date` $(id)
EOF

cat <<EOF            # unquoted: parameter, command and arithmetic expansion happen
hello $name
EOF

cat <<-EOF           # <<- strips leading TABS (not spaces) so you can indent
	indented in source, flush in output
	EOF

tr a-z A-Z <<< "$name"      # here-string: one line on stdin
wc -c <<< "abc"             # 4 — a here-string APPENDS a newline
printf abc | wc -c          # 3
L0.cloze:
cat <<{{c1::'EOF'}}    # quote the delimiter to stop $ and backticks being expanded
...
EOF

cat <<{{c2::-}}EOF     # this form strips leading TAB characters so the here-doc can be indented

tr a-z A-Z {{c3::<<<}} "$name"   # here-string
wc -c <<< "abc"       # {{c4::4}} — a here-string adds a trailing newline

concepts.L1: A here-document feeds literal text to a command's stdin, ending at a line containing only the delimiter. Quoting the delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) suppresses all expansion inside the body; leaving it bare allows parameter, command and arithmetic expansion.
concepts.L2: The quoting decision is a security boundary, not a style choice: an unquoted here-doc containing a `$(...)` from untrusted data executes it. And `<<-` strips only tab characters, so an editor configured to insert spaces silently breaks the closing delimiter.
concepts.L3: The commonest real failure is generating a script or config with an unquoted delimiter, so every `$VAR` in the template is expanded by the generating shell instead of written out. `cat > run.sh <<'EOF'` is almost always what you want. The `<<-` variant lets an indented here-doc avoid being flush-left, but it strips tabs only: mix it with space indentation and the delimiter line reads `    EOF`, which does not terminate the document - bash warns that the here-doc was delimited by end-of-file and swallows the rest of the script as data. A here-string always appends a newline, which matters when the consumer is `wc -c` or a checksum.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`name={n}`
  `cat <<'EOF'`
  `hello $name`
  `EOF`
  `cat <<EOF`
  `hello $name`
  `EOF`
What are the two output lines?
L4.answer: hello `$name` (literally, with the dollar sign) then hello world (or hello ada).
L4.explanation: Quoting the delimiter in any way - <<'EOF', <<"EOF", <<\EOF - turns the entire body into literal text. Leaving it bare enables parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion inside the body.

L4.prompt_tpl:
printf '{s}' | wc -c
  wc -c <<< '{s}'
What two numbers are printed?
L4.answer: For abc: 3 then 4. For hello: 5 then 6. The here-string appends a newline that printf did not.
L4.explanation: Here-strings are defined to supply the word followed by a newline. This shows up as an off-by-one in byte counts and in hashes: sha256sum <<< "`$v`" and printf %s "`$v`" | sha256sum produce different digests.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`n={n}`
  `cat <<EOF`
  `total: $((n * 2 + 1))`
  `EOF`
What number appears after "total: "?
L4.answer: n*2+1. For n=3: total: 7. For n=5: total: 11. For n=8: total: 17. For n=12: total: 25.
L4.explanation: The delimiter is unquoted (<<EOF, not <<'EOF'), so arithmetic expansion $((...)) runs before the line reaches cat's stdin, exactly as it would outside a here-document; only a quoted delimiter would print the literal text $((n * 2 + 1)).

L4.prompt_tpl:
`cat <<EOF`
  `result: $(echo {w} | tr a-z A-Z)`
  `EOF`
What is the one output line?
L4.answer: result: CAT (for w=cat), result: DOG (for w=dog), or result: SUN (for w=sun).
L4.explanation: An unquoted heredoc delimiter allows command substitution, not just parameter expansion: $(echo w | tr a-z A-Z) runs before cat ever sees the line, so cat's stdin already contains the uppercased word, not the literal $(...) text.

L4.prompt_tpl: A shell function opens with a line containing only an opening brace, then runs `cat <<-EOF`, then two tab-indented lines `line one` and `line two`, then a closing `EOF` line indented with {spaces} plain spaces (not a tab), then a line containing only a closing brace to end the function. The script then calls the function and runs `echo after`. What happens when the script runs?
L4.answer: Bash never finds a line that is only the delimiter, because <<- strips leading TAB characters only, not spaces; the here-document silently swallows the rest of the file, including the function's closing brace, and bash reports a syntax error before the function ever runs, so nothing is printed.
L4.explanation: Verified in bash 5.2: with a space-indented closing EOF, bash reports a here-document delimited by end-of-file warning, then a syntax error for the now-unclosed function, and exits 2 with no other output at all; the whole file fails to parse, so cat never runs.
options: cat prints line one and line two, then the script prints after; the space-indented EOF line is harmless.

Bash never finds a line that is only the delimiter, because <<- strips leading TAB characters only, not spaces; the here-document silently swallows the rest of the file, including the function's closing brace, and bash reports a syntax error before the function ever runs, so nothing is printed.
Bash strips the leading spaces exactly like tabs and prints a one-line deprecation warning, but the output is otherwise identical to the tab-indented version.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script reads hostnames from a here-document and runs a remote command on each: `while read -r host; do`, `  ssh "$host" {cmd}`, `done <<EOF`, `web1`, `web2`, `web3`, `EOF`. Only web1 is ever processed, and web2/web3 appear to vanish. Why, and what is the standard one-flag fix to the ssh invocation?
L4.answer: ssh reads from its own stdin by default, and it inherits the same stdin as the loop, which is the here-document. On the first iteration ssh consumes the remaining here-doc lines (web2, web3) as its own input before the loop's read ever sees them, so the loop exits after one pass. Fix: run ssh -n (or redirect ssh's stdin from /dev/null) so it never touches file descriptor 0.
L4.explanation: A here-document becomes the whole loop's stdin, and every command inside the loop body shares that same file descriptor unless it is redirected away. ssh beyond login covers -n and the other flags that control what ssh does with stdin on the remote side, which is exactly the tool for this trap.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need diff to compare the sorted contents of two files, {a} and {b}, without writing temp files. Which construct actually gives diff two independent inputs, and why do the here-document and here-string alternatives fail?
L4.answer: diff <(sort file1.txt) <(sort file2.txt) - each process substitution hands diff a separate readable path, such as /dev/fd/63, so diff gets the two distinct file arguments it expects.
L4.explanation: A here-string or here-document only ever targets one file descriptor, the command's stdin; a second <<< or heredoc on the same command just replaces the first one instead of adding a second input. diff wants two positional file arguments, which only process substitution's named /dev/fd path can supply.
options: diff <(sort file1.txt) <(sort file2.txt) - each process substitution hands diff a separate readable path, such as /dev/fd/63, so diff gets the two distinct file arguments it expects.
diff <<< "$(sort file1.txt)" <<< "$(sort file2.txt)" - each here-string adds another input for diff to read in turn, so both sorted streams reach it correctly.
diff with two separately quoted here-documents, one feeding each sorted file's content - quoting the delimiters keeps the two here-documents from interfering with each other before diff runs.

L0.body:
declare -A count            # REQUIRED — without it, count[foo] means count[0]

count[alpha]=1
count[beta]=2

echo "${!count[@]}"         # alpha beta          the KEYS (order unspecified)
echo "${count[@]}"          # 1 2                the values
echo "${#count[@]}"         # 2
echo "${count[alpha]}"      # 1
echo "${count[nope]-absent}" # absent

[[ -v count[beta] ]] && echo present     # test for a key

for k in "${!count[@]}"; do printf '%s=%s\n' "$k" "${count[$k]}"; done
# for large streams, awk does the same in one process: awk '{c[$1]++} END{...}'
L0.cloze:
{{c1::declare -A}} count        # without this line, count[foo] is an INDEXED array subscript
echo {{c2::"${!count[@]}"}}     # the keys
echo "${count[@]}"      # the values
[[ {{c3::-v}} count[beta] ]]    # test whether a key exists
for k in "${!count[@]}"; do ... done   # iteration order is {{c4::unspecified}}

concepts.L1: `declare -A name` creates a hash map with string keys. Subscripts are strings rather than arithmetic expressions, `${!m[@]}` lists the keys and `${m[@]}` the values, and `${#m[@]}` is the number of entries.
concepts.L2: Without the `declare -A`, bash treats the variable as an indexed array and evaluates the subscript arithmetically, so `m[foo]` and `m[bar]` both resolve to index 0 and silently overwrite each other.
concepts.L3: The silent-collision failure is worth seeing once: in an indexed array the subscript is an arithmetic expression, and an unset name in arithmetic context is 0, so every string key maps to slot 0 and the map appears to hold one entry - the last one written. `declare -A` before first use is not optional. Iteration order is hash order and undefined, so sort the keys when output stability matters. Associative arrays arrived in bash 4.0, which means macOS's system bash 3.2 lacks them entirely - the usual reason a Linux script fails on a Mac. For large streams, awk's arrays do the same job in one process.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`count[{a}]=1`
  `count[{b}]=2`
  `echo "${{#count[@]}}"`
The author expects 2. What is printed and why?
L4.answer: 1. Without a prior `declare -A count`, bash creates an indexed array and evaluates each subscript as an arithmetic expression. Unset names evaluate to 0 in that context, so both assignments write index 0 and the second overwrites the first. Adding `declare -A count` before the assignments gives the expected 2.
L4.explanation: The failure is silent and the array looks plausible, which is what makes it expensive. ShellCheck flags each bare subscript as SC2154 ('referenced but not assigned'), because it parses `apple` as an unset arithmetic variable - the habit of declaring the type first is the real defence.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`declare -A m`
  `m[a]={x}`
  `m[b]={y}`
  `echo "${{#m[@]}} ${{m[a]}} ${{m[missing]-none}}"`
What is printed?
L4.answer: For x=1,y=2: '2 1 none'. For x=10,y=20: '2 10 none'. Two entries, the value under key a, and the default because key 'missing' is absent.
L4.explanation: The `${m[k]-default}` form works on array elements exactly as it does on scalars, which makes it the idiomatic way to accumulate counts: m[`$k`]=`$(( ${m[$k]:-0} + 1 ))` needs no separate existence check.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`declare -A m`
`m[{k1}]={v1}`
`m[{k2}]={v2}`
`unset "m[{k1}]"`
How many keys does m have now? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: 1. unset "m[key]" deletes exactly that key-value pair; the untouched key survives, so the array holds one entry no matter which two keys or values were used.
L4.explanation: unset needs the fully-qualified element reference, m[key] (best quoted) - not the bare array name - unset m with no subscript would instead destroy the whole array, which is a different and much more common mistake.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`declare -A m=( [{k1}]={v1} [{k2}]={v2} [{k1}]={v3} )`
How many keys does m have after this single compound assignment? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: 2. The parenthesised initializer runs the assignments left to right exactly like separate m[key]=value statements: the second occurrence of a repeated key simply overwrites the first, so 2 distinct keys remain regardless of how many key-value pairs were listed.
L4.explanation: declare -A m=( [k]=v ... ) is sugar for a sequence of ordinary subscript assignments, not a set literal - bash never rejects or merges a repeated key, so only the last value written under it survives, same as anywhere else in the script.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`declare -A m`
`m[{k}]=""`   the value is deliberately the empty string
`[[ -v m[{k}] ]] && echo present || echo absent`   test A: is the key present
Separately, test B checks whether the value stored under key {k} is a non-empty string, printing present or absent the same way.
What does test A print, what does test B print, and why do the two disagree?
L4.answer: Test A prints present; test B prints absent. -v m[key] asks only whether the key exists in the array, and it does - it was explicitly set, just to an empty string. The non-empty-string test treats an empty string as false, which conflates 'key absent' with 'key present but empty'. Use -v when presence itself is the question.
L4.explanation: This is the general bash presence-versus-truthiness confusion applied to array elements: -v tests whether the variable or element was ever assigned, never whether its value is non-empty, zero, or otherwise falsy-looking.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`unset counts`
`counts[{k1}]=1`
`counts[{k2}]=1`
Neither statement is preceded by declare -A, and {k1} and {k2} are ordinary alphabetic words. How many entries does counts end up with, and would the answer differ if the keys were the digit strings 7 and 42 instead? Explain why.
L4.answer: One entry, not two. Without declare -A, counts is an indexed array and each subscript is evaluated as an arithmetic expression; an unset name like cat or dog evaluates to 0 in that context, so both statements write index 0 and the second overwrites the first. With the digit-string keys 7 and 42 the outcome differs: a numeral in arithmetic context evaluates to itself, so counts[7] and counts[42] are genuinely distinct indices and both entries survive. The bug is invisible exactly when test data happens to use numbers.
L4.explanation: This is why a hand-rolled counting loop (the same job as sort | uniq -c in the counting idiom, done inside bash instead of piped text tools) can work fine on numeric IDs during testing and then silently lose data on the first word-shaped key; the fix is the same: declare -A before first use.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to count occurrences of each distinct value in a {n}-line log file and print the results. Three ways to do it: build the histogram in a bash while-read loop into a declare -A array, build it in a single awk program using its built-in associative arrays, or run sort then uniq -c on the piped text. Which would you choose for a {n}-line file, and why?
L4.answer: For a small file any of the three works, and sort | uniq -c is the simplest to reach for since it needs no scripting beyond piping two text tools together. For a five-million-line file a bash while-read loop is the wrong choice: testing and updating an associative-array element on every line pays bash's per-line interpreter overhead with no compensating benefit, and that dominates the runtime. awk reads the file once, updates its own associative array natively in a single process, and is the standard choice at this scale. sort | uniq -c also works but pays an O(n log n) sort first, so awk's single O(n) pass is the more efficient of the two for pure counting, though sort | uniq -c stays simpler when the input is already expected to be small or already sorted.
L4.explanation: The concept to internalise is where the cost lives: a bash loop pays per-line interpreter and subshell overhead that dwarfs the actual work, while awk and the coreutils pipeline do the looping in C. Reach for declare -A inside bash for small, already-in-memory collections, not as a general counting engine at scale.

L0.body:
grep -r 'TODO' src/          # recursive
grep -i 'error' app.log      # case-insensitive
grep -v '^#' conf           # invert: everything that is NOT a comment
grep -c 'GET' access.log    # count matching LINES (not matches)
grep -l 'panic' *.log       # just the filenames
grep -o '[0-9]\+' f         # print only the matched part, one per line

grep -F 'a.c' f             # literal: the dot is a dot
grep    'a.c' f             # BRE: the dot is any character
grep -E '(cat|dog)s?' f     # extended regex
grep -P '(?<=id=)\d+' f     # PCRE: lookbehind, \d
L0.cloze:
grep {{c1::-o}} '[0-9]\+' f     # print only the matched text, not the whole line
grep {{c2::-c}} 'GET' access.log  # count matching LINES
grep {{c3::-F}} 'a.c' f          # treat the pattern as a literal string
grep {{c4::-P}} '(?<=id=)\d+' f  # the only flavour with lookbehind

concepts.L1: `-r` recursive, `-i` case-insensitive, `-v` invert, `-c` count, `-l` filenames only, `-o` matched part only, `-A/-B/-C` context, `-E` extended regex, `-F` fixed strings, `-P` PCRE.
concepts.L2: `grep -F` is dramatically faster for literal strings because it skips regex compilation and uses Aho-Corasick. On a large log with a literal search term it's routinely several times faster, and nobody uses it.
concepts.L3: `-c` counts matching LINES, not matches: a line with the pattern three times still counts once, so `grep -c` and `grep -o | wc -l` disagree and only the second counts occurrences. For one literal pattern, `-F` is fast because GNU grep skips regex compilation and runs Boyer-Moore, skipping most of the buffer per comparison; with several literals (repeated `-e`, or `-f patternfile`) it builds a multi-pattern automaton instead. Either way, `-F` is right whenever the pattern is data, not literal text you wrote - an unescaped `.` or `*` in user input is a regex injection, the same bug class as an unescaped quote in SQL. `-r` recurses without following symlinks met along the way, `-R` follows them too, and `-q` stops at the first hit, testing cheaply inside `if` rather than scanning fully. Passing matched names on safely needs `-Z` with `xargs -0`, in find and xargs as an execution engine.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A file contains exactly one line: `{line}`. What do these print?
  A: grep -c 'a' f
  B: grep -o 'a' f | wc -l
L4.answer: For the line 'a b a b a': A (grep -c 'a' f) prints 1, B (grep -o 'a' f | wc -l) prints 3, because 'a' occurs three times but on only one line. For the line 'x-x-x': A prints 0 and B prints 0, because 'a' never occurs. -c always counts matching LINES, never occurrences; -o prints one line of output per match, so piping it to wc -l is what actually counts occurrences.
L4.explanation: This trips people building metrics from logs. If you want occurrences rather than lines, -o piped to wc -l is the honest way; if you want lines, -c is faster because it never formats output.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`read -r term`
  `grep "$term" /var/log/{f}`
A user enters a term containing regex metacharacters. Describe two failure modes and the one-flag fix.
L4.answer: First, wrong results: a term like 'a.c' matches 'abc', and '.*' matches every line, so the search silently lies. Second, denial of service: a catastrophically backtracking pattern such as '(a+)+b' can make a backtracking engine take exponential time - GNU grep's default engine is not backtracking, but grep -P is. The fix is grep -F "`$term`", which treats the input as a literal string.
L4.explanation: Treating user input as a regex is the same category of error as treating it as SQL or as shell. Use -F whenever the pattern is data, and note that -F is also the faster path, so there is no cost to being correct here.

L4.prompt_tpl: Three files: a.txt has one line 'ERROR disk full'. b.txt has one line 'INFO nothing to see'. c.txt has two lines, both 'ERROR disk full' and 'ERROR retrying'. What does `grep -c '{pat}' a.txt b.txt c.txt` print, one line per file?
L4.answer: For pattern ERROR: a.txt:1, b.txt:0, c.txt:2. For pattern INFO: a.txt:0, b.txt:1, c.txt:0. For pattern WARN: a.txt:0, b.txt:0, c.txt:0. grep -c prints one line per file even when a file has zero matches, unlike -l, which lists only the files that matched.
L4.explanation: This is the flag people mix up: -l lists only matching filenames, but -c prints a count for every file named on the command line, including a 0 for files with no match at all, which is what makes it useful for building a per-file table.

L4.prompt_tpl: A log file has {n} lines total, and {k} of those lines contain the string 'ERROR' (some of them more than once). What single number does `grep -c 'ERROR' file` print? Answer with that number.
L4.answer: grep -c counts matching lines, not occurrences and not total lines, so the answer is exactly k: for example 20 lines with 3 matching lines gives 3, and 100 lines with 12 matching lines gives 12, regardless of how many times ERROR appears within those lines.
L4.explanation: grep -c counts matching lines, not occurrences, and does no other arithmetic: it is exactly the number of lines containing at least one match. This is the base fact the later trap template (grep -c versus grep -o piped to wc -l) depends on.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file has one line: `{line}`. What exactly does `grep -o 'ab' f` print, each line of output in order, and how many lines is that?
L4.answer: For 'ababab': grep -o prints three lines, each just 'ab' (ab, then ab, then ab) - 3 lines. For 'grabbed a cab': it prints two lines, each 'ab' (from 'gr-ab-bed' and 'c-ab') - 2 lines. For 'no match here': it prints nothing - 0 lines, and the command exits with status 1.
L4.explanation: -o replaces each matched line with just the matched text, once per non-overlapping match, so a line with three occurrences becomes three lines of output. This is what makes grep -o piped to wc -l the way to count occurrences rather than matching lines.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script parses `grep -c '{pat}' "$f"` output as filename-then-count by splitting on the first colon. It passes testing, where a glob always matched several files, then breaks in production when the glob matches exactly one file. Which flag makes the output format consistent no matter how many files are searched?
L4.answer: -H, which forces grep to prefix the filename even when only one file is given
L4.explanation: grep only prefixes the filename when more than one file is given, or when -H is set; with exactly one file it drops the prefix, so filename:count split on the first colon returns one field instead of two and the parser silently misreads the count as the filename. -H makes the prefix unconditional, matching -c's usual multi-file shape.
options: -H, which forces grep to prefix the filename even when only one file is given
-h, which suppresses the filename prefix entirely
-l, which prints matching filenames instead of counts

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to delete every file under a directory tree whose contents match the literal string '{pat}', and filenames may contain spaces or newlines. Which pipeline is safe: `grep -rl '{pat}' . | xargs rm`, or `grep -rlZ '{pat}' . | xargs -0 rm`, and why?
L4.answer: grep -rlZ ... | xargs -0 rm, because -Z null-terminates each filename and xargs -0 splits on that null byte instead of whitespace or newlines
L4.explanation: grep -rl separates filenames with newlines, which xargs's default parser also treats as a word-splitting delimiter, so a filename with a space or an embedded newline gets torn into two arguments. -Z makes grep emit NUL bytes instead, and xargs -0 reads NUL-delimited input, so any byte except NUL is safe inside a filename. The same -0/-Z pairing works with find -print0, covered in find and xargs as an execution engine.
options: grep -rlZ ... | xargs -0 rm, because -Z null-terminates each filename and xargs -0 splits on that null byte instead of whitespace or newlines
grep -rl ... | xargs rm, because -l already lists one filename per line and xargs handles embedded newlines correctly by default
Neither is safe: xargs always re-splits on whitespace, so filenames with spaces must be renamed before this can work

L0.body:
sed 's/-/_/'   <<< 'a-b-c'    # a_b-c   first occurrence on each line
sed 's/-/_/g'  <<< 'a-b-c'    # a_b_c   every occurrence
sed 's|/usr|/opt|' <<< '/usr/local'   # any delimiter; | avoids escaping slashes
sed 's/l\+/[&]/' <<< 'hello'  # he[ll]o   & is the whole match
sed -E 's/(\w+) (\w+)/\2, \1/' <<< 'john smith'   # smith, john

sed -n '3,5p' f              # -n suppresses output; p prints the range
sed '2d' f                   # delete line 2
sed -n '5{p;q}' f            # print line 5 and stop reading
sed -i.bak 's/a/b/g' f       # in place, keeping f.bak (portable form)
L0.cloze:
sed 's/-/_/{{c1::g}}'  <<< 'a-b-c'   # a_b_c — without this flag only the FIRST match changes
sed 's/l\+/[{{c2::&}}]/' <<< 'hello'  # he[ll]o — this character means 'the whole match'
sed {{c3::-n}} '3,5p' f            # print only the selected lines
sed {{c4::-i.bak}} 's/a/b/g' f      # edit in place with a backup suffix — the portable form

concepts.L1: `s/pat/repl/flags` with `g` global and `I` case-insensitive. Address ranges `sed -n '10,20p'`. `-i` in place. `d` delete, `a`/`i` append/insert.
concepts.L2: `sed -i` behaves differently on GNU and BSD/macOS — BSD requires an explicit backup suffix argument. Scripts that work on Linux and fail on a Mac usually fail here.
concepts.L3: GNU `sed -i` takes an optional suffix attached to the flag; BSD and macOS `sed -i` require a separate argument, so `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` on a Mac consumes `s/a/b/` as the backup suffix and then treats `f` as the script. `sed -i.bak` works on both. GNU sed also accepts `\+`, `\?` and `\|` in BRE where BSD sed does not, so explicit `-E` is the safer default. `&` in a replacement is the whole match and needs `\&` to be literal. And sed reads line by line with no lazy quantifiers, so `s/<.*>/X/` on `<a><b>` eats both tags; `s/<[^>]*>/X/` is the standard workaround.

L4.prompt_tpl:
echo '<{tag1}><{tag2}>' | sed 's/<.*>/X/'
  echo '<{tag1}><{tag2}>' | sed 's/<[^>]*>/X/'
What are the two output lines?
L4.answer:
X
X<{tag2}>
L4.explanation: This is the single most common sed surprise and the reason 'parse HTML with sed' fails: greedy .* spans from the first '<' to the LAST '>' on the line, eating both tags, while the negated class [^>]* stops at the very next '>'. [^>]* is the standard substitute for a lazy .*?, which POSIX regex has no syntax for.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CI script runs `sed -i 's/{a}/{b}/g' config.yml` and works on the Linux runners but fails on the macOS runner with 'command c expects \ followed by text'. Explain and give a form that works on both.
L4.answer: BSD sed's -i requires an explicit backup-suffix argument, so it consumes 's/{a}/{b}/g' as that suffix, leaving config.yml to be parsed as the sed SCRIPT. Its first character 'c' is read as the change command, which needs a literal backslash before its replacement text — 'onfig.yml' is not that, hence 'command c expects \ followed by text'. Portable forms: sed -i.bak 's/.../.../g' config.yml (leaves a .bak behind, works on both), or write to a temp file and mv it over the original.
L4.explanation: The empty-suffix GNU form sed -i '' is not portable in the other direction either: GNU sed reads the empty string as the script. If a script must run on both, use the suffix form or avoid -i entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file has 25 lines, numbered 1 to 25, one number per line. Running `sed -n '{a},{b}p' file` prints how many lines? Answer with just the count.
L4.answer: The address range {a},{b} is inclusive on both ends, so the number of lines printed is b - a + 1.
L4.explanation: sed line ranges, like most Unix range syntax (awk, cut -f), are inclusive on both ends rather than half-open, so the count is (end - start + 1), not (end - start). Forgetting the +1 is the usual off-by-one here.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file contains three lines: 1, 2, 3, one number per line. What does `sed '2a\{text}' file` print, one line per output line?
L4.answer:
1
2
{text}
3
L4.explanation: The a command appends the given text as a new line immediately after the addressed line (here line 2); every other line, matched or not, still passes through unchanged and in order, so only one new line is inserted.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does `echo '{c} {c} {c} {c}' | sed 's/{c}/X/2'` print?
L4.answer: {c} X {c} {c}
L4.explanation: A trailing digit on s/pat/repl/N is an occurrence count: it rewrites only the Nth match on the line, not the first (the default with no flag) and not every match (that needs g). N and g combine as /Ng to mean 'from the Nth match onward'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file has three lines: apple, banana, cherry, one per line, in that order. What does `sed '/{w}/s//X/' file` print, and what does the empty pattern in `s//X/` mean here?
L4.answer: An empty regex inside s///  reuses the last regex that matched — here, the address /{w}/ that just matched. So the line containing {w} is rewritten to X and the other two lines pass through unchanged, giving the same three lines in order with only the {w} line replaced.
L4.explanation: s//repl/ with an empty pattern is a genuine idiom for not repeating a regex you just matched in an address, but it silently reuses whichever regex matched most recently anywhere earlier in the script — including inside an unrelated command — which is a common source of an s command that substitutes the wrong text.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need a `sed -E` one-liner that turns a URL like '{example}' into just its domain (drop the scheme and everything from the next slash onward). Derive the command using a capturing group, then explain why the capturing group needs `-E` (or escaped parentheses) here, connecting this to the distinction covered in "Regex flavours: BRE, ERE and PCRE".
L4.answer: sed -E 's#^[a-z]+://([^/]+).*#\1#'  — ([^/]+) captures every character up to (not including) the next /, and \1 in the replacement is a backreference to that captured group. In BRE, ( and ) are literal characters and must be escaped as \( \) to become a group; -E switches to ERE, where ( ) are already metacharacters and grouping is written bare — exactly the BRE/ERE split named in "Regex flavours: BRE, ERE and PCRE".
L4.explanation: Backreferences only work once you have escaped this correctly: BRE needs \( \) for a group and \1 for the backreference, ERE (and -E) needs bare ( ) for the group but still \1 for the backreference. Mixing the two conventions is the most common reason a sed capture-and-rewrite one-liner silently does nothing.

prereqs: Regex flavours: BRE, ERE and PCRE

L0.body:
# access.log:  10.0.0.1 GET /a 200 120

awk '{sum+=$5} END {print sum}' access.log            # total bytes
awk '$4==200 {sum+=$5} END {print sum}' access.log    # ...for 200s only
awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}' a.log | sort -rn   # top talkers
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd                      # field separator
awk 'NR==1 {next} {print NR, NF, $NF}' f              # skip a header row
awk 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} {$1=$1; print}' f                 # re-emit tab separated

# replaces:  grep X f | cut -d' ' -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
L0.cloze:
awk '{sum+=${{c1::5}}} END {print sum}' access.log    # sum the fifth field
awk '{c[$1]{{c2::++}}} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}'   # count by first field
awk {{c3::-F:}} '{print $1}' /etc/passwd            # set the input field separator
awk '{{c4::NR==1}} {next} {...}' f                    # skip the header line

concepts.L1: `awk '{sum+=$3} END {print sum}'`. Fields via `$1..$NF`, `NR` record number, `-F` separator, associative arrays, `BEGIN`/`END` blocks, pattern-action pairs.
concepts.L2: Most multi-stage `grep | cut | sort | uniq` pipelines are one awk invocation that's shorter, faster, and clearer. Learning awk properly — a genuine afternoon — replaces a large fraction of what people write shell scripts for.
concepts.L3: One awk pass beats a five-process pipeline on process count and on how much data gets sorted. `grep | cut | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` forks five processes: `sort` makes an $O(n \log n)$ pass over every record so `uniq -c` can collapse runs into $k$ distinct keys, then a second sort orders only those $k$ lines. awk instead forks once, makes a single $O(n)$ pass, and accumulates the $k$ keys in a hash - no sort needed to group. On a multi-gigabyte log with low key cardinality that is minutes versus seconds; the two approaches converge only as $k$ approaches $n$. The model is small: a program is `pattern { action }` pairs; awk reads one record at a time, splits it on FS into `$1..$NF`, and runs every pair whose pattern matches - why associative arrays make counting one line. The same fork cost is why `find | xargs` batches arguments into few invocations, not one process per file.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A file has these lines:
  a 1
  b 2
  a 3
What does `awk '{{s[$1]+=${n}}} END {{for (k in s) print k, s[k]}}' f | sort` print?
L4.answer: Two lines: 'a 4' and 'b 2'.
L4.explanation: Sums are accumulated in an associative array keyed by the first field, in a single pass. The pipe to sort is necessary because for-in iteration order over an awk array is unspecified and differs between mawk, gawk and BusyBox awk.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`printf 'x y z\n' | awk -v OFS={sep} '{{print $1,$2,$3}}'`
  `printf 'x y z\n' | awk -v OFS={sep} '{{ print }}'`
  `printf 'x y z\n' | awk -v OFS={sep} '{{$1=$1; print}}'`
What are the three lines?
L4.answer: With OFS set to '{sep}': line 1 is 'x{sep}y{sep}z' (print joins the comma-listed fields with OFS); line 2 is 'x y z' unchanged (a bare print emits $0, which OFS never touches); line 3 is 'x{sep}y{sep}z' again (the no-op $1=$1 forces $0 to be rebuilt, and the rebuild uses OFS).
L4.explanation: OFS is used when awk joins a comma-separated print list, and when it rebuilds `$0` - but `$0` is only rebuilt if a field is assigned. A bare `print` emits the untouched original record, which is why the no-op assignment `$1`=`$1` is the standard idiom for re-separating a line.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n} GB log needs the top ten client IPs by request count. Compare `awk '{{c[$1]++}} END{{...}}' | sort -rn | head` with `cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` on time and memory.
L4.answer: awk makes one linear pass over the file and sorts only the distinct IPs at the end, so its memory is proportional to the number of unique keys and its time is dominated by reading the file. The cut pipeline sorts every record - two full external sorts of n lines, spilling to disk - and forks four extra processes. For a log with few unique IPs relative to its size, awk is faster by a large margin; only when the key cardinality approaches the record count do they converge.
L4.explanation: The general rule: sorting to group is O(n log n) in the number of records; hashing to group is O(n) in records and O(k) in memory for k distinct keys. Reach for sort|uniq -c when k is close to n or the data does not fit in memory.

L4.prompt_tpl: In `awk '$2 > {n}' file`, with no action after the pattern, what decides whether a line gets printed?
L4.answer: Whether the value of the second field, compared numerically, is greater than {n}
L4.explanation: A bare pattern with no action block is a full awk program on its own: when the pattern is true for a record, awk falls back to the implicit default action, `print $0`. Here the pattern is a numeric comparison on field two, not on the raw line or on NF.
options: Whether the value of the second field, compared numerically, is greater than {n}
Whether the entire line, compared as text, is greater than {n}
Whether the line contains more than {n} fields

L4.prompt_tpl: In awk, what must you do before using a variable like count or an array like seen for the first time?
L4.answer: Nothing - a variable or array element springs into existence on first use, starting at numeric 0 and empty string
L4.explanation: awk has no declarations. An unset variable reads as 0 in numeric context and "" in string context, and an array key that has never been assigned is simply absent from `in` until you touch it - which is exactly what lets `c[$1]++` count without any setup line.
options: Declare its type first, with a keyword such as int or array
Nothing - a variable or array element springs into existence on first use, starting at numeric 0 and empty string
Initialize every variable inside a DECLARE block placed before BEGIN

L4.prompt_tpl: A file `nums` has four lines, in order: `10`, `10.0`, one leading space then `10`, and `abc`. What does `awk '$1 == "10"'` print, and how does that differ from what `awk '$1 == 10'` prints on the same file?
L4.answer: `$1 == "10"` compares a field against a string constant, so it is a string comparison: it prints '10' and the leading-space line (its field value trims to the string "10"), two lines - '10.0' and 'abc' are excluded. `$1 == 10` compares against a bare numeric constant, so every field that looks like a number is converted and compared numerically: it prints '10', '10.0', and the leading-space line, three lines - only 'abc' is excluded. Field splitting trims the leading space off $1 for the comparison, but $0 (what gets printed) still has it.
L4.explanation: POSIX says a comparison is numeric only if both sides are numeric, or one side is numeric and the other is a numeric string; a quoted constant like "10" is a string, not numeric, so it forces a string comparison even against a field that looks like a number. This is the classic awk trap behind bugs like `if ($status == "200")` silently failing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague wrote `awk '$1=1' file` where every line of file has its two fields separated by two spaces, meaning to print only the lines whose first field is 1. Instead every line comes back single-spaced with the first field always 1 - for example a line that was `10` then two spaces then `x` becomes `1 x`. What is the bug, and what is the one-character fix?
L4.answer: The bug is `=` where `==` was meant: `$1=1` assigns 1 to the first field on every record instead of comparing it. An assignment's value is 1 (truthy), so the implicit pattern is true for every line and awk runs the default action, `print $0` - but assigning to a field also forces `$0` to be rebuilt from the fields using OFS, which is why the double space collapsed to one. The fix is `awk '$1==1' file`.
L4.explanation: This is one of the best-known awk typos: `=` (assignment, always true, and it mutates the record) versus `==` (comparison). Any field assignment - not just to `$1` - triggers a full `$0` rebuild joined by OFS, so it silently reformats spacing even on lines the pattern was never meant to touch.

prereqs: numeracy:Sigma notation: a sum written as a loop
