L0.body:
sort -n         # numeric: 2 9 10 100     (lexical gives 10 100 2 9)
sort -r         # reverse
sort -u         # unique, no counts
sort -t, -k2,2n f     # field 2 only, numeric, comma separated
sort -k2 f            # field 2 TO END OF LINE — usually not what you meant
sort -s -k2,2n  # stable: preserve input order within equal keys

uniq -c         # prefix each group with its count — INPUT MUST BE SORTED
uniq -d         # only lines that repeat
uniq -u         # only lines that never repeat

LC_ALL=C sort   # byte order, and faster: what scripts silently assume
L0.cloze:
sort {{c1::-n}}            # numeric rather than lexical order
sort -t, {{c2::-k2,2}}n f     # restrict the key to field 2 ONLY (the ,2 matters)
sort {{c3::-s}} -k2,2n     # stable — equal keys keep their input order
{{c4::LC_ALL=C}} sort      # byte order rather than locale collation

concepts.L1: `sort -k2,2 -n -r -u`, `-t` field separator, `-h` human-readable sizes. `uniq -c` counts but requires sorted input; `uniq -d` duplicates only.
concepts.L2: `sort -u` and `sort | uniq` differ: `uniq -c` gives counts, `sort -u` doesn't. And `sort` respects the locale — `LC_ALL=C sort` is both faster and gives byte order, which is what you usually want and what scripts silently depend on.
concepts.L3: `-k2` means 'from the start of field 2 to the end of the line', so `sort -k2` on `x 2 zz` and `y 2 aa` puts `y` first, while `sort -k2,2` ties on the key and falls back to comparing whole lines, putting `x` first. That last-resort comparison is also why `sort -k2,2n` is not stable - `-s` disables it. `uniq` only ever compares adjacent lines, which is why it needs sorted input and why `sort -u` is faster than `sort | uniq` but cannot produce counts. Locale matters too: UTF-8 collation ignores punctuation and case in ways that break `join` and `comm`, so `LC_ALL=C` is both byte order and measurably faster.

L4.prompt_tpl:
printf 'x 2 zz
y 2 aa
' | sort -k2
  printf 'x 2 zz
y 2 aa
' | sort -k2,2
What is the first line of each output?
L4.answer: First command: 'y 2 aa'. Second command: 'x 2 zz'.
L4.explanation: -k2 extends the key to the end of the line, so it compares '2 zz' against '2 aa' and aa sorts first. -k2,2 restricts the key to the single field '2', the keys tie, and sort falls back to comparing the entire lines, where x precedes y.

L4.answer: 'a {n}|b {n}|' then 'b {n}|a {n}|'
L4.explanation: The keys are equal, so the default sort uses the last-resort whole-line comparison and reorders the records. -s disables that fallback, making the sort stable and preserving input order - which is what you want when a previous stage already ordered the data.

L4.prompt_tpl:
printf '2
9
10
100
' | sort
What is the first line of the output (no flags, so this is plain lexical order)?
L4.explanation: Default sort compares lines byte-by-byte like strings: the character '1' is less than '2' and '9', so both 10 and 100 sort ahead of 2 and 9. Between 10 and 100, '10' is a prefix of '100' and a prefix sorts first, giving the order 10, 100, 2, 9. `sort -n` instead gives 2, 9, 10, 100.

L4.prompt_tpl:
printf 'a
a
b
' | uniq -c
This input is already sorted. What does the command print?
L4.answer: '      2 a' then '      1 b'
L4.explanation: uniq -c collapses each run of identical adjacent lines into one line prefixed with the run's count, right-justified. The two 'a' lines are adjacent so they collapse to a count of 2; the single 'b' line stays a count of 1.

L4.prompt_tpl:
printf 'a
b
a
' | uniq -c
This input is NOT sorted. Does uniq -c print one line, two lines, or three lines, and is any count greater than 1?
L4.answer: Three lines, and every count is 1 - no count is greater than 1.
L4.explanation: uniq only ever compares each line to the one immediately before it. The two 'a' lines here are not adjacent, so they are counted as two separate groups of size 1 rather than one group of size 2. A real count of 2 only appears once the input is grouped first, e.g. `sort | uniq -c`.

L4.prompt_tpl:
printf 'a
a
b
' | uniq -d
printf 'a
a
b
' | uniq -u
What does each command print?
L4.answer: uniq -d prints 'a' (the only line that repeats, shown once). uniq -u prints 'b' (the only line that never repeats).
L4.explanation: -d keeps one copy of each run that has a duplicate and drops every run of length one; -u does the opposite, keeping only runs of length one and dropping every run that repeats. Both still require sorted input first, for the same reason as uniq -c: uniq only ever compares adjacent lines.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script sorts a log by response time, field 3, with `sort -k3 access.log`. Whenever two lines have the same response time, the URL field (later in the line) ends up deciding the order, which is not what the author wanted. What is the minimal fix to the sort invocation, and why does the bug happen?
L4.answer: Use `sort -k3,3` (add `n` for numeric response times: `-k3,3n`) instead of `-k3`. `-k POS1` with no POS2 makes the key run from field 3 to the end of the line, not just field 3, so ties on the response time fall through to comparing the rest of the line, including the URL.
L4.explanation: `-k POS1[,POS2]` without POS2 extends the key from POS1 to the end of the line - the single most common sort mistake. Restricting it to `-k3,3` isolates exactly field 3, so ties are resolved by sort's own last-resort whole-line comparison instead of being silently dominated by it (add `-s` if even that fallback is unwanted).

L4.prompt_tpl: A pipeline runs plain `sort` (no LC_ALL set) on two files under a UTF-8 locale, then feeds them to `join` on a shared key. join warns that one file is not sorted, even though sort produced it and it looks alphabetical by eye. Under most UTF-8 locales, punctuation is ignored when comparing lines. Explain why this can make join reject sort's own output, and give the one-line fix.
L4.answer: Locale collation (LC_COLLATE) can order lines by rules other than raw byte value - e.g. ignoring punctuation - so two lines that differ only in punctuation compare as near-ties under that locale even though the file 'looks' alphabetically sorted. join and comm expect the traditional byte-value order and do not replicate sort's locale logic, so they can see the very same file as unsorted. Fix: run both `sort` and `join` under `LC_ALL=C`, so both use byte order and agree.
L4.explanation: This is why `LC_ALL=C sort` is the standard opener of any pipeline that feeds `join` or `comm`: the same file can be 'sorted' under one locale's collation and 'unsorted' under a program that compares by raw bytes, and `LC_ALL=C` is the one setting both sort and join honour identically.

L0.body:
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#      3 10.0.0.1
#      2 10.0.0.2
#      1 10.0.0.3

# read it as: extract key -> group -> count -> rank -> truncate

# the one-pass version, for large inputs:
awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}' access.log | sort -rn | head

# count status codes instead:
awk '{c[$4]++} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}' access.log | sort -rn
# awk '{c[$0]++}' counts whole lines rather than the first field
L0.cloze:
cut -d' ' -f1 f | {{c1::sort}} | uniq {{c2::-c}} | sort {{c3::-rn}} | head
# the one-pass alternative, one process instead of four:
awk '{ {{c4::c[$1]++}} } END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}' f | sort -rn | head

concepts.L1: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` — the frequency count. Probably the most-used analysis pipeline in existence.
concepts.L2: For large inputs `awk '{c[$0]++} END {for(k in c) print c[k], k}'` is one pass instead of two sorts, and on a multi-gigabyte log that's minutes versus seconds.
concepts.L3: Every stage earns its place. `sort` exists only because `uniq` compares adjacent lines; without it the counts are per-run rather than per-value, and the result is silently wrong rather than empty. `uniq -c` emits a right-padded count before the value, which is why the second sort needs `-n` - lexically `10` sorts before `2` - and `-r` puts the largest first so `head` truncates the tail. The awk rewrite replaces group-by-sorting with group-by-hashing: one linear pass, memory proportional to the distinct keys, one process instead of four. Keep the pipeline for interactive work; switch to awk when the file is large or the script runs often.

L4.answer: The first prints three groups of one each (1 x, 1 y, 1 x) because the two x lines are not adjacent. The second prints '2 x' and '1 y' after sorting brings the duplicates together.
L4.explanation: uniq is a streaming filter with a one-line memory. Forgetting the sort does not error - it produces plausible-looking counts that are wrong, which is the worst kind of bug in an analysis pipeline.

L4.prompt_tpl: A log has {n} lines and {k} distinct values in the counted field. State the time complexity in comparisons and the peak memory for (A) the sort|uniq -c pipeline and (B) the awk one-pass version.
L4.answer: A: $O(n \log n)$ comparisons, and peak memory $O(n)$ (external sort spills to disk, so disk rather than RAM, but proportional to n). B: $O(n)$ hash operations, peak memory $O(k)$. With n far larger than k, B wins on both axes; when k approaches n, B's memory becomes $O(n)$ and the external sort is the safer choice.
L4.explanation: This is the whole reason to learn awk's associative arrays. The crossover is about key cardinality, not file size: a 100 GB log with 200 distinct status codes is trivial for awk and expensive for sort.

L4.prompt_tpl: A log has {ka} lines whose value is 'A' and {kb} lines whose value is 'B', and no other values. Piping it through `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1` prints exactly one line. Answer with the integer count on that line.
L4.answer: The pipeline ranks by count descending and keeps only the top line, so the printed count is $\max(k_a, k_b)$: for ka=20 it is 20, for ka=30 it is 30, for ka=50 it is 50 (kb is always the smaller one here by construction).
L4.explanation: sort -rn ranks uniq -c's lines by the leading count field, largest first, and head -1 keeps just that one line. Writing the answer as max(ka, kb) rather than always 'ka' keeps it correct even if the two counts were swapped.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which single flag combination, given to the second `sort` right after `uniq -c`, ranks its lines by count with the largest count first?
L4.answer: -rn
L4.explanation: -n makes sort compare the count field numerically instead of lexically, so '9' sorts before '10'; -r reverses ascending order into descending. Either flag alone gets only half of what ranking-by-count-descending needs; -rn combines both.
options: -rn
-r
-n

L4.prompt_tpl: In `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`, which single command actually does the counting?
L4.answer: uniq -c
L4.explanation: The first sort only brings identical lines together so uniq -c can see duplicates as adjacent; head only truncates the ranked list at the end. uniq -c is the one stage that turns runs of repeated lines into a count.
options: uniq -c
the first sort
head

L4.prompt_tpl: A log's method field is sometimes uppercase and sometimes lowercase but means the same thing either way, e.g. 'GET' and 'get'. Piped through `sort | uniq -c`, are these two spellings counted together or kept as two separate lines? Why?
L4.answer: Kept separate: uniq compares lines byte-for-byte with no case folding, so 'GET' and 'get' are different lines to it, and the output shows two lines, e.g. '2 GET' and '1 get', instead of one combined count of 3. Normalising case first - e.g. with `tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'` or awk's tolower() - is required before counting if you want them merged.
L4.explanation: The counting idiom is purely textual: uniq -c has no notion of 'the same value spelled differently'. Any byte-level variation - case, trailing whitespace, a stray tab versus a space - silently creates an extra group instead of erroring, which is exactly the kind of bug this idiom hides well.

L4.prompt_tpl: The one-pass idiom counts by a single field with `c[$1]++`. Explain how to extend it to count by two fields together, say $1 and $4, instead of one, and why `sort -rn | head` afterward still needs no change. Name the Whetstone concept that covers the array mechanism this relies on.
L4.answer: Use a composite key, e.g. `c[$1,$4]++` - awk joins multiple subscripts with its internal SUBSEP character, so each distinct ($1,$4) pair gets its own counter; equivalently write it out as `c[$1"\t"$4]++` with an explicit separator that cannot occur in either field. The END loop still emits one 'count key' line per distinct combination, and `sort -rn | head` only ever looks at the leading number, so it needs no change regardless of what the key contains. The mechanism is awk's associative arrays, covered in 'awk: BEGIN, END and associative arrays'.
L4.explanation: This is the generalisation that makes the idiom useful beyond single-column counts - grouping by (status, path) or (user, action) is the same trick with a wider key. The forward connection is deliberate: this concept teaches the one-key case, the named awk concept teaches the general array mechanism underneath it.

L0.body:
jq '.items[] | select(.status=="error") | .id' data.json    # 2 3
jq -r '.items[].status' data.json | sort -u                  # error ok
jq '[.items[].n] | add' data.json                            # 23
jq -r '.items[] | [.id,.status] | @tsv' data.json   # tab separated, for cut/awk
jq -r '.a.missing // "none"' data.json    # default for null/false
jq -s 'add' <<< $'1\n2\n3'                # 6 — slurp a stream into one array

jq '.x' f    # "ok"   quoted JSON string
jq -r '.x' f # ok     raw, ready for the shell
# for shell use always -r:  v=$(jq -r '.x' f)  — otherwise you get JSON quotes
L0.cloze:
jq '.items[] | {{c1::select}}(.status=="error") | .id'    # filter, then project
jq {{c2::-r}} '.items[].status'                          # raw output, no JSON quotes
jq -r '.items[] | [.id,.status] | {{c3::@tsv}}'           # emit columns for cut/awk
jq -r '.a.missing {{c4:://}} "none"'                     # supply a default for null

concepts.L1: `jq '.items[] | select(.status=="error") | .id'`. Filters, pipes, `-r` raw output, `-c` compact, `map`, `group_by`, `to_entries`.
concepts.L2: jq is the correct tool for JSON and grep is not — JSON has no line structure and grepping it produces bugs that appear only when the formatting changes. `jq -r` for shell-consumable output is the flag to internalize.
concepts.L3: JSON has no line structure, so every grep-based approach depends on the producer's formatting: re-serialise the document with different indentation, or let a value contain a newline, and the grep breaks by matching a different number of lines. jq parses the document, so its filters are structural. The model that unlocks it is that a jq program is a filter from a stream of values to a stream of values - `|` composes filters, `.items[]` emits one value per element rather than an array, and `[ ... ]` collects a stream back into one. That is why `[.items[].n] | add` works and `.items[].n | add` does not. `-r` strips JSON quoting for shell consumption.

L4.prompt_tpl:
For the document {{"items":[{{"n":{a}}},{{"n":{b}}}]}}, what do these print?
  A: jq '[.items[].n] | add'
  B: jq -r '.items[0].missing // "none"'
L4.answer: A prints the sum (12 for 5 and 7; 18 for 7 and 11). B prints none.
L4.explanation: The brackets collect the stream of n values into a single array so that add has something to fold. The // operator supplies its right-hand side when the left is null or false, which is the idiomatic default for an absent key.

L4.prompt_tpl: A deploy script extracts a value with `grep '"{key}"' cfg.json | cut -d'"' -f4`. Give two inputs that make it return the wrong value, and the jq replacement.
L4.answer: First, a value containing an escaped quote, such as "image": "a\"b" - the cut counts quote characters and returns a truncated value. Second, the same key appearing inside a nested object elsewhere in the file, or the file being re-serialised onto one line, which makes the grep match a different line or all of them. Replacement: jq -r '.image' cfg.json, or jq -r '.spec.image' for the specific path.
L4.explanation: The general point: text tools operate on a serialisation, jq operates on the document. Any grep of JSON is a bet that the producer will never change its whitespace, key order, or escaping - a bet that eventually loses in production.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file readings.json holds a JSON object with one field, readings, whose value is a JSON array containing the three numbers {r1}, {r2} and {r3}. What number does the command jq '(.readings | add) / (.readings | length)' readings.json print?
L4.answer: The arithmetic mean of the three numbers. r1=10,r2=20,r3=30 -> 20. r1=5,r2=15,r3=25 -> 15. r1=12,r2=18,r3=24 -> 18. add sums the array, length counts its elements, and jq divides as floating point.
L4.explanation: jq's add sums an array's elements and length counts them, so dividing gives the arithmetic mean, computed as ordinary floating-point division - exactly (r1+r2+r3)/3 for any three numbers under the readings key, whatever their values.

L4.prompt_tpl: A shell pipeline feeds {m} separate top-level JSON number values, one per line, into jq -s 'length' on stdin. How many elements does the command report?
L4.answer: m itself: 4 values in gives 4, 6 values in gives 6, 9 values in gives 9, regardless of the numbers' signs or magnitudes.
L4.explanation: Without -s, jq runs the filter once per top-level value in the stream, and length on a bare number returns its absolute value - not a count. -s (slurp) first collects every value in the stream into one JSON array, so length then counts array elements: exactly m of them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A JSON field named {field} can legitimately hold the boolean false. A script reads it with jq -r '.{field} // "{default}"'. When {field} is actually false, what does the command print?
L4.answer: The fallback string on the right of //, silently masking the real false
L4.explanation: jq's // treats both null and false as its left operand as "absent" and falls through to the right-hand side, unlike most languages' null-coalescing operators which check only for null. A field that is meaningfully false is therefore indistinguishable from a missing one under //; use has("field") or an explicit == null check when false is a real, distinct value.
options: The fallback string on the right of //, silently masking the real false
The word false, exactly as stored
An error, because // only accepts null on its left

L4.prompt_tpl: A log file holds one JSON object per line (JSON Lines), each with a field named {field}. Without ever holding the whole file as one array in memory, derive a jq command that counts how many lines have {field} equal to the string {value}, then say in one sentence why passing -s (slurp) first would be worse for a large file.
L4.answer: jq -c 'select(.level == "error")' file.ndjson | wc -l (substituting the actual field and value asked for). jq's default mode already treats a whitespace-separated sequence of top-level JSON values as a stream, so no -s is needed; -c prints one compact line per matching object so wc -l counts them. An equivalent single-jq form is jq -n '[inputs | select(.level=="error")] | length' file.ndjson. -s would first slurp the entire file into one JSON array in memory before filtering, which defeats streaming and can exhaust memory on a large file, whereas the native stream mode discards each object right after it is tested.
L4.explanation: jq's ordinary (non -s) mode is already a streaming pipeline over the input's top-level values, which is exactly why JSON Lines files need no special handling; -s throws that property away by materialising every value into one array before any filter runs, the opposite of what a large file needs.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CI script runs curl against an authentication endpoint and gets back a JSON response body with a field named {field} holding a short-lived credential as a plain string. The script must pass that value as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of a second curl call. Using command substitution and jq -r, write the two-line shell snippet, and say in one sentence why -r matters here rather than plain jq.
L4.answer: TOKEN=$(curl -s https://api.example.com/login -d '...' | jq -r '.token') then curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.example.com/data (substitute the field name actually asked for in place of token). -r matters because without it jq prints the string wrapped in its own JSON double quotes, e.g. "abc123" instead of abc123; those quote characters would then sit literally inside the header value, producing a malformed Authorization: Bearer "abc123" header that the server rejects.
L4.explanation: jq's default output is JSON, so a string result is printed with its surrounding double quotes; -r (raw output) strips them so the value drops cleanly into a shell variable and then into plain text like an HTTP header, the same -r-for-shell-consumption point this concept's own L1 already makes.

L0.body:
rg TODO                 # recursive by default, skips .gitignored files, parallel
rg -t py TODO           # only Python files
rg --no-ignore TODO     # include ignored files
rg -F 'a.c'             # literal
# rg is case-sensitive by default; -S makes it smart-case (lowercase pattern -> insensitive, mixed -> sensitive)

fd '\.log$' /var        # find, with sane defaults
fzf                     # interactive fuzzy filter over any stdin

grep -rn TODO .         # the version that exists on every server you will ssh into
# fzf is a filter, not a search tool:  sel=$(ls | fzf)  selects one line
L0.cloze:
{{c1::rg}} TODO                # recursive by default and respects .gitignore
rg {{c2::--no-ignore}} TODO    # ...unless you ask for the ignored files too
{{c3::fzf}}                    # interactive fuzzy filter over anything on stdin
grep {{c4::-rn}} TODO .        # the equivalent that is installed everywhere

concepts.L1: `ripgrep` (rg) for search, `fd` for find, `bat` for cat, `delta` for diffs, `fzf` for fuzzy selection, `sd` for sed.
concepts.L2: ripgrep is genuinely much faster and respects .gitignore by default. But learn the classic tools first — they're on every server you'll ever ssh into, and the modern ones are on your laptop only.
concepts.L3: ripgrep's speed comes from three separate things, and knowing which is which stops you expecting the same from a `grep` alias. It uses a finite-automata regex engine with no backtracking, so pathological patterns stay linear. It walks directories in parallel and applies `.gitignore` during the walk, so it never opens the files you did not want - on a repo with a large `node_modules` that alone is most of the win. And it memory-maps files and uses SIMD substring search for a pattern's literal prefix. The gitignore default is its one surprise: `rg` will not match inside an ignored file, which is right for source and wrong when debugging a build artefact.

L4.prompt_tpl: A repository has {n} matches for TODO in tracked files and {m} more inside a directory listed in .gitignore. What does `rg -c TODO | wc -l` report versus `grep -rc TODO . | wc -l`, and which flag reconciles them?
L4.answer: rg reports only the tracked files (its count of files containing matches excludes everything .gitignore covers), while grep -r descends into the ignored directory and reports those files too. `rg --no-ignore` reconciles the gap; -uu (two -u/--unrestricted flags) does the same and also un-hides dotfiles, though binary files are still skipped until a third -u (-uuu).
L4.explanation: Neither default is wrong; they answer different questions. The failure is silent - you conclude a string does not appear anywhere when it appears in a vendored dependency - so make --no-ignore a reflex when a search comes back empty and you expected a hit.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have ssh access to a production host with a minimal base image and need to find every line containing a literal IP address in {f}. What do you run?
L4.answer: grep -F on the literal, or grep -E with a pattern - because ripgrep, fd and bat are not installed on a stock server image and installing tools on a production host during an incident is not an option.
L4.explanation: The modern tools are strictly better on your laptop and absent everywhere else. Learning the classic flags is not nostalgia; it is the difference between diagnosing an incident and not.
options: grep -F on the literal, or grep -E with a pattern
Install ripgrep first, then rg
scp the log to your laptop and use rg there

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `fd '{pattern}'` in a git repository. Like rg, fd skips dotfiles and anything covered by .gitignore by default. Which single flag makes fd also search hidden (dotfile) entries, without changing how it treats .gitignore?
L4.answer: -H (--hidden)
L4.explanation: -H/--hidden adds hidden dotfile entries to the results without touching ignore-file behaviour. -I/--no-ignore does the opposite job (stop respecting .gitignore) and leaves hidden files excluded. -a only changes whether printed paths are absolute or relative.
options: -H (--hidden)
-I (--no-ignore)
-a (--absolute-path)

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `bat {file}` at an interactive terminal and it opens in a pager (less) with line numbers and a git-diff gutter. You then run the exact same command as `bat {file} | wc -l`. What does bat do differently the second time, and why?
L4.answer: bat detects that stdout is no longer a terminal (it is piped into wc -l) and falls back to behaving like plain cat: no pager is invoked, so the raw file text streams straight through with no line-wrapping or interactive controls. --paging defaults to auto, which only pages when output is going to an interactive terminal.
L4.explanation: bat's --paging (and --color) default to 'auto', meaning 'only when stdout is a terminal'. That is why the identical command behaves like a fancy pager interactively and like plain cat once redirected or piped, which is exactly what makes bat safe to drop into a script in place of cat.

L4.prompt_tpl: In sed you replace every literal dot with an underscore in {file} using sed's s/\./_/g syntax, where the backslash is required because a bare dot means 'any character' in sed's regex. Using sd instead of sed for the same job, what do you type, is the dot still special, and what does sd do differently from sed the moment you give it a file argument?
L4.answer: sd '\.' '_' file - the dot is still special, because sd matches with the same kind of regex sed uses by default. What sd removes is sed's s/find/replace/flags delimiter syntax and its escaping headaches, not regex metacharacter meaning; to match a dot with zero regex thinking at all, add -F/--fixed-strings: sd -F '.' '_' file. The other difference is more consequential: unlike sed (which needs -i to edit in place and otherwise just prints to stdout), sd edits the given file in place by default the instant you pass it a filename, with no undo - you must use -p/--preview to see the diff first without writing it.
L4.explanation: sd's advantage over sed is surface syntax - plain 'pattern' 'replacement' arguments instead of a delimiter-bound s/.../.../ expression - not a different notion of what counts as a special character (. * ( ) still need escaping or -F). The real trap for sed muscle memory is that sd's default with a file argument is sed -i's behaviour, not sed's default stdout behaviour.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `fd '{lit}'` to find files whose name contains that literal text, and it exits with a regex parse error instead of listing any matches. What causes this, and name two different fixes.
L4.answer: fd treats its pattern as a regular expression by default, and none of these strings is a syntactically valid one on its own: an unbalanced ( opens a group that is never closed, an unbalanced [ opens a character class that is never closed, and [z-a] closes its character class but gives it a backwards range (start after end). Fix 1: escape or correct the special construct, e.g. \(cache, or [a-z]. Fix 2: pass -F/--fixed-strings to match the text literally with no regex interpretation at all.
L4.explanation: fd, like rg, defaults to regex matching rather than literal substring matching - the same default that makes fd's own README example work also turns a filename with an unescaped (, an unclosed [, or a backwards range like [z-a] into a parse error. -F/--fixed-strings (present on fd, rg and grep -F) is the general fix whenever the text you want matched literally happens to contain regex metacharacters.

L4.prompt_tpl: Both `rg -l {pattern} | xargs {cmd}` and a `find -exec` pipeline run a command across every matching file, and both silently mishandle a filename containing a space or a newline unless you take one extra step on each side. What is that step for the rg/xargs half, and what does it rely on from xargs?
L4.answer: Add -0/--null to rg (rg -l0 pattern) so matched filenames are separated by a NUL byte instead of a newline, and add -0 to xargs (xargs -0) so it splits its input on NUL instead of whitespace and newlines. NUL cannot appear in a POSIX filename, so this is the only fully safe delimiter; without it, a filename containing a space is split into two arguments and one containing a newline breaks xargs' parsing outright.
L4.explanation: This is the same failure mode as find without -print0 piped into xargs without -0 (see Handling filenames safely and find and xargs as an execution engine): any tool that hands filenames to another tool over a text stream needs an unambiguous separator, and NUL is the one byte guaranteed not to appear in a filename.

L4.prompt_tpl: This concept's L3 says ripgrep's default engine guarantees linear-time matching by using finite automata with no backtracking. Given that guarantee, predict what happens when you run `rg` with the backreference pattern {pattern} to match repeated text, and say what flag changes the outcome.
L4.answer: A backreference like \1 requires the engine to remember and re-match text it already captured, which a finite automaton cannot do while staying linear-time - so rg's default engine rejects the pattern with an unsupported-syntax error rather than silently miscompiling it. Passing -P/--pcre2 switches rg to the PCRE2 engine, which does support backreferences (and lookaround), at the cost of the linear-time guarantee - a PCRE2 pattern can backtrack catastrophically the same way grep -P or a Perl regex can.
L4.explanation: The no-backtracking guarantee and the missing backreference support are the same fact from two angles: anything that needs backtracking to evaluate - backreferences, lookaround - is exactly what the default engine cannot bound the running time of, so ripgrep excludes that syntax rather than quietly break its own guarantee.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `rg {pattern}` against a file. Give the exit status rg returns in each of these three cases: (1) at least one line matches, (2) the file exists and is readable but zero lines match, (3) the target path does not exist at all.
L4.answer: 0 when at least one line matches; 1 when the search ran cleanly but found no matches; 2 when rg itself hit an error (such as a missing file) and could not complete the search at all.
L4.explanation: rg follows the same three-way exit-status convention as grep: 0 means 'found', 1 means 'ran fine, found nothing' (not an error - safe to test with if rg ...; then), and 2 means 'something went wrong' (bad path, bad pattern, permissions). Treating 1 as a failure in a script is a common bug, since a clean no-match is exit 1, not 2.

concepts.t: Regex flavours: BRE, ERE and PCRE

L0.body:
# input lines:  aaa   ab   a+b

grep    'a+b'   f    # BRE: + is LITERAL  -> matches the line a+b
grep -E 'a+b'   f    # ERE: + is a quantifier -> matches ab
grep -E 'a\+b'  f    # ERE: escaped -> literal -> matches a+b

grep    '\(ab\)\1' f  # BRE: groups need backslashes
grep -E '(ab)\1'   f  # ERE: bare parentheses

grep -P '(?<=id=)\d+' f   # PCRE only: lookbehind, \d, \w shorthands
grep -oP '<.+?>'          # PCRE only: lazy quantifier
sed -E / awk / rg         # ERE-ish;  rg and sd use Rust regex (no backreferences)
L0.cloze:
grep 'a+b'      # {{c1::BRE}}: + is a literal plus sign
grep -E 'a+b'   # {{c2::ERE}}: + is the one-or-more quantifier
grep {{c3::-P}} '(?<=id=)\d+'   # the only common grep flavour with lookbehind
grep -oP '<.+{{c4::?}}>'        # the lazy quantifier — POSIX regex has no equivalent

concepts.L1: Three incompatible regex dialects are in daily use. POSIX basic (BRE), grep/sed's default: `{ }` `( )` are literal unless backslashed, per POSIX; backslashed `+ ? |` becoming special is a GNU extension, not POSIX. POSIX extended (ERE) is grep -E, sed -E, awk: those chars are special; backslash makes them literal.
concepts.L2: The rule is not 'ERE has more features'; it is that the two dialects invert the meaning of the same backslash. A pattern that works in one is frequently a valid but different pattern in the other, so it fails silently rather than erroring.
concepts.L3: PCRE (`grep -P`) is a third thing again: `\d`, `\w`, `\s`, lazy quantifiers, lookahead and lookbehind — none exist in POSIX regex, which is why sed has no `.*?` and the negated class `[^>]*` is the standard substitute. PCRE backtracks, so `(a+)+b` can take exponential time on a non-matching input. Ripgrep's Rust engine refuses backreferences to guarantee linear-time matching; GNU grep's default engine is normally linear too, but it does support backreferences (`\1`, and `(...)\1` as a GNU ERE extension) by falling back to backtracking whenever one appears, so a backreferenced pattern can be as slow as PCRE's. The same ERE dialect resurfaces in awk, whose multi-character field separator is compiled as an ERE. Rule: pass `-E` or `-P` explicitly, single-quote the pattern, and use `-F` (fixed string) once the pattern comes from data.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A file contains three lines: `aaa`, `ab`, `a+b`. Which lines does each command print?
  A: grep '{p}' f
  B: grep -E '{p}' f
L4.answer: A prints only the line a+b (in BRE the plus is a literal character). B prints only the line ab (in ERE the plus is a one-or-more quantifier, so it matches one-or-more 'a' followed by 'b').
L4.explanation: The same six characters produce two disjoint answers depending on one flag. This is why patterns copied from a blog post into a script silently stop matching, and why -E should be explicit rather than assumed.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to extract the digits that follow `{key}=` from a log, without the key itself, using one command. Which flavour and why?
L4.answer: grep -oP '(?<=id=)\d+' — a lookbehind matches the prefix without including it in the output, and only PCRE has lookbehind.
L4.explanation: grep -oE '(?<=id=)[0-9]+' fails outright: POSIX ERE has no lookbehind, so grep treats '(?<=id=)' as an invalid group and prints 'grep: warning: ? at start of expression' with no matches. grep -o 'id=\d+' also fails: without -P, \d is not a digit shorthand, so the backslash before the ordinary character d is a no-op and the pattern just searches for the literal text id=d+, which is not in the log line. Only grep -oP with a real PCRE lookbehind both matches and excludes the prefix.
options: grep -oP '(?<=id=)\d+'
grep -o 'id=\d+'

L4.prompt_tpl: sed's default dialect is BRE, the same as grep without -E. A file contains the single line `{line}`. What does `sed 's/a+/X/' f` print, and what does `sed -E 's/a+/X/' f` print?
L4.answer: sed 's/a+/X/' f prints aaa unchanged: in BRE the + is a literal plus sign, and the line has no literal plus, so nothing matches. sed -E 's/a+/X/' f prints X: in ERE + is the one-or-more quantifier, so it matches the whole run 'aaa' and replaces it.
L4.explanation: sed inherits grep's BRE/ERE split exactly: the same flag, -E, turns on the same quantifier meaning for +. This is the single most common reason a sed one-liner copied from a modern blog post does nothing on a machine where -E was left off.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file contains two lines: `{l1}` and `{l2}`. What does `grep '{pat}' f` print (no flags), and what does `grep -F '{pat}' f` print?
L4.answer: grep 'a.b' f prints both lines: the dot is a BRE metacharacter meaning 'any one character', so it matches the literal dot in a.b and also matches the x in axb. grep -F 'a.b' f prints only a.b: -F disables regex entirely and searches for the three literal characters a, dot, b.
L4.explanation: This is why grep -F (or fgrep) is the right choice whenever the search string comes from data rather than from the person writing the command: an unescaped dot, bracket or plus in that data would otherwise be read as regex syntax instead of as itself.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script was written and tested as `grep '\(foo\)\1' f` (BRE; it matches a line 'foofoo'). Someone 'modernizes' it by adding -E without touching the pattern: `grep -E '\(foo\)\1' f`. What actually happens, and why?
L4.answer: grep exits with an error ('Invalid back reference'), because under -E the backslash now makes the parentheses literal, so \1 refers to a group that was never opened.
L4.explanation: Verified here: grep -E '\(foo\)\1' on a file containing foofoo prints 'grep: Invalid back reference' and exits 2. Under -E the backslash flips \( from 'start a group' to 'literal parenthesis', so \1 backreferences a group that was never opened.
options: It matches nothing new; -E only changes how + and ? behave, so the output is unchanged.
grep exits with an error ('Invalid back reference'), because under -E the backslash now makes the parentheses literal, so \1 refers to a group that was never opened.
It silently matches every line in the file, because -E makes GNU grep ignore backslashes entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: In awk, a multi-character -F value is compiled as an ERE — the same dialect grep -E uses. Given the line `{line}` and the command `{cmd}`, how many fields does awk report, and why?
L4.answer: 2 fields. FS values longer than one character are compiled as an ERE, so 'a+' is the one-or-more quantifier from this concept, not three separate literal separators; it matches the whole run 'aaa' as a single field separator, splitting baaab into the two fields b and b.
L4.explanation: The BRE/ERE distinction is not a grep-only quirk: awk's field splitter uses the exact same ERE dialect once FS is more than one character, so a pattern's quantifier meaning here transfers directly to how awk parses input records.

L4.prompt_tpl: A web server builds the command grep -P with a pattern taken directly from an HTTP request, then runs it against a log file. What specific denial-of-service risk does -P introduce here that the default BRE engine would not, and what is one concrete mitigation?
L4.answer: PCRE backtracks, so a crafted pattern like `(a+)+$` run against a crafted non-matching input can take exponential time (a ReDoS), tying up the process indefinitely; GNU grep's default DFA-based engine does not backtrack unless the pattern itself contains a backreference, so ordinary user patterns cannot trigger this against it. Mitigations: never let untrusted input become the -P pattern, run the match under a hard timeout (timeout 1 grep -P ...), or validate the pattern against a strict allowlist before use.
L4.explanation: This connects the exponential-time property of PCRE backtracking, established for (a+)+b, to a real security posture: letting user data become a PCRE pattern is a denial-of-service surface the same way an unbounded regex in application code would be.

concepts.t: awk: records, fields and the implicit loop

L0.body:
# an awk program is:  pattern { action }  repeated
# no pattern = every record;  no action = { print $0 }

awk '$4==500' f          # pattern only -> the implicit { print }
awk '{print $1,$NF}' f   # action only  -> runs on every record
awk 'NR>1' f             # skip the header row
awk 'NR==FNR {a[$1]; next} $1 in a' keys data   # load a table, filter

#  $0 record   $1..$NF fields   NF count
#  NR overall record number   FNR record number within THIS file

printf 'a  b\n' | cut -d' ' -f2    # (empty): two adjacent delimiters
printf 'a  b\n' | awk '{print $2}' # b: default FS collapses runs
L0.cloze:
awk '$4==500' f          # a pattern with no action means {{c1::{ print }}}
awk '{print $1, ${{c2::NF}}}' f   # this variable is the number of fields
awk '{{c3::NR}}==FNR {a[$1]; next} $1 in a' keys data   # NR is global, {{c4::FNR}} restarts per file
printf 'a  b\n' | awk '{print $2}'   # prints b — the default FS collapses runs of whitespace

concepts.L1: awk's main loop is implicit: it reads one record at a time, splits it into fields on FS, and evaluates every pattern-action pair in order. A bare pattern implies `{ print }` and a bare action implies 'every record'.
concepts.L2: The default FS is not a space; it is the special value that splits on runs of whitespace and strips leading and trailing whitespace. That special-casing survives `-F' '` too - POSIX ties it to the value " " itself, so only a regex like `-F'[ ]'` truly splits on one literal space, the way `cut -d' '` does.
concepts.L3: That default is why `awk '{print $2}'` is correct on ragged, space-aligned output like `ps` or `df` where `cut -d' ' -f2` returns an empty string. If your data really is delimiter-separated with meaningful empty fields, `-F:` makes awk behave like cut, empty fields included. `NR==FNR {...; next}` is the standard two-file idiom: NR counts records across all inputs while FNR restarts per file, so the test is true exactly while the first file is being read - it loads a lookup table, and `next` skips the rest of the program so the second file falls through. That one pattern replaces most uses of `join`, with no sorting required.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`printf 'a  b\n' | cut -d' ' -f{n}`
  `printf 'a  b\n' | awk '{{print ${n}}}'`
The input has two spaces between a and b. What are the two lines?
L4.answer: The first prints an empty line; the second prints b.
L4.explanation: cut treats every delimiter character as a field boundary, so two spaces create an empty field 2. awk's default FS collapses runs of whitespace into one separator and strips leading and trailing whitespace, so field 2 is b. For whitespace-aligned output, awk is correct and cut is not.

L4.prompt_tpl:
keys.txt contains the single line `{k}`. data.txt contains `{k} 100` and `other 200`. What does
  `awk 'NR==FNR {{a[$1]; next}} $1 in a' keys.txt data.txt`
print?
L4.answer: One line: the matching data.txt record, for example 'alpha 100'.
L4.explanation: While the first file is being read, NR and FNR are equal, so the first rule fires, records the key, and `next` skips the remaining rules. Once the second file starts, FNR resets to 1 while NR keeps climbing, the first rule stops firing, and the bare pattern `$1 in a` applies its implicit print.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file f contains three lines: `web01 200`, `web02 500`, `web03 500`. What does `awk '$2=={threshold}' f` print?
L4.answer: threshold 500 selects the two lines whose second field equals 500: web02 500 and web03 500. threshold 200 selects only web01 200.
L4.explanation: A pattern with no action block defaults to `{ print $0 }`, so this line filters records by a field comparison and prints the whole matching record with no print needed - the way grep filters lines, but on one numeric field instead of the whole line.

L4.prompt_tpl: A record reaches awk's default field splitter: `{line}`. Ignoring the surrounding backticks, what value does awk report for NF on that record?
L4.answer: 3 in both cases: leading and trailing whitespace is discarded and every run of spaces between words counts as one separator, so extra spaces never add empty fields.
L4.explanation: The default FS is not a literal space character; it is the special value meaning split on any run of blanks, and drop leading and trailing blanks first. That is why doubled internal spaces and outer padding never change NF, unlike splitting on a fixed single-character delimiter.

L4.prompt_tpl: The record `a b c` contains no `{delim}` character at all. Under `-F{delim}` (using {delim} as the field separator), what are the values of NF and $1?
L4.answer: NF is 1 and $1 is the whole record, 'a b c': a delimiter that never occurs leaves the record unsplit, one field containing everything including the spaces.
L4.explanation: A literal single-character FS (anything other than the special space value) turns off whitespace collapsing entirely: awk only breaks the record where that exact character occurs. If it never occurs, there is nothing to split on, so the record stays intact as field one.

L4.prompt_tpl: The two-file idiom is normally written as: while NR equals FNR, run 'a[$1]; next'; then the bare pattern '$1 in a' prints matches. Someone deletes 'next', leaving only 'a[$1]' as the first rule's action. keys.txt has one line, `{k}`. data.txt has two lines, `{k} 100` then `other 200`. Reading keys.txt then data.txt in that order, what does this buggy version print, and why does dropping next cause it?
L4.answer: It prints two lines instead of one: first the keys.txt record itself (e.g. alpha), then the matching data.txt record (alpha 100). Without next, once the first rule records a[$1] while NR==FNR, execution falls through to the second rule on that same keys.txt record; since $1 was just added to a, '$1 in a' is now true and its implicit print fires on the keys.txt line too, before data.txt is even read.
L4.explanation: next is not decoration: it is what stops a record from also being tested by the rules after the one that just matched, while the first file is still open. Drop it and every line of the lookup file gets evaluated by the whole program, not just the loading rule, so the keys file's own lines leak into the output.

L4.prompt_tpl: GNU join requires both input files sorted on the join field: it detects out-of-order records, warns on stderr, and returns only the partial matches found before the ordering broke, not the full join. The NR==FNR awk idiom needs no such sort. You have two large unsorted files and must keep every record of file B whose key also appears in file A. Which tool do you reach for, and why?
L4.answer: The NR==FNR awk idiom: it loads file A's keys into an associative array in one pass, then filters file B in a second pass, with no ordering requirement at all, whereas join would force an extra sort step on data that was never sorted, or silently miss matches if you skipped that step.
L4.explanation: join's algorithm is a merge join: it walks both files in lockstep assuming ascending order, so unsorted input breaks that assumption and it can miss matches past the point where order is violated, even though it warns. awk's array-based lookup makes no such assumption, which is why the two-file idiom is the standard join replacement for messy, unsorted, real-world data.

concepts.t: awk: BEGIN, END and associative arrays

L0.body:
awk 'BEGIN {FS=":"; OFS="\t"; total=0}
     $3 >= 1000 {shells[$7]++; total++}
     END {print "users:", total
          for (s in shells) print s, shells[s]}' /etc/passwd

#  BEGIN runs once before any input — set FS/OFS, print a header
#  END   runs once after all input — totals, averages, the report
#  arrays are ALWAYS associative; the key is a string

awk '{s+=$1; n++} END {print (n ? s/n : 0)}' nums     # mean, guarding n==0
awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}' f | sort -rn   # group-by
# for (k in arr) order is UNSPECIFIED — pipe to sort if it matters
L0.cloze:
awk '{{c1::BEGIN}} {FS=":"} ... {{c2::END}} {print total}'   # run once before input / once after
awk '{c[$1]{{c3::++}}} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}'   # group-by in one pass
# `for (k in arr)` iteration order is {{c4::unspecified}} — pipe to sort for stable output

concepts.L1: BEGIN runs once before the first record is read and END once after the last, so BEGIN is where FS, OFS and constants are set and END is where totals are printed. Arrays are always associative: the subscript is converted to a string, and `for (k in a)` walks the keys.
concepts.L2: Changing FS is not retroactive: a BEGIN assignment splits record one correctly, since BEGIN completes before input is read, but FS assigned inside a later rule only takes effect on the next record - the current one keeps its old split. `for (k in a)` order is undefined and differs between mawk, gawk and BusyBox awk.
concepts.L3: The three-part shape - BEGIN to configure, pattern-action rules to accumulate, END to report - is what makes awk a report generator rather than a filter. Uninitialised variables are simultaneously 0 and the empty string, so `c[$1]++` needs no existence check and `s+=$1` no initialisation; that is what makes the counting idiom one line. Comparisons follow strnum rules: a field that looks numeric compares numerically, but a quoted string constant compares as text even against a field. `length(a)` for array size started as a gawk-only extension but is not gawk-exclusive - mawk has it too - and is broadly supported across modern awks; confirm it exists before relying on it, and count with `for (k in a) n++` for portability. The same no-declaration array model is why awk never needs bash's `declare -A`, and why skipping that declaration in bash silently aliases every key to index 0.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A file has the lines `a {x}`, `b {y}`, `a {z}`. What does
  `awk '{{s[$1]+=$2; n[$1]++}} END {{for (k in s) print k, s[k], n[k]}}' f | sort`
print?
L4.answer: Two lines. For x=1,y=2,z=3: 'a 4 2' and 'b 2 1'. For x=10,y=20,z=30: 'a 40 2' and 'b 20 1'.
L4.explanation: Two associative arrays are accumulated in the same pass, keyed by the first field, with no declaration and no zero-initialisation. The pipe to sort is what makes the output deterministic, because for-in order is unspecified.

L4.prompt_tpl: Write the awk one-liner that prints the mean of field {f}, printing 0 rather than dividing by zero on empty input.
L4.answer: awk '{s+=`$1`; n++} END {print (n ? s/n : 0)}' file — substituting `$3` and the same guard for field 3.
L4.explanation: n++ counts records that were actually read, so on empty input END still runs with n unset, which is 0, and the ternary avoids a division by zero. Note that END always runs even when no records matched, which is what makes the guard necessary and also what makes 'print a total of zero' possible.

L4.prompt_tpl: An awk program has a BEGIN action that prints start, a main rule with no pattern that prints a line for every record read, and an END action that prints done. Run it against a totally empty input file, zero records. What gets printed?
L4.answer: start, then done - BEGIN and END both run exactly once, whether or not any records were read
L4.explanation: BEGIN executes once before the first record is read and END once after the last, and both are unconditional on there being any input at all. Only the middle, pattern-action rules depend on records existing to test against - with zero input lines that rule never fires, but BEGIN and END still do, in order.
options: start, then done - BEGIN and END both run exactly once, whether or not any records were read
Nothing at all - none of BEGIN, the main rule or END run without at least one record
start only - END never runs unless the main rule matched at least once

L4.prompt_tpl: In a BEGIN block, the statement count[3]++ runs once, then count["3"]++ runs once, and nothing else touches count. What is length(count) afterward, and why?
L4.answer: 1 - every array subscript is converted to a string, so the number 3 and the string "3" address the same element
L4.explanation: awk has exactly one array type, and every subscript - however it is written - is converted to a string before use. The number 3 converts to the string "3" by the ordinary number-to-string rule, so count[3] and count["3"] name the identical element; the two increments land on it together, leaving length(count) at 1 with a stored value of 2.
options: 1 - every array subscript is converted to a string, so the number 3 and the string "3" address the same element
2 - awk keeps a separate integer-indexed array and a separate string-indexed array
0 - a bare numeric subscript like 3 is invalid until it is written as a string

L4.prompt_tpl: In a BEGIN block, count[3.14159265]++ runs, then count["3.14159"]++ runs, with CONVFMT left at its default. What is length(count) afterward, and why do the two subscripts collide?
L4.answer: length(count) is 1. A numeric subscript is converted to a string using CONVFMT, whose default is the printf format %.6g - six significant digits. Under that format, 3.14159265 becomes the string "3.14159", which is exactly the second subscript, so both increments hit the same element and its value ends up 2.
L4.explanation: CONVFMT governs every implicit conversion of a non-integer number to a string, subscripts included, and defaults to %.6g; integer-valued subscripts bypass it and always render as plain integers, which is why count[3] and count["3"] collide regardless of CONVFMT in the sibling question above. OFMT is separate and only affects what print writes. Two non-integer numbers that render identically under CONVFMT are indistinguishable as array keys.

L4.prompt_tpl: Before array a has been touched, a BEGIN block runs: if (a["{key}"]) print "true"; else print "false". What does this print, and what is length(a) immediately afterward? Then say whether testing with ("{key}" in a) instead of a["{key}"] would change that length.
L4.answer: It prints false, since a["{key}"] is empty and empty is falsy - but merely referencing a["{key}"] creates that key as a side effect, with an empty value, so length(a) becomes 1 right after, even though nothing was ever deliberately assigned. Testing with ("{key}" in a) instead never touches the array: it checks membership without creating the key, so length(a) would stay 0.
L4.explanation: Any reference to an array element - even just reading it inside a condition - auto-vivifies that element in awk if it did not already exist, because there is no way to read a[k] without awk first deciding it exists. The `in` operator is the one construct built specifically to test membership without that side effect, which is why `if (k in a)` is the safe idiom and `if (a[k])` is not.

L4.prompt_tpl: awk's count[$1]++ needs no setup line, while bash's associative-array equivalent needs declare -A count before first use, or a silent bug appears. What is the actual mechanism difference that makes awk safe without a declaration and bash unsafe without one?
L4.answer: awk has exactly one array type - always associative, every subscript converted to a string - so there is no ambiguity a declaration could resolve; count[$1]++ is unambiguous from the first use. bash has two array types sharing the same subscript syntax, and without declare -A it defaults to an indexed array, where a subscript is evaluated as an arithmetic expression; an unset name like foo evaluates to 0 there, so every distinct string key silently maps to the same index 0 and overwrites the last write.
L4.explanation: This is the same silent-collision failure the bash 'Associative arrays' concept covers from the other side: declare -A is not stylistic, it switches which subscript rule bash uses. awk never needed that switch because it only ever had the one rule - string subscripts - which is also why awk arrays need no bash-4.0-style version floor.

L4.prompt_tpl: Extend the counting idiom count[$1]++, with an END rule that loops over count with for k in count, so the program prints only the single key with the highest count. Write the complete, correct awk one-liner.
L4.answer: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) if (c[k]>mx) {mx=c[k]; best=k} print best, mx}' file - tested here on the records a b a a c c, which prints 'a 3'.
L4.explanation: The END block needs a second reduction over the array it just built: track a running maximum mx and the key best that achieved it as the for-k-in loop visits every entry, then print only that pair once the loop finishes. Because for-k-in order is unspecified and the test is a strict greater-than, ties go to whichever tied key the loop happens to visit first.

L0.body:
cut -d: -f1   /etc/passwd    # field 1, colon separated
cut -d: -f1,3 /etc/passwd    # fields 1 and 3
cut -d: -f3,1 f              # STILL prints 1 then 3 — no reordering
cut -d' ' -f2 f              # breaks on 'a  b': every space counts

paste a.txt b.txt            # side by side, tab separated
paste -s -d, col.txt         # a COLUMN -> one comma-separated row

tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' <<< hello     # HELLO
tr -s ' '    <<< 'a   b'     # a b   squeeze runs
tr -cd '0-9' <<< ab12        # 12    complement then delete
tr -d '\r' < win.sh          # fixes: bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M
L0.cloze:
cut -d: {{c1::-f1,3}} /etc/passwd    # select fields 1 and 3
cut -d: -f3,1 f              # output order is always {{c2::ascending field order}} — cut cannot reorder
paste {{c3::-s}} -d, col.txt         # turn a column into one comma-separated row
tr {{c4::-s}} ' '                    # squeeze runs of the character into one

concepts.L1: These three are the fixed-function tools: `cut` selects columns by delimiter or character position, `paste` joins files column-wise, and `tr` maps or deletes individual characters. All three stream in constant memory and are much faster than awk for what they do.
concepts.L2: Each has one hard limit people trip over. `cut` cannot reorder or reformat - `-f3,1` still prints field 1 first. `cut -d' '` treats every single space as a separator, so it breaks on whitespace-aligned output. `tr` is character-to-character and cannot replace a string.
concepts.L3: Reach for awk the moment you need any of the things they cannot do: reordering columns, a computed column, a different output separator, or whitespace-run splitting. Two idioms are worth memorising anyway. `paste -s -d,` collapses a column of values into a single comma-separated line, which is the shortest way to build an IN-list or a comma-joined argument. `tr -d '\r'` strips the carriage returns that a file written on Windows carries, which is the actual cause of the mystifying `bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M` error - the shebang line's last character is a CR, so the kernel looks for an interpreter whose name ends in a control character.

L4.answer: The first prints an empty line (two adjacent delimiters make field 2 empty). The second prints 'a:c' - cut always emits selected fields in ascending order with the delimiter between them, regardless of the order you listed them in.
L4.explanation: Both limits are by design and documented, and both produce quiet wrong answers. For whitespace-aligned input use awk; for reordering use awk -F: '{print `$3`, `$1`}'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script downloaded from a Windows machine fails with `bash: ./{f}: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory`. Explain and give the one-line fix.
L4.answer: The file has CRLF line endings, so the shebang line is `#!/bin/bash\r` and the kernel searches for an interpreter literally named '/bin/bash' followed by a carriage return, which does not exist. Fix: tr -d '\\r' < deploy.sh > tmp && mv tmp deploy.sh, or dos2unix deploy.sh.
L4.explanation: The same invisible CR causes subtler failures inside the script: a variable read from a CRLF file ends in \r, so string comparisons fail and the mismatched value prints identically to the expected one because the CR moves the cursor to column zero.

L4.prompt_tpl: `cut -c{lo}-{hi} file` prints the characters at positions {lo} through {hi} of every line. Both ends are included. How many characters does that select?
L4.answer: hi - lo + 1 characters. cut -c ranges are inclusive at both ends: cut -c2-9 keeps positions 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9, which is 8 characters (verified: `echo abcdefghij | cut -c2-9` prints `bcdefghi`), not 7 as an exclusive-end reading would give.
L4.explanation: The off-by-one trap runs the other way from most range syntax people know: cut -c ranges include the end position, so the count is hi-lo+1, not hi-lo. Getting this wrong under- or over-selects by exactly one character on every line.

L4.prompt_tpl: `paste` with no `-d` option joins {n} files line by line, inserting one tab between each pair of adjacent fields and none at the very end. Merging {n} files this way, how many tab characters appear on each output line?
L4.answer: n - 1 tabs: paste places exactly one delimiter between every pair of adjacent files, never after the last one. Verified: `paste <(echo a) <(echo b) <(echo c)` prints a, tab, b, tab, c - two tabs for three files, not three.
L4.explanation: People expect one delimiter per file and are surprised the last field has no trailing tab. This matters when the output is fed to something that splits on a fixed field count, since a trailing empty field never appears.

L4.prompt_tpl: A string of exactly {len} characters contains {digits} digit characters (0-9) and no other digits; the rest are letters, and the input has no trailing newline. Piped through `tr -cd 0-9`, how many characters does the output contain?
L4.answer: digits characters. -c complements the set 0-9, giving every character that is NOT a digit; -d then deletes whatever falls in that complemented set, so only the digit characters survive. Verified: `printf ab12 | tr -cd 0-9` prints 12 - the 2 digits, with the 2 letters gone.
L4.explanation: tr -cd is complement-then-delete, not delete-then-complement: -c rewrites the working set first, and -d always deletes members of whatever set it is finally given, which is why the surviving characters are the ones matching the original pattern, not its opposite.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file mixed.txt has two lines: `a:b:c` and `plaintext` (no colon on the second line). What does `cut -d: -f2 mixed.txt` print for each line, and what would change if you added `-s`?
L4.answer: For 'a:b:c': b. For 'plaintext': the whole line, plaintext, unchanged - by default cut passes through any line that contains no delimiter at all, rather than printing nothing for it. Verified: `cut -d: -f2 mixed.txt` prints `b` then `plaintext`. Adding -s suppresses that second line entirely, so only `b` is printed.
L4.explanation: This is the most common cause of cut appearing to silently misbehave on messy input: a header row or a malformed line without the delimiter sails through untouched instead of erroring or vanishing. There is no way to get 'blank instead of whole line'; the choice is pass-through or -s suppression.

L4.prompt_tpl: `tr -s ' '` squeezes runs of spaces to one. What does `printf 'a   b  c\n' | tr -s ' :'` print, given the string has no colons at all?
L4.answer: a b c
L4.explanation: Listing a character in SET1 that never appears in the input is harmless: tr -s only squeezes characters that are both in SET1 and actually repeated in the stream, so an unused member of the set (here a colon) simply never triggers and every run of spaces still collapses to one.

L4.prompt_tpl: `tr -s 'ab' 'xx' <<< 'ab'` maps both a and b to x, then squeezes if `-s` applies. Does -s squeeze based on the original characters (SET1) or the characters already produced (SET2, after translation)? Give the exact output and justify from that.
L4.answer: Output is x (verified). This proves squeezing runs on the translated (output) stream: a and b are different input characters, so a squeeze based on SET1 would leave 'ab' untouched and translation would then still produce 'xx'. Instead both characters map to x, become adjacent and identical only after translation, and get squeezed to one x.
L4.explanation: The textbook example tr -s 'a-z' 'A-Z' <<< aabbaa giving ABA does not actually settle the ordering question, because squeezing the input first or the output first gives the same answer when SET1 maps letter-for-letter to SET2; only a many-to-one mapping like ab->xx tells the two theories apart.

L4.prompt_tpl: usernames.txt has one username per line: alice, bob, carol. Using only cut, paste, tr and sed (no awk), write a one-line pipeline that prints a single line: 'alice','bob','carol' - each name single-quoted, comma-separated, no trailing comma.
L4.answer: sed "s/.*/'&'/" usernames.txt | paste -sd, - : sed wraps every line in single quotes, then paste -sd, - reads that from stdin (the - argument) and serialises all lines into one comma-separated row. Verified on alice/bob/carol: prints 'alice','bob','carol' exactly, with no trailing comma because paste -s never adds a delimiter after the last line.
L4.explanation: This chains the two facts the concept already states: paste -s -d, collapses a column into one comma-joined line, and since cut and tr can only select or map characters, never insert new ones, sed is the piece that adds the quotes before paste joins the lines.

prereqs: awk: records, fields and the implicit loop
literacy:Text is bytes: UTF-8 in one concept

concepts.t: join and comm: relational operations on sorted text

L0.body:
# users.txt      scores.txt
#   1 alice         1 10
#   2 bob           2 20
#   4 dave          3 30

join users.txt scores.txt          # 1 alice 10
                                   # 2 bob 20
join -a1 -a2 -e NULL -o 0,1.2,2.2 users.txt scores.txt   # full outer join
#   1 alice 10 / 2 bob 20 / 3 NULL 30 / 4 dave NULL

# A: a b c     B: b c d
comm A B      # col1 = only in A, col2 = only in B, col3 = both
comm -12 A B  # b c   intersection
comm -23 A B  # a     only in A
comm -13 A B  # d     only in B

# BOTH require input sorted the same way. Use LC_ALL=C sort on both sides.
L0.cloze:
join a.txt b.txt              # inner join on field {{c1::1}} by default
join {{c2::-a1 -a2}} -e NULL -o 0,1.2,2.2 a b   # full outer join with a placeholder
comm {{c3::-12}} A B                  # intersection: suppress columns 1 and 2
comm {{c4::-23}} A B                  # lines only in A

concepts.L1: `join` is a relational join over two sorted text files, defaulting to an inner join on field 1; `-a` adds unmatched rows from a side, `-o` chooses the output columns and `-e` fills the blanks. `comm` compares two sorted files line-by-line and emits three columns: only-in-A, only-in-B, in-both.
concepts.L2: Both silently assume their inputs are sorted in the same collation and both misbehave when they are not - comm's disorder check is a content-dependent heuristic: it often warns, but can just as easily emit wrong output with no warning and exit status 0. A locale mismatch between the sort and the join is the usual root cause.
concepts.L3: The digits in `comm`'s flags suppress columns rather than select them, which is the opposite of most people's first guess: `-12` hides columns 1 and 2, leaving only the shared lines. That gives three set operations free - intersection `-12`, difference `-23`, symmetric difference `-3`. The sorting requirement is not a formality: both are single-pass merge algorithms with no memory of what they have seen, which is why they run in constant space on files larger than RAM. Sort both sides with the same `LC_ALL=C sort`. When the inputs are unsorted, `awk 'NR==FNR{a[$1]=$2; next} $1 in a'` does the same by hashing.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A contains the sorted lines a, b, c. B contains the sorted lines b, c, d. What does each print?
  1: comm -12 A B
  2: comm -{x}{y} A B
L4.answer: comm -12 prints b and c (the lines in both). comm -23 prints a (the lines only in A).
L4.explanation: The digits name the columns to SUPPRESS: column 1 is only-in-A, column 2 is only-in-B, column 3 is in-both. So -12 leaves column 3 and -23 leaves column 1.

L4.prompt_tpl:
join users.txt scores.txt > joined.txt
users.txt was produced by `sort users.raw` on a machine with {loc}, scores.txt by `LC_ALL=C sort`. joined.txt is missing rows that clearly match. Diagnose and fix.
L4.answer: The two files are sorted under different collations, so their orderings disagree - UTF-8 locales ignore case and punctuation in ways byte order does not. join is a single-pass merge and simply walks past keys it thinks are already behind it, dropping matches without an error. Fix: re-sort both files with the same collation, LC_ALL=C sort, and set LC_ALL=C for the join itself.
L4.explanation: The same trap applies to comm and to sort -u used across two files. Making LC_ALL=C explicit in any script that sorts, joins or compares is cheap insurance and is also faster than locale-aware collation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two sorted files A and B are compared with plain comm (no flags). A has {a} lines with no duplicates, B has {b} lines with no duplicates, and {shared} of those lines are identical text appearing in both files. How many lines does `comm -12 A B` print?
L4.answer: comm -12 prints only column 3 (lines common to both files), so the count equals the shared-line count regardless of how large A and B are on their own.
L4.explanation: comm's -12 flag suppresses columns 1 and 2, leaving only the lines present in both files - exactly the shared lines, independent of A's and B's own sizes.

L4.prompt_tpl: The same A and B as above (comm with no flags, three columns). A has {a} lines, B has {b} lines, and {shared} lines are common to both. How many lines total does plain `comm A B` print across all three columns combined?
L4.answer: Column 1 gets a-shared lines, column 2 gets b-shared lines, column 3 gets shared lines; summed that is a+b-shared lines total, never a+b.
L4.explanation: comm partitions every line of A and every line of B into exactly one of the three columns, so the total line count is the size of the union, a+b-shared, never a+b.

L4.prompt_tpl: file1 has {n1} lines that all share the identical join key (and are otherwise correctly sorted among themselves); file2 has {n2} lines that all share that same key. Both files are sorted overall. How many output lines does plain `join file1 file2` print for that key?
L4.answer: join pairs every matching line of file1 with every matching line of file2 for a shared key, so it emits n1 times n2 lines - the full cross product, not min(n1,n2) or n1+n2.
L4.explanation: join has no notion of a unique key; when a key repeats on both sides it behaves like a relational inner join and emits the Cartesian product of the matching rows for that key.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using users.txt (keys 1, 2, 4) and scores.txt (keys 1, 2, 3) from this concept's own example, run `join -a1 -a2 -o 0,1.2,2.2 users.txt scores.txt` WITHOUT `-e`. On the output line for key 3, file1 contributes nothing (it has no key 3). How many space characters separate the printed 3 and 30 on that line? Answer with just the number of spaces.
L4.answer: Two spaces: 3, then two spaces, then 30. The explicit -o format still requests three output fields (0, 1.2, 2.2) even though file1 contributes nothing, so the empty field 1.2 survives as a zero-length token between two field separators.
L4.explanation: Explicit -o formats always print every named field slot, even when it is empty; only the plain default FORMAT (no -o) collapses a missing field so the line looks shorter. Always pair -o with -e STRING when a side may be missing, or the blank field becomes an invisible parsing trap for whatever reads this output next.

L4.prompt_tpl: Files A, B and C are each already sorted with the same collation and contain no duplicate lines. comm and join only accept two files at a time. Using comm -12 twice, with the second call reading one input from standard input via a dash, write a single pipeline that prints exactly the lines common to all three files.
L4.answer: comm -12 A B | comm -12 - C  --  comm -12 A B first reduces to the lines common to A and B, in the same sorted order; because that output is still correctly sorted, it can be fed as the dash operand of a second comm -12 against C, whose surviving column-3 output is then the three-way intersection of A, B and C.
L4.explanation: This works only because comm's output on sorted, duplicate-free inputs is itself sorted, so composition is safe. The same trick composes join twice: join A B | join - C, since join's default output field is the sort key. It generalizes to n-way intersection by chaining n-1 calls.
