L0.body:
kill -TERM $pid  # 15  polite: catchable, so cleanup can run
kill -INT  $pid  #  2  what Ctrl-C sends to the foreground GROUP
kill -HUP  $pid  #  1  terminal gone; often repurposed as 'reload config'
kill -KILL $pid  #  9  UNCATCHABLE: the kernel acts, the process cannot
kill -STOP $pid  # 19  suspend, uncatchable;  kill -CONT resumes
kill -USR1 $pid  # 10  meaning is the application's to define

# the correct escalation — never kill -9 first:
kill -TERM "$pid"; sleep 10
kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null && kill -KILL "$pid"   # -0 sends nothing
# a shell reports a signalled child as $? = 128 + N
L0.cloze:
kill -{{c1::TERM}} $pid     # 15 — the polite request a process can catch
kill -{{c2::KILL}} $pid     #  9 — cannot be caught, blocked or ignored
kill -{{c3::HUP}} $pid      #  1 — sent when the controlling terminal goes away
kill {{c4::-0}} "$pid"      # send NO signal; just test whether you may signal it

concepts.L1: SIGTERM (15) polite, SIGKILL (9) uncatchable, SIGINT (2) Ctrl-C, SIGHUP (1) terminal closed, SIGSTOP/SIGCONT, SIGUSR1/2 for application use.
concepts.L2: `kill -9` skips the process's cleanup entirely — no flush, no temp file removal, no graceful connection drain. Reaching for it first is a habit that causes data loss. Try TERM, wait, then escalate.
concepts.L3: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are the only signals a process cannot catch, block or ignore, because the kernel acts on them without ever scheduling the process's handler. That is the whole reason `kill -9` is destructive: no `atexit` handlers, no flush of buffered stdout, no pidfile or temp-directory removal, no application-level goodbye on an open connection - the process is torn down mid-instruction, so nothing it would have chosen to do on the way out happens. SIGTERM is the same delivery with a handler that gets to run, which is why orchestrators and systemd send it first: TERM, wait, then `kill -0` to test, then KILL. SIGHUP is what the kernel sends when a controlling terminal disappears, repurposed by many daemons as 'reload config'.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`sleep 30 & p=$!`
  `kill -{sig} $p`
  `wait $p 2>/dev/null`
  `echo "$?"`
What is printed?
L4.explanation: A process terminated by signal N reports exit status 128+N: SIGTERM is signal 15, so 128+15 = 143. SIGHUP is 1, SIGINT 2, SIGKILL 9, SIGTERM 15 - the 128+N encoding is how the shell distinguishes 'exited with status N' from 'died from signal N' in a single byte-sized status.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service is not responding on port {port}. What is the correct first action and why?
L4.answer: kill -TERM, wait, then kill -KILL only if still running
L4.explanation: SIGTERM lets the process flush buffers, finish in-flight requests and release resources before it exits; reaching for kill -9 first costs data - unflushed writes, orphaned temp files and pidfiles, and no application-level goodbye on open connections. SIGHUP is a reload convention in some daemons, a no-op or a terminate in others, so it is not a general stop. Escalate to SIGKILL only once `kill -0` shows the process outlived the grace period.
options: kill -TERM, wait, then kill -KILL only if still running
kill -9 immediately, then investigate
kill -HUP, since it is gentler than TERM

L4.prompt_tpl: You own process {pid} and run `kill -0 {pid}`. How many signals does the kernel actually deliver to process {pid}?
L4.answer: 0. Signal number 0 is the null signal: `kill -0` makes the kernel perform its normal permission and existence checks on the PID and delivers nothing, which is why it is the standard way to test whether you may still signal a process without disturbing it.
L4.explanation: Every other signal number maps to a real action; 0 is reserved for exactly this probe. `kill -0 PID` returns exit status 0 if the process exists and is signalable, and a nonzero status otherwise, which is why scripts use it to poll liveness without perturbing the target.

L4.prompt_tpl: Process {pid} installed a SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown, but a bug in that handler makes it hang forever, so `kill -TERM {pid}` never actually ends the process. Which signal is guaranteed to end it regardless of what the process's own code does?
L4.answer: SIGKILL (kill -9)
L4.explanation: SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored: the kernel terminates the process directly and never schedules its handler, so a broken or hung handler is irrelevant. A second SIGTERM reaches the same broken handler and hangs the same way. SIGSTOP only suspends the process - kill -CONT would resume it exactly where the hung handler left off.
options: SIGKILL (kill -9)
SIGTERM (kill -15), sent a second time
SIGSTOP (kill -19)

L4.prompt_tpl: `yes | head -n {n}` finishes instead of running forever. Which signal does `yes` receive when `head` exits and closes its end of the pipe, and what is that signal's default action on Linux?
L4.answer: SIGPIPE, default action terminate
L4.explanation: Writing to a pipe with no reader raises SIGPIPE (13); its default disposition is Term, so `yes` is killed the moment `head` stops reading - nobody called kill. That silent death is why a pipeline can end with no error message: no process complained, one was just signalled.
options: SIGPIPE, default action terminate
SIGCHLD, default action ignore
SIGTERM, default action terminate

L4.prompt_tpl: A script blocks SIGTERM inside a critical section. While blocked, an operator runs `kill -TERM {pid}` three times in a row. Once the script unblocks the signal, how many times does its TERM handler run?
L4.answer: Once -- standard signals do not queue
L4.explanation: POSIX standard signals are not queued: the kernel just marks one instance pending, so three deliveries of the same signal while it is blocked collapse into a single pending flag and the handler runs exactly once after it unblocks. Only real-time signals (SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX) queue multiple instances; relying on a count for standard signals is a real bug.
options: Once -- standard signals do not queue
Three times, once per kill
Zero -- a blocked signal is dropped, not delivered

L4.prompt_tpl: A non-interactive cleanup script runs `long_task & pid=$!; trap 'kill $pid' TERM; wait $pid`. `long_task` itself starts its own background subprocess before doing its work. An operator sends SIGTERM to the script. Does that subprocess also die? Explain from how `kill $pid` addresses processes, and name the fix that reaches the whole tree.
L4.answer: Not automatically. `kill $pid` addresses exactly one PID; it does not walk down to children, so long_task's own subprocess keeps running as an orphan once the script exits. You cannot fix this with `kill -TERM -- -$pid` (negative PID = process group) as the script stands: this is a non-interactive script, so job control is off and the backgrounded `long_task` never becomes its own process-group leader - it shares the script's own PGID, not $pid, so `-$pid` names a group that does not exist and `kill` fails with 'No such process'. (Verified: `ps -o pgid=` on the backgrounded child shows the parent script's PGID; `kill -- -$pid` there errors and the subprocess survives.) The fix that actually applies here is to enumerate descendants: `trap 'pkill -TERM -P $pid; kill -TERM $pid' TERM`. `kill -- -$pid` only becomes correct if long_task is first put in its own group, e.g. `set -m` before backgrounding it, or `setsid long_task & pid=$!`.
L4.explanation: The kernel signals exactly the PID (or PGID, for a negative target) you name - it has no notion of a job's process tree, and a plain `cmd &` in a script (job control off) does not get its own process group for free. Scripts that background work and expect one signal to clean up everything need either an explicitly created process group (set -m, or setsid) paired with a group-kill, or recursive cleanup via pkill -P / enumerating children; assuming 'kill -- -$pid just works' without one of those is a common source of orphaned processes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A script does `kill -19 {pid}` to pause a worker and `kill -18 {pid}` to resume it. It works on every x86-64 and ARM64 Linux box the author tests. A teammate reports it does the wrong thing on an old MIPS Linux server. What is the bug, and what is the portable fix?
L4.answer: The bug is hardcoding signal numbers. 19 and 18 are SIGSTOP and SIGCONT on x86-64, ARM64 and most Linux architectures, but MIPS numbers signals differently - SIGSTOP is 23 there - so `kill -19` silently sends the wrong signal instead of failing loudly. The portable fix is the symbolic names, `kill -STOP $pid` / `kill -CONT $pid`, which libc and kill(1) translate to the correct number for whatever architecture they run on.
L4.explanation: Signal numbers 1-31 match across x86, x86-64 and ARM (32- and 64-bit) because they share the generic asm-generic/signal.h layout, but Alpha, SPARC and MIPS number several signals differently - exactly the trap a hardcoded number sets. Symbolic names are the only genuinely portable spelling for a script meant to run on more than one architecture.

L0.body:
long_task &          # run in the background; prints [1] 12345
echo "$!"            # PID of the most recent background job
jobs                 # list this shell's jobs with their job numbers
fg %1                # bring job 1 to the foreground
# Ctrl-Z             suspends the foreground job (SIGTSTP)

disown -h %1         # keep the job but stop the shell sending it SIGHUP
nohup long_task &    # immune to SIGHUP; stdout goes to nohup.out

tmux new -s work     # the answer for anything that must outlive the connection
# %1 is a SHELL label, not a PID — use $! for the PID
L0.cloze:
long_task &          # background;  {{c1::$!}} holds its PID
{{c2::jobs}}                 # list this shell's jobs
fg %1 / {{c3::bg}} %1        # foreground it / resume it in the background
{{c4::disown}} -h %1         # keep it running but stop the shell HUPping it on exit

concepts.L1: `&` background, `jobs`, `fg`, `bg`, Ctrl-Z suspends, `disown` detaches from the shell, `nohup` ignores HUP.
concepts.L2: A backgrounded job still dies when the terminal closes unless disowned or nohup'd. `tmux` or `screen` is the right answer for anything long-running, because it survives your ssh connection dropping.
concepts.L3: Job control is a property of the shell, not the kernel: `%1` is a shell-local label, `jobs` reads the shell's own table, and none of it survives the shell exiting. What the kernel provides is process groups - the foreground group is the one the terminal signals on Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z. An exiting interactive bash sends SIGHUP to its jobs; `disown -h` marks a job so bash skips it, while `nohup` starts the process with SIGHUP ignored, which is why nohup survives even a killed shell. Neither moves the process to a new session, so it still shares a terminal that may be gone - which is why tmux, whose server owns its own session, is the real answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have already started a {n}-hour migration in the foreground over ssh and your connection is unreliable. What is the correct recovery sequence?
L4.answer: Press Ctrl-Z to suspend it, `bg` to resume it in the background, then `disown -h %1` so the shell will not send it SIGHUP on exit. Redirect its output if you still need it, since it will keep writing to the terminal. Next time, start it inside tmux, which is the only option that lets you reattach and see the output.
L4.explanation: disown is a rescue, not a plan: it saves the process but not your ability to watch it, and it does not detach the process from the terminal's session, so output can still fail once the pty is gone.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a job started with `&` still dies when the ssh connection drops, and name the two mechanisms that prevent it.
L4.answer: When the connection drops, the terminal disappears and the kernel sends SIGHUP to the session's foreground process group; the shell also HUPs its own jobs as it exits. Backgrounding changes which group is foreground, not whether the process is in the session. The preventions are: nohup (start the process with SIGHUP ignored) or disown -h (tell the shell not to send it), and separately tmux or screen, which move the work into a session owned by a long-lived server process that the disconnect does not touch.
L4.explanation: The distinction that matters: nohup and disown suppress a signal, tmux removes the dependency entirely and also preserves the output and the ability to reattach.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Running `jobs -l` prints:
[1]- {pid_a} Running                 sleep 50 &
[2]+ {pid_b} Running                 sleep 60 &
With no argument, `fg` brings which job number to the foreground? Answer with just the job number, 1 or 2.
L4.explanation: Bash marks the current job with `+` and the previous job with `-` in its jobs table. A bare `fg`, `bg`, or the specifier `%+` always targets the current job, not the highest job number - they agree here only because job 2 was started most recently.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `rsync -a src dst &` and then `make -j8 &`. Which job specifier refers to the rsync job without needing to know its job number?
L4.answer: %rsync
L4.explanation: `%string` refers to the job whose command line begins with string, so `%rsync` names the rsync job directly. `%+` is the current job - here that is the more recently started make job. `%2` refers to job 2, which here is the make job (started second), not rsync - and even if it were rsync's number, you would still need to already know it, unlike `%rsync`, which names the command directly.
options: %rsync

L4.prompt_tpl: In an interactive bash shell, which key sequence sends SIGTSTP to stop the foreground job (suspending it, without terminating it)?
L4.answer: Ctrl-Z
L4.explanation: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, whose default action is Stop - the job halts but stays in the job table, resumable with `fg` or `bg`. Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which by default terminates the process. Ctrl-D is not a signal at all; it sends end-of-file on the terminal's input.
options: Ctrl-Z
Ctrl-C
Ctrl-D

L4.prompt_tpl: You background {k} jobs and one of them will exit with status {code}. If you call bare `wait` (no PID argument) and let all {k} finish, what exit status does `wait` itself return, regardless of whether any of the jobs failed?
L4.explanation: `wait` with no operands waits for every currently active background job and always returns 0 - it does not report the jobs' own failures. To capture one job's real exit status, wait on it by PID or job spec, e.g. `wait $!`, and read `$?` right after that call.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A script `deploy.sh` contains:
sleep {n} &
fg
echo done
You run it as `bash deploy.sh` (non-interactively, no terminal prompt). What happens at the `fg` line, and why?
L4.answer: It fails: bash prints `deploy.sh: line 2: fg: no job control` and, since `fg`'s own failure doesn't abort the script by default, execution falls through to `echo done`. `sleep {n} &` still worked - backgrounding a command is unconditional - but job control itself (`fg`, `bg`, Ctrl-Z, %-specifiers) is enabled only for interactive shells, or a script that explicitly turns it on with `set -m`, because its whole job is arbitrating which process group owns the controlling terminal, and a plain script run this way was never given that role.
L4.explanation: Verified: `bash -c 'sleep 100 & fg'` prints `bash: line 1: fg: no job control` while the backgrounding itself succeeds. Job control needs an interactive shell (or `set -m`) because `fg`/`bg` call `tcsetpgrp()` to hand the terminal to a process group, which only a monitoring shell is set up to do.

L4.prompt_tpl: A background job running `{cmd}` that tries to read from the terminal stops itself, with nobody sending a signal by hand and no permission error printed. Which signal does the kernel send it, and why does terminal input work this way instead of the read simply blocking or returning nothing?
L4.answer: SIGTTIN. A terminal has exactly one foreground process group at a time, set by the shell via `tcsetpgrp`, and only that group is allowed to read from it; when a process in a background group calls read() on the controlling terminal, the tty driver sends SIGTTIN to that process's whole group instead of returning data, and SIGTTIN's default disposition is Stop, the same as SIGTSTP - which is why `jobs` shows it stopped rather than hung or erroring. This exists so exactly one job at a time consumes keystrokes; without it, two programs racing to read the same input would be undefined. `fg` fixes it by moving the job into the terminal's foreground process group, after which its read succeeds and it resumes.
L4.explanation: Writing to the terminal from a background group only triggers the matching signal, SIGTTOU, if the tty's `tostop` option is set (off by default on Linux), which is why a background job that just prints output usually runs to completion while one that reads stdin stops immediately - the same foreground-process-group mechanism as job control's %-current-job bookkeeping, enforced by the kernel instead of the shell.

L0.body:
ps -ef                   # or ps aux, the BSD spelling
ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,stat,comm -p "$pid"   # pick your columns
pgrep -af nginx          # PIDs and command lines, by pattern
pkill -TERM -f "$pattern"

lsof -p "$pid"           # every file this process has open
lsof -i :8080            # who is listening on that port
lsof +L1                 # deleted-but-open files: the df/du gap

tr '\0' ' '  < /proc/$pid/cmdline   # the real argv (NUL separated)
tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/$pid/environ   # the env it was STARTED with
ls -l /proc/$pid/fd                 # open descriptors, as symlinks
L0.cloze:
ps -o pid,ppid,{{c1::pgid,sid}},comm -p $pid   # process group and session ids
{{c2::pgrep}} -af nginx        # find PIDs by command-line pattern
lsof {{c3::-i :8080}}          # which process holds that port
tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/$pid/{{c4::environ}}   # the environment the process was started with

concepts.L1: `ps aux`, `ps -ef`, `pgrep`/`pkill` by name, `lsof -p` open files, `lsof -i :8080` for a port, `/proc/PID/` for everything.
concepts.L2: `/proc/PID/environ`, `cmdline`, `limits`, `status`, `fd/` answer questions no tool exposes cleanly — including which file descriptor a process leaked and what environment it was actually started with, which is often different from what you think.
concepts.L3: `/proc/PID/` is the kernel's own view and answers questions no formatted tool exposes cleanly. `environ` is the environment at exec time, not the current one - exactly the question you want when a service behaves as though it has a different config than the file you edited, because the restart it never got would have picked it up. `cmdline` is the true argv, NUL-separated, so arguments containing spaces are unambiguous where `ps` output is already flattened. `fd/` is a directory of symlinks, so a leaked descriptor or a deleted-but-open file holding disk space shows up immediately. `limits` shows the rlimit behind 'Too many open files'.

L4.prompt_tpl: `df` reports the filesystem is {pct}% full but `du -sh` on every directory accounts for far less. What do you inspect and why?
L4.answer: lsof +L1, or ls -l /proc/PID/fd looking for links marked (deleted) - a process still holding an unlinked file keeps its blocks allocated, so the space is invisible to du (no directory entry) but counted by df (still allocated).
L4.explanation: Restarting the holding process releases the space immediately, which is why the usual fix is to find the process rather than to hunt for files. A log rotated by deletion rather than truncation is the most common cause.
options: lsof +L1, or ls -l /proc/PID/fd for links marked (deleted)
du -sh again with --apparent-size, since du was measuring wrong
Reboot the host to clear the filesystem cache

L4.prompt_tpl: A service is reading the old value of an environment variable you changed {n} deploys ago. Which single file tells you definitively what it is running with, and why is `env` in your shell not the answer?
L4.answer: /proc/PID/environ, read with tr '\\0' '\\n'. It is the environment captured at exec time for that specific process. Your shell's env shows your own environment, which says nothing about a daemon started by systemd or by an init script possibly weeks ago with a different environment file.
L4.explanation: Note the corollary: because environ is fixed at exec, editing an EnvironmentFile or a .env has no effect until the process is re-executed. Confirming this one fact usually ends the investigation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A daemon should already be listening on port {port}, but a health check keeps failing. Which single command tells you directly which process, if any, holds that port right now?
L4.answer: lsof -i :{port}
L4.explanation: lsof -i :{port} lists the network sockets bound to that port together with the PID and command holding it, in one step. Grepping ps output only works if the process happens to print the port on its command line; /proc/self/environ shows your own shell's environment, not the target process's socket.
options: lsof -i :{port}
ps -ef | grep {port}
cat /proc/self/environ

L4.prompt_tpl: `ls /proc/{pid}/fd | wc -l` shows {open} open file descriptors for a process, and `/proc/{pid}/limits` reports a soft Max open files limit of {lim}. How many more descriptors can it open before the kernel returns EMFILE, 'Too many open files'? Give the count.
L4.answer: Headroom = limit minus current count: the soft Max open files rlimit caps the whole fd table, including 0/1/2, which ls /proc/PID/fd already counts. E.g. limit 1024, 7 open: 1017 more. Limit 4096, 250 open: 3846 more.
L4.explanation: RLIMIT_NOFILE bounds the size of the entire per-process file-descriptor table, not just descriptors 'beyond the first three', so the count from ls /proc/PID/fd already includes stdin/stdout/stderr and the arithmetic is a plain subtraction against the limits file's soft value.

L4.prompt_tpl: This reproduces exactly what the L0 idiom does to read /proc/PID/cmdline: `printf '{a}\0{b}\0{c}\0' | tr '\0' ' '`. What single line does it print (on x86-64 Linux, GNU coreutils tr)?
L4.explanation: tr '\0' ' ' replaces every NUL byte with a space, including the one after the final field, so the three NUL-separated argv entries print on one line separated by single spaces - the same transform the L0 command applies to a real process's cmdline.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cleanup script does exactly this: `pid=$(pgrep -f {name}); sleep {secs}; kill -TERM "$pid"`. On a churny box it occasionally sends SIGTERM to an unrelated, newly started process instead of {name}. Name the race condition, and the Linux mechanism (added 5.1 and 5.3) that removes it.
L4.answer: PID reuse. Between the pgrep snapshot and the kill sent seconds later, the target process can exit and the kernel can recycle its now-free PID (Linux allocates PIDs cyclically up to /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max and wraps around) for a completely unrelated process, so the stored $pid no longer names the process you meant. pidfd_send_signal(2) (Linux 5.1+), paired with a stable file descriptor from pidfd_open(2) (5.3+), signals the exact process the fd was opened for; if it has already exited the call fails instead of silently hitting whoever reused the number.
L4.explanation: A PID is only a name the kernel can hand to a different process once its holder exits; kill -TERM $pid never re-checks that the name still points at the process you looked up (see Signals). Capturing a direct child's PID with $! right after launch (see wait, $! and parallelism in bash) is safer than a pgrep snapshot, since the PID is guaranteed yours until reaped.

L4.prompt_tpl: /proc/PID/stat records a process's user-mode and kernel-mode CPU time as utime and stime, in clock ticks, plus a starttime field: the ticks since boot at which the process began. getconf CLK_TCK on this box reports {hz} ticks per second, /proc/uptime's first field (system uptime) is {uptime} seconds, and this process shows utime = {ut} ticks, stime = {st} ticks, starttime = {starttime} ticks. Derive its percent CPU the way ps and top do: total CPU time divided by how long the process has actually been alive (elapsed real time), as a percentage.
L4.answer: Two steps. First, elapsed real time = uptime - starttime/CLK_TCK (how long ago the process started, in seconds). Second, %CPU = 100 * ((utime+stime)/CLK_TCK) / elapsed. E.g. hz=100, ut=4500, st=800, starttime=36000, uptime=7200: elapsed = 7200 - 360 = 6840 s, CPU time = 53.0 s, %CPU = 100*53/6840 = 0.775%. hz=250, ut=30000, st=5000, starttime=36000, uptime=7200: elapsed = 7200 - 144 = 7056 s, CPU time = 140.0 s, %CPU = 100*140/7056 = 1.984%.
L4.explanation: ps(1) defines %cpu as the cputime/realtime ratio: CPU time used divided by how long the process has been running. CPU time is (utime+stime)/CLK_TCK; realtime is current uptime minus the process's own start time, itself stored in ticks (starttime/CLK_TCK). Skipping the second division and reporting raw CPU seconds as a percentage is the bug this item is built to catch.

L0.body:
true;  echo $?     # 0    success
false; echo $?     # 1    generic failure
grep -q zz /nope   # 2    grep uses 1 for 'no match' and 2 for a REAL error

./not-executable   # 126  found but not executable
nosuchcommand      # 127  not found: a typo, a bad PATH, a missing .so

# 128+N when killed by signal N:
#   129 = HUP   130 = INT (Ctrl-C)   137 = KILL (9)   143 = TERM (15)

exit 300           # 44   — the status is one byte, taken modulo 256
# 137 in a container log means OOM-killed, essentially always

concepts.L1: 0 success, 1 general error, 2 misuse, 126 not executable, 127 not found, 128+N killed by signal N — so 137 is SIGKILL, 143 is SIGTERM.
concepts.L2: Exit code 137 in container logs means OOM-killed, essentially always. Recognizing that number instantly saves a great deal of time and is a small piece of knowledge with a very high hit rate.
concepts.L3: The status is a single byte, which is why `exit 300` becomes 44 - the shell takes it modulo 256. The 128+N convention partitions that byte so a caller can distinguish 'exited with 9' from 'killed by signal 9'; imperfectly, since a program may exit 137 itself, but reliably in practice. 137 in a container log is the highest-value number here: the OOM killer sends SIGKILL, so a pod that vanishes with 137 was over its memory limit. 143 means something asked it to stop politely. 127 usually means a wrong entrypoint path or a missing library. And non-zero is not always an error: grep uses 1 for 'no match' and 2 for a real failure.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`bash -c 'exit {n}'; echo $?`
What is printed?
L4.answer: 300 gives 44, 257 gives 1, 256 gives 0, 255 gives 255. The status is the value modulo 256.
L4.explanation: Exit statuses are a single unsigned byte in the wait status word. This is why scripts that return a count as an exit status silently report 0 when the count is a multiple of 256, and why counts belong on stdout instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A container in a {n}-replica deployment repeatedly terminates with exit code 137 and no application error in the logs. What happened?
L4.answer: It was killed by SIGKILL (128+9), and in a container that is essentially always the kernel OOM killer enforcing the memory limit. Raise the limit or reduce the footprint; there is no application bug to find in the logs because SIGKILL leaves no chance to log anything.
L4.explanation: The absence of application logs is itself the evidence: a process killed with SIGKILL never runs a handler, never flushes stdout, and so cannot record its own death. 143 would mean a graceful shutdown request; 1 would mean the process chose to fail.
options: Killed by SIGKILL, almost certainly the OOM killer hitting the memory limit
The application called exit(137) after an internal error
The orchestrator sent SIGTERM and the app shut down cleanly

L4.prompt_tpl:
The file named by {path} does not exist. Bash runs:
  `{util} {path}`
  `echo $?`
What number does the second line print?
L4.answer: 1. cat, wc and head all follow the ordinary coreutils convention (0 for success, 1 for a runtime error) rather than one of the documented exceptions such as sort or ls; a missing input file is a runtime error, so `$?` is 1 regardless of which of the three tools ran, even though the error message itself went to stderr.
L4.explanation: GNU coreutils documents one shared exit-status convention used by the large majority of its programs: 0 on success, nonzero (typically 1) on any failure. A named, short list of exceptions (ls, sort, test, expr, timeout among them) assign other meanings to 1 and 2; cat, wc and head are not on that list, so a missing file gives them exit status 1.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A directory named {dir} already exists. Bash runs:
  `mkdir {dir}`
  `echo $?`
What number does the second line print?
L4.answer: 1. mkdir follows the ordinary coreutils convention (0 for success, 1 for a runtime error) and is not one of the documented exceptions; trying to create a directory that already exists is a runtime error, so $? is 1 even though the diagnostic text goes to stderr, not to the exit status.
L4.explanation: Exit status is the machine-readable half of an error report and the stderr message is the human-readable half; a script that only checks $? never sees mkdir's own wording, which is exactly why the number, not the message, is what conditionals and CI systems act on.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Bash runs:
  `(exit {n})`
  `echo $?`
What number does the second line print?
L4.answer: n itself. `exit N` sets the subshell's exit status to N and the subshell exits immediately, so `(exit 0)` yields 0, `(exit 4)` yields 4, `(exit 200)` yields 200; the parentheses run it in a child shell so the parent script keeps going and $? reports exactly the N that was passed.
L4.explanation: exit N is the base case every other exit-status fact builds on: it sets the shell's (or subshell's) own exit status to N directly, with no translation, so long as 0 <= N <= 255. The parent's $? after the subshell finishes is that same N.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Bash runs:
  `{a} && echo yes || echo no`
  `echo $?`
What number does the second line print?
L4.answer: 0 either way. Whether the first word is true or false only decides which branch runs - echo yes or echo no - and both are plain echo calls that succeed. `$?` always reflects the most recently executed command, not the earlier one that chose the branch, so it is 0 whichever way the chain went.
L4.explanation: `$?` is overwritten by every command that runs, including ones that only exist to print a message. Reading `$?` right after a chain like this tells you about the last link in the chain, never about an earlier test - a frequent source of scripts that believe a failure never happened.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Bash runs:
  `result=$(exit {n})`
  `echo $?`
What number does the second line print?
L4.answer: n itself: a bare assignment is not a command with an outcome of its own, so bash defines the exit status of `var=$(cmd)` to be exactly the exit status of cmd. `result=$(exit 3)` leaves `$?` at 3, `result=$(exit 42)` leaves it at 42 - the assignment does not quietly reset the status to 0.
L4.explanation: This is why `if ! result=$(risky_cmd); then ...` works without a separate check: the assignment carries risky_cmd's status through. It stops working the moment `local` is added in front, because local is itself a command and overwrites `$?` with its own status - a known ShellCheck SC2155 trap.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A script:
  `trap '{cmd}' EXIT`
  `exit 7`
runs to completion and is invoked as `bash script.sh; echo $?` from the calling shell. What does the outer echo $? print?
L4.answer: 7, whichever of the three commands the trap runs. exit 7 fixes the script's own pending exit status the instant it executes; the EXIT trap then runs on top of that, and none of true, false or echo cleanup calls exit itself, so none of them can override the 7 the script already committed to.
L4.explanation: bash records the status passed to exit and reports that status to the caller once the EXIT trap finishes, unless the trap body itself calls exit with a different value. A trap command that merely succeeds or fails changes $? only while the trap is still executing, never the value the script eventually hands back. See Traps and cleanup.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A script:
  `grep -q {pattern} {file}`
  `if [ "$VERBOSE" = "1" ]; then echo checking; fi`
  `if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "grep failed"; fi`
never prints grep failed, even on a run where {pattern} truly is not in {file} and VERBOSE is unset. What is wrong?
L4.answer: The second if reads the exit status of the first if statement (0, because its condition was false and no branch ran), not grep's status, which is already gone by then
L4.explanation: POSIX defines the exit status of an if construct whose condition is false and which has no else as 0 - not the status of the failed condition test, and not grep's. Whatever grep returned was overwritten the moment the VERBOSE check ran, one line before anyone reads `$?`.
options: The second if reads the exit status of the first if statement (0, because its condition was false and no branch ran), not grep's status, which is already gone by then
grep -q always exits 0, so a failed match can never be detected this way
The test [ "$VERBOSE" = "1" ] itself exits 0 whenever VERBOSE is unset, and that is what the second if reads

L0.body:
ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,tty,stat,comm -p $$
#   PID   PPID   PGID    SID TTY   STAT COMMAND
#  4622   4610   4622   4610 pts/0 S    bash

#  SID  = session id      one login / one terminal
#  PGID = process group   what Ctrl-C signals (the FOREGROUND group)
#  TTY  = controlling terminal, or ? if there is none

setsid mycmd            # new session: SID = PID, and NO controlling terminal
ps -o pid,pgid,sid -p $$   # under setsid all three are equal

# hierarchy:  session  >  process groups  >  processes
# terminal disappears -> kernel SIGHUPs the session's foreground group
L0.cloze:
SID = the {{c1::session}} id — one per login or terminal
PGID = the {{c2::process group}} id — Ctrl-C signals the whole FOREGROUND group, not one process
{{c3::setsid}} mycmd   # start in a brand new session with no controlling terminal
# when the terminal goes away the kernel sends {{c4::SIGHUP}} to the foreground group

concepts.L1: The kernel groups processes three deep: a session contains process groups, a process group contains processes. A session has at most one controlling terminal, and exactly one of its process groups is the foreground group - the one the terminal delivers SIGINT, SIGQUIT and SIGTSTP to.
concepts.L2: Ctrl-C does not signal 'the command'; it signals every process in the foreground group. That is why interrupting `a | b | c` stops all three, and why a shell script that spawns children can be half-killed if it puts them in a different group.
concepts.L3: This is the machinery underneath every 'my job died when I closed the laptop' story. Closing the terminal destroys the pty; the kernel sends SIGHUP to that session's foreground process group, and bash additionally HUPs its own jobs on exit. A background job is still in the same session, so `&` alone does not save it. `setsid` calls setsid(2), making the process a session leader with a new session, a new process group and no controlling terminal - genuinely unreachable by the terminal's signals, which is what a daemon needs. tmux takes the same step: its server runs in its own session and allocates a pty per pane.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash -c 'ps -o pid,pgid,sid --no-headers -p $$'
  setsid bash -c 'ps -o pid,pgid,sid --no-headers -p $$'
For the second command, what relationship holds between the three numbers, and why not for the first?
L4.answer: Under setsid all three are equal: the process is a session leader, so its PID, PGID and SID are the same number. Without setsid the PID and PGID match but the SID is inherited from the parent shell's session, so it is a different, lower number.
L4.explanation: setsid(2) creates a new session with the caller as leader and a new process group with the caller as leader, and detaches the controlling terminal. That is the definition of daemonising, and it is why a setsid'd process is unaffected by the terminal's SIGHUP.

L4.prompt_tpl: Ctrl-C is pressed while `{a} | {b} | {c}` is running. Which processes receive SIGINT and why?
L4.answer: All three. The shell puts every stage of a pipeline into a single process group and makes that group the terminal's foreground group; the terminal driver delivers SIGINT to every member of the foreground group, not to one process. That is what makes Ctrl-C feel like it interrupts 'the command' even though a command is often several processes.
L4.explanation: The corollary matters in scripts: a background process started with & is in a different group and does not receive the Ctrl-C, so a script that launches helpers must trap INT and kill them explicitly, or start them in the same group.

L4.prompt_tpl: The kernel's response to a terminal hangup is SIGHUP, not SIGKILL, even though {daemon} could just as easily be killed outright. Which of these is the real reason the kernel uses SIGHUP here?
L4.answer: SIGHUP can be caught, blocked or ignored, so a well-behaved process gets the chance to clean up or opt out - exactly what nohup relies on by setting SIGHUP to ignore.
L4.explanation: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) are the two signals POSIX makes uncatchable and unblockable, on purpose, as an admin's last resort. The kernel does send SIGKILL itself in other contexts (the OOM killer is the well-known example) - the point here is that hangup is an ordinary, survivable event, not a last resort.
options: SIGHUP can be caught, blocked or ignored, so a well-behaved process gets the chance to clean up or opt out - exactly what nohup relies on by setting SIGHUP to ignore.
SIGKILL cannot be sent by the kernel itself, only by a user process calling kill(2), so it was never an option here.
SIGHUP is delivered faster than SIGKILL because it has a lower signal number and skips a scheduler round-trip.

L4.prompt_tpl: In one interactive bash session, `{x} & {y} &` starts two commands as two separate background jobs, while `{x} | {y}` starts them as one pipeline. How many process groups exist in each case, and why the difference?
L4.answer: Two process groups for the `&  &` form - each backgrounded command is its own job, and bash's job control gives every job its own process group. One process group for the `|` form - every stage of a single pipeline is one job, so all its processes share one process group, which is exactly why a signal aimed at that job reaches every stage together.
L4.explanation: A job, not a command, is the unit bash hands a process group to. A pipeline is one job with several processes; two backgrounded commands are two jobs, each with one process (or more, if either is itself a pipeline) - so the group boundary follows the job boundary, not the process count.

L4.prompt_tpl:
This runs as a non-interactive script (bash with job control off, i.e. `monitor` unset - the default outside an interactive shell):
  {cmd} &
  `echo "script pgid=$(ps -o pgid= -p $$)"; echo "bg pgid=$(ps -o pgid= -p $!)"`
Are the two printed numbers the same or different, and why would typing the identical `{cmd} &` at an interactive prompt behave differently?
L4.answer: The same number. Moving a backgrounded command into its own process group is part of job control, and bash's job control (the `monitor` option) is off by default whenever the shell is non-interactive, so `&` never creates a new group here - the child simply stays in the script's own process group. Typed at an interactive prompt, job control is on, so the identical command would get its own, different process group instead.
L4.explanation: Verified: in a non-interactive bash, `set -o | grep monitor` shows monitor off, and a backgrounded child's pgid matches the script's own pgid. This is why intuitions about backgrounding built at the interactive prompt do not automatically transfer into scripts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A background job running `{job}` is suspended with Ctrl-Z, and then the shell that owns its session exits without ever resuming or waiting on it. Its process group is now orphaned: no process outside the group is left in the session to control it. What does the kernel do to it, and why does POSIX specify exactly that instead of leaving it stopped forever?
L4.answer: It sends SIGHUP to every process in the newly orphaned group, immediately followed by SIGCONT. SIGHUP gives a well-behaved process a chance to catch it and exit cleanly, or at least die instead of lingering; SIGCONT guarantees the group actually resumes rather than staying stopped. Without this rule a stopped, orphaned group would sit stopped forever, since nothing is left able to send it a SIGCONT - it would waste its process slot and any memory or file locks it holds indefinitely.
L4.explanation: This is the same session/process-group machinery as the rest of this concept, applied to a case the L3 does not walk through: orphaning can happen without any terminal closing at all, purely because the controlling shell went away.

L4.prompt_tpl: The classic Unix daemonizing recipe forks, has the parent exit immediately, calls setsid() in the surviving child, then forks a second time and exits that first child too - only the second child, the grandchild, keeps running. Given that setsid() already makes the child a session leader with no controlling terminal, what does the second fork actually buy, and how would {app} be exposed without it?
L4.answer: On traditional System V/Linux terminal semantics, a session leader that has no controlling terminal acquires one automatically the moment it opens a terminal device without O_NOCTTY - so the child right after setsid() is still eligible to accidentally reacquire a controlling terminal (and with it, exposure to SIGHUP and the other terminal-generated signals) just by opening one, say to log an error to /dev/console. The second fork produces a process that is a member of the session but is not the session leader, and a non-leader can never acquire a controlling terminal by opening one - so only the grandchild is genuinely, permanently detached.
L4.explanation: This is fork(2)'s mechanics (see 'fork and copy-on-write') put to a specific, narrow use: dodging a single POSIX corner case in controlling-terminal acquisition, which is why the double fork looks like folklore until you trace the session rule it defeats.

concepts.t: nohup, disown and what actually survives

L0.body:
cmd &                 # backgrounded, SAME session — dies on SIGHUP
nohup cmd &           # starts with SIGHUP ignored; stdout -> ./nohup.out
cmd & disown -h %1    # tells THIS SHELL not to HUP it on exit
setsid cmd            # new session, no controlling terminal: a real daemon

# none of the first four detaches stdio from the terminal. Do it yourself:
nohup cmd > run.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &

tmux new -d -s work 'cmd'     # or just use tmux and keep the output
L0.cloze:
{{c1::nohup}} cmd &          # starts the process with SIGHUP set to IGNORE
cmd & {{c2::disown -h}} %1   # asks the SHELL not to send HUP to that job on exit
{{c3::setsid}} cmd           # new session + no controlling terminal — the real detach
nohup cmd > run.log 2>&1 {{c4::< /dev/null}} &   # detach stdin too, or it may block on read

concepts.L1: The three tools solve different halves of the same problem. `nohup` sets the process's SIGHUP disposition to ignore before exec. `disown` changes the shell's own jobs table so it does not send HUP. `setsid` moves the process into a new session with no controlling terminal.
concepts.L2: None of them redirects the process's standard streams away from the terminal, except `nohup`'s fallback of writing stdout to nohup.out. A surviving process whose stdout still points at a destroyed pty gets EIO on its next write and often dies anyway.
concepts.L3: Work through what a dropped ssh session actually does. The pty is destroyed; the kernel SIGHUPs the session's foreground group; the login shell, receiving HUP, HUPs its own jobs before exiting. `nohup` defeats the first path and `disown` the second, which is why people who use only one still occasionally lose jobs. But the process remains in the dead session with fds pointing at a gone terminal, so the honest form redirects all three streams: `nohup cmd > log 2>&1 < /dev/null &`. `setsid` is the clean version of all of this. In practice run long work under tmux or systemd: both give you the output back, which nohup's flat blob does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer runs `nohup ./migrate.sh &` over ssh and disconnects. {h} hours later the process is gone and nohup.out ends mid-line. Give two plausible causes that nohup does not protect against.
L4.answer: First, stdin was left attached to the destroyed pty: when the script reached a `read` (a confirmation prompt, or a tool that probes stdin) it got an I/O error rather than input and aborted. Second, nohup only ignores SIGHUP - the process is still in that session and can still be killed by anything else, and it is still a child of the dead shell's session for accounting purposes; an OOM kill, a SIGTERM from a deploy, or the machine's session-cleanup all end it. Redirecting < /dev/null and running under tmux or systemd address both.
L4.explanation: The general lesson: nohup is a single-signal shield, not a supervision strategy. Anything that must genuinely run for hours belongs in a session-scoped multiplexer or under an init system that will restart and log it.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to start a {n}-hour job on a remote host, watch its output tomorrow, and survive disconnection. Which approach?
L4.answer: tmux new -s job, run it inside, detach with the prefix key then d, and reattach later with tmux attach -t job. It survives disconnection, keeps the scrollback, and lets you interact with the process again.
L4.explanation: nohup survives the disconnect but discards interactivity and dumps output into a flat file with no scrollback search. Running it in the foreground and hoping is the failure this whole concept exists to prevent.
options: tmux new -s job, run it inside, detach and reattach later
nohup ./job.sh & and read nohup.out tomorrow
Run it in the foreground and keep the laptop awake

L4.prompt_tpl: Before nohup execs {cmd}, what has it already done to the SIGHUP signal's disposition for the process about to start?
L4.answer: Set it to be ignored (SIG_IGN), so a later hangup has no default action left to deliver
L4.explanation: POSIX's nohup spec and the GNU nohup(1) man page agree: nohup sets SIGHUP to be ignored before it invokes the named utility, and an ignored disposition is preserved across exec, so the child starts already immune to it.
options: Set it to be ignored (SIG_IGN), so a later hangup has no default action left to deliver
Blocked it with sigprocmask so it queues until the process explicitly unblocks it
Left it at the default action and relies on the nohup.out redirection to protect the process instead

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `nohup {cmd}` and {cmd} is not on PATH, so it can never be invoked at all. What exit status does nohup itself return?
L4.answer: 127, the coreutils convention for a command that could not be found
L4.explanation: Per the nohup(1) man page: nohup exits 125 if nohup itself fails, 126 if the command is found but cannot be invoked, 127 if the command cannot be found, and otherwise passes through the command's own exit status.
options: 127, the coreutils convention for a command that could not be found
0, because nohup itself ran fine even though the command did not exist
1, the generic catch-all shell failure code

L4.prompt_tpl: You background a job as {job} and then run `disown -h {job}` instead of plain `disown {job}`. What is the practical difference?
L4.answer: -h keeps the job visible in `jobs` but marks it so the shell will not send it SIGHUP if the shell itself receives SIGHUP; plain disown removes it from the jobs table entirely
L4.explanation: The bash reference manual is explicit: without -h, disown removes the job from the jobs table; with -h, the job stays in the table but is marked so the shell will not resend SIGHUP to it before exiting.
options: -h keeps the job visible in `jobs` but marks it so the shell will not send it SIGHUP if the shell itself receives SIGHUP; plain disown removes it from the jobs table entirely
-h immediately sends SIGHUP to the job as a test that it survives; plain disown waits until the shell exits to test it
They are equivalent; -h only exists for compatibility with old scripts and changes nothing about signal delivery

L4.prompt_tpl: Inside a script whose own stdout is already redirected to a file, it runs `nohup {cmd} | tee out.log &`. Does a nohup.out file appear anywhere, and where does {cmd}'s output actually go?
L4.answer: No nohup.out appears. nohup only substitutes nohup.out for standard output when standard output is connected to a terminal at the moment nohup runs; here stdout is already the write end of a pipe into tee, which is not a terminal, so nohup leaves it alone. {cmd}'s output flows down that pipe into tee, which writes it to out.log.
L4.explanation: The nohup.out fallback is conditional on isatty(stdout), not automatic. People who redirect or pipe nohup's output and then go looking for nohup.out are chasing a file that was never going to be created.

L4.prompt_tpl: A deploy script runs `ssh {host} 'nohup ./release.sh > release.log 2>&1 < /dev/null & disown -h'` and returns immediately. Trace why release.sh keeps running after the ssh connection closes, then name one failure mode this setup still does not protect against.
L4.answer: nohup already set SIGHUP to be ignored before exec, so release.sh cannot be torn down by any HUP forwarded its way; redirecting all three fds away from the pty means nothing later tries to read or write a terminal that is about to disappear and gets EIO; disown -h stops the remote shell from resending it HUP on the way out too, so both of the usual delivery paths are closed. What it still does not protect against: anything else that can kill the process outright, such as an OOM kill, a deploy script that pattern-kills stray processes, or the host rebooting - nothing here restarts it or lets you see its output live, which is exactly what a supervisor like systemd, or a multiplexer like tmux, would give you.
L4.explanation: This is the whole concept in one instance: nohup and disown each close one HUP delivery path, the explicit redirects close the stdio-to-dead-terminal path, and none of that is process supervision. Unlike `wait, $! and parallelism in bash`, there is no shell left here to wait on anything.

L0.body:
sleep 2 & a=$!
sleep 2 & b=$!
wait "$a" "$b"          # both ran concurrently: ~2s, not 4s

bash -c 'exit 5' & wait "$!"; echo "$?"    # 5 — wait returns the CHILD's status

wait                    # wait for ALL children; status is 0
wait -n                 # return as soon as ANY one child finishes

# bounded parallelism without a job queue:
for f in *.log; do
    process "$f" &
    while (( $(jobs -rp | wc -l) >= 4 )); do wait -n; done
done
wait

xargs -P4 -n1 -0 process < <(printf '%s\0' *.log)   # usually the better tool
L0.cloze:
cmd & p={{c1::$!}}          # PID of the most recent background job
{{c2::wait}} "$p"; echo "$?"    # blocks, then reports THAT child's exit status
wait {{c3::-n}}              # return as soon as any one child finishes
{{c4::xargs -P4}} -n1 cmd       # bounded parallelism, without hand-rolling a job queue

concepts.L1: `&` starts a child and returns immediately; `$!` is its PID and must be captured on the very next line because the next `&` overwrites it. `wait PID` blocks until that child exits and returns its exit status; bare `wait` waits for all children and always returns 0.
concepts.L2: Because bare `wait` returns 0 regardless, a loop that backgrounds N jobs and then calls `wait` reports success even when every job failed. You must wait on each PID individually, or collect statuses with `wait -n`.
concepts.L3: The pattern that actually works: keep an array of PIDs, then `for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p" || rc=1; done`. That gives concurrency and a truthful overall status. `wait -n` (bash 4.3+) returns when any child finishes, which is what lets you cap concurrency - launch, then block until a slot frees. Two cautions. Backgrounded jobs are subshells, so nothing they assign is visible to the parent; results must come back through files or a pipe. And under `set -e` a failing background job does not abort the script - only the `wait` that observes it can. Beyond a handful of items, `xargs -P` is less code and handles queue and status for you.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`bash -c 'exit {n}' & p=$!`
  `wait "$p"; echo "single=$?"`
  `bash -c 'exit {n}' &`
  `bash -c 'exit {n}' &`
  `wait; echo "all=$?"`
What are the two lines?
L4.answer: single= the chosen status (5, 3 or 9), and all=0.
L4.explanation: wait with a PID argument reports that child's exit status, which is what makes it usable for error handling. Bare wait waits for every child and returns 0 unconditionally, so a fan-out loop followed by a bare wait cannot detect failures.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`for f in *.{ext}; do`
      `convert "$f" &`
  `done`
  `wait`
  `echo "all converted"`
Several conversions fail but the script reports success and exits 0. Fix it.
L4.answer: Bare wait always returns 0. Collect the PIDs and wait on each: pids=(); for f in *.png; do convert "`$f`" & pids+=(`$!`); done; rc=0; for p in "`${pids[@]}`"; do wait "`$p`" || rc=1; done; exit "`$rc`". Alternatively use xargs -P4 -0, which propagates a non-zero status when any command fails.
L4.explanation: Also note that unbounded & over a large glob will fork thousands of processes at once. The PID-array form fixes correctness; xargs -P or a wait -n throttle fixes both correctness and resource use.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`bash -c "exit {n}" & wait -n; echo "$?"`
Only one background job exists when `wait -n` runs. What number does this print?
L4.answer: n itself (4, 6 or 11 depending on the draw): with a single background job, wait -n has nothing to pick between, so it behaves exactly like wait on that job's PID and reports its real exit status.
L4.explanation: wait -n returns as soon as any one background job finishes and reports THAT job's exit status. With only one job running, that is the only job it can return, so it prints the job's real status, not an unconditional 0.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`sleep 0.3 & first=$!`
`bash -c "exit {n}" & second=$!`
`wait "$second"`
`echo "$?"`
Two jobs are running in the background. What does the final echo print?
L4.answer: n itself (5, 8 or 23 depending on the draw): wait given an explicit PID (or `wait "$!"` captured right after backgrounding) waits for that one job specifically and reports its own real exit status.
L4.explanation: `wait PID` (or `wait "$!"`) waits only for that one job and returns its real exit status, unlike bare wait, which always returns 0 no matter which child failed. Passing wait an explicit PID or job spec is how a script actually recovers one background job's exit code.

L4.prompt_tpl:
`x=0`
`( x={val} ) &`
`wait`
`echo "$x"`
What does the final echo print?
L4.answer: 0. The parenthesised assignment runs in a subshell that is then backgrounded, so it has its own private copy of x; the parent's x is never touched, whatever {val} was.
L4.explanation: `cmd &` (and `( ... )` on its own) runs in a subshell: it gets a copy of the parent's variables, not a reference. Assignments inside it die with the subshell. Results from a background job must come back through a file, a pipe, or command substitution, never a plain variable.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop backgrounds {N} independent jobs, each taking exactly {T} seconds, capped to {P} concurrent jobs by `while (( $(jobs -rp | wc -l) >= {P} )); do wait -n; done`. Assuming every job takes the same {T} seconds, about how many seconds of wall-clock time does the whole loop take?
L4.answer: T * ceil(N/P). Because every job takes the same T, the pool fills, empties, and refills in lockstep: the N jobs finish in ceil(N/P) equal-length rounds of P jobs each, so total time is T times that many rounds (e.g. N=10, P=4, T=2 -> ceil(10/4)=3 -> 6 seconds).
L4.explanation: With uniform job duration, wait -n only ever frees a slot when the whole current batch of P jobs has finished at once, so the loop advances in ceil(N/P) rounds of length T. This is the same batch-size reasoning behind xargs -P's throughput, and it breaks down as soon as job durations differ.

L4.prompt_tpl:
On x86-64 Linux, bash 5.x:
`trap "echo TRAP_FIRED" {signum}`
`sleep 5 & child=$!`
`( sleep 1; kill -{signum} $$ ) &`
`wait "$child"`
`echo "$?"`
After TRAP_FIRED prints, what number does the final echo print?
L4.answer: 128 + signum (138, 143 or 140 for signum 10, 15 or 12): a signal that has a trap set, delivered while wait is blocked, makes wait return immediately with status 128+signal-number and then runs the trap, even though the sleep it was waiting on has not actually died.
L4.explanation: Per the Bash Reference Manual's Signals section, wait interrupted by a trapped signal returns at once with an exit status greater than 128, and only then does the trap run. This is the same 128+n convention Signals uses for a process actually killed by n, and it is why Traps and cleanup must check `$?` rather than assume wait always reports the child.

L0.body:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host prod-*
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_prod
    ProxyJump bastion.example.com
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p
    ControlPersist 10m

Host bastion.example.com
    User jump

# then:
ssh prod-web01                  # first connection opens the master
ssh prod-web01 uptime           # subsequent ones reuse the TCP+TLS session

ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 bastion    # local port -> remote-side host
ssh -R 8080:localhost:3000 remote       # expose a local service on the remote
L0.cloze:
Host prod-*
    ProxyJump {{c1::bastion.example.com}}   # reach it through a jump host, no nested ssh
    ControlMaster {{c2::auto}}
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p
    ControlPersist {{c3::10m}}          # keep the master open this long after the last session

ssh {{c4::-L}} 5432:db.internal:5432 bastion   # forward a LOCAL port to a remote-side address

concepts.L1: `~/.ssh/config` with Host aliases, `ProxyJump` for bastions, `ControlMaster` for connection reuse, `-L`/`-R` for tunnels, `ssh-agent` forwarding (carefully).
concepts.L2: `ControlMaster auto` with `ControlPersist` makes subsequent ssh connections to the same host near-instant by reusing the TCP session. On a workflow with many short ssh calls it's transformative and almost unknown.
concepts.L3: Every fresh ssh connection pays a TCP handshake, a key exchange, host-key verification and authentication - typically 200 ms to over a second across a WAN, per invocation, so a deploy script making forty `ssh host cmd` calls pays it forty times. `ControlMaster auto` opens one multiplexed connection and routes later sessions down it as channels; `ControlPersist 10m` keeps that master alive after the last session closes. `ProxyJump` replaces the old `ProxyCommand ssh -W` incantation and terminates the inner encryption at the target, so the bastion never sees your traffic. `ssh -G host` prints the fully resolved config, which settles most 'why is it using that key' questions.

L4.prompt_tpl: A deploy loop makes {n} separate `ssh host cmd` calls. Connection setup costs {ms} ms and the command itself {c} ms. Give total wall time with and without ControlMaster, and the speedup. Answer with the total wall time in milliseconds with ControlMaster.
L4.answer: Without reuse: $n \times (ms + c)$. With reuse: $ms + n \times c$ (one setup, then per-command cost). For n=40, ms=250, c=50: 12000 ms versus 2250 ms, a speedup of about 5.3. For n=100, ms=400, c=20: 42000 ms versus 2400 ms, about 17.5.
L4.explanation: The speedup approaches ms/c as n grows, so multiplexing matters most exactly where it is used most - short commands over a high-latency link. This is why an unfamiliar deploy script can get several times faster from four lines of ssh_config.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CI job needs to reach db.internal:{port}, which only listens on the private network, from a runner outside it. Compare `ssh -L` against enabling agent forwarding to a bastion and connecting from there.
L4.answer: ssh -L is the right tool: it binds a local port on the runner and tunnels the traffic, and the private key never leaves the runner. Agent forwarding puts a socket on the bastion that lets anyone with root there sign challenges with your key for as long as the session lasts - it grants use of the key, not just of the connection. If a jump is genuinely needed, use ProxyJump, which forwards the connection rather than the credential.
L4.explanation: The rule: forward ports, not agents. When agent forwarding is unavoidable, restrict it to specific hosts in ssh_config, use a hardware-backed key that requires touch confirmation, and never enable ForwardAgent globally.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run ssh with {n} separate -L flags in one invocation, each forwarding a different local port to a different remote-side destination over the same connection. How many local TCP listening sockets does ssh open on your machine for these forwards? Answer with the count.
L4.answer: Each -L flag asks ssh to open its own local listening socket and route accepted connections down the one shared encrypted channel to its own destination - the forwards multiplex the underlying connection, not the local sockets themselves. For n=2: 2 sockets. For n=5: 5 sockets.
L4.explanation: A single ssh session can multiplex many independent forwards, but each `-L` still claims its own local listening socket - the sharing is over the one underlying TCP-plus-encryption channel to the far end, not over local sockets themselves.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to reach {target} through two bastion hosts in sequence: first {jump1}, then {jump2}. Which single ssh command establishes that chain?
L4.answer: ssh -J {jump1},{jump2} {target}
L4.explanation: -J takes a comma-separated list of hops traversed in order from nearest to you to farthest, so `-J {jump1},{jump2}` reaches {jump1} first and tunnels through it to {jump2} and on to {target}. A colon inside one hop separates host from port ({jump1}:port), not one hop from the next, and reversing the list changes which host your machine must reach directly.
options: ssh -J {jump1},{jump2} {target}
ssh -J {jump1}:{jump2} {target}
ssh -J {jump2},{jump1} {target}

L4.prompt_tpl: A teammate adds `ControlMaster auto` and `ControlPath {dir}/%r@%h:%p` to their ssh_config, but never creates the `{dir}` directory. They say ssh still works but ControlMaster does not seem to do anything - connections are not noticeably faster. What is actually happening, and how would you confirm it?
L4.answer: ssh cannot create the control socket because its parent directory does not exist: the bind fails with ENOENT and ssh prints `unix_listener: cannot bind to path <path>: No such file or directory` to stderr, then degrades gracefully - every call falls back to an ordinary, unshared connection rather than aborting. That line is not suppressed, it is just one line among the rest of the session's output, easy to miss in scrollback or a redirected/scripted run. Confirm it with `ssh -O check host`: a live master answers `Master running (pid=NNNN)`, while no master gives `Control socket connect(...): No such file or directory`.
L4.explanation: ControlMaster's fallback is graceful, not silent: ssh does print a `unix_listener: cannot bind to path ...` error to stderr when the ControlPath directory is missing, but a missing directory still produces ssh that works but is not sped up, and one stderr line is easy to miss without connecting it to ControlMaster. `mkdir -p` the directory once and the same config starts multiplexing.

L4.prompt_tpl: From your laptop you run `ssh -R {port}:localhost:{svc} {remote}` to expose a local dev server to a colleague. They ssh separately into {remote} and try to curl localhost:{port} from a different machine on the same network as {remote} - not from {remote} itself. Does that work, and why?
L4.answer: No, not by default: OpenSSH's server-side GatewayPorts setting defaults to no, so a -R forward binds only to the loopback interface on {remote} itself, reachable from a process running on {remote} but not from another host on {remote}'s network. Reaching it elsewhere needs GatewayPorts yes (bind all interfaces) or clientspecified (client chooses the bind address) in {remote}'s sshd_config, or a further hop from {remote} to that other machine.
L4.explanation: The trap: -R looks like it exposes a port on the network, but by default it only opens a loopback-bound listener on the ssh server. GatewayPorts is a server-side setting the client cannot override with -R alone unless the server permits clientspecified.

L4.prompt_tpl: A backup script calls `rsync -e ssh` against the same host {n} times in a row, once per directory, and each call pays its own ssh handshake because -e ssh spawns a fresh ssh client process per invocation. Design the one change to ~/.ssh/config that removes the repeated handshake cost without touching the rsync command at all, and explain why it works.
L4.answer: Add a Host block for that host with ControlMaster auto, a ControlPath such as ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p, and a ControlPersist like 10m. rsync -e ssh still launches a plain ssh client each call, but ssh itself checks ControlPath before opening a new connection: the first of the {n} calls creates the master and pays the handshake, and the rest reuse it as multiplexed channels at near-zero connect cost - no rsync flag changes, because the reuse happens inside the ssh client rsync shells out to.
L4.explanation: The same mechanism this concept's ControlMaster template applies to `ssh host cmd` loops applies to any tool that shells out to ssh per call, including rsync and scp, because the reuse decision is made inside the ssh client itself before the caller's own logic ever runs.

prereqs: SSH keys, the agent, and forwarding risk

L0.body:
tmux new -s work          # create a named session
tmux ls                   # list sessions
tmux attach -t work       # reattach after a disconnect
tmux new -d -s job 'cmd'  # start detached, running one command

# default prefix is Ctrl-b:
#   d    detach (the session keeps running)
#   c    new window        n / p   next / previous window
#   %    split vertically  "       split horizontally
#   [    copy mode: scroll back, then / to search

# tmux runs a SERVER in its own session: your client disconnecting is not its problem
L0.cloze:
tmux new {{c1::-s}} work        # create a NAMED session so you can find it again
tmux {{c2::attach}} -t work     # reattach after your connection drops
# prefix then {{c3::d}}          detach, leaving the session running
# prefix then {{c4::[}}          copy mode: scroll back and search the output

concepts.L1: Sessions survive disconnection. Windows and panes, `tmux attach`, copy mode for scrollback search.
concepts.L2: Starting long-running work inside tmux by reflex is the habit that prevents 'my deployment died because my wifi dropped'. It costs nothing and the failure it prevents is expensive.
concepts.L3: The mechanism explains why tmux is categorically different from `nohup`. tmux starts a long-lived server in its own session, and every pane is a pseudo-terminal owned by that server rather than by your ssh connection; your `tmux` command is just a client talking to it over a socket. When the connection drops the client dies and the server notices nothing - the pty is still there, the shell inside still has a valid controlling terminal, and no SIGHUP is generated. That is also why the scrollback survives, why two machines can attach the same session, and why `tmux new -d -s job 'cmd'` is a complete solution for a long job.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a job inside tmux survives a dropped ssh connection while `./job.sh &` does not, in terms of sessions and SIGHUP.
L4.answer: The backgrounded job is in the ssh login session and its controlling terminal is the pty ssh created; when the connection drops that pty is destroyed and the kernel SIGHUPs the session's foreground group, and the exiting shell HUPs its jobs too. A tmux pane's controlling terminal is a pty owned by the tmux server, which lives in its own session that the ssh disconnect does not touch - so no terminal is destroyed and no SIGHUP is generated.
L4.explanation: The corollary is that tmux also preserves the output and the ability to type into the process, which nohup does not. It is a different mechanism, not a stronger version of the same one.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want to kick off a {n}-hour job on a remote host right now and check on it from a different laptop tomorrow. Which command?
L4.answer: tmux new -d -s job './run.sh' — it creates a named detached session owned by the tmux server, so the job starts immediately, survives your disconnect, and `tmux attach -t job` from any client tomorrow shows the live output and scrollback.
L4.explanation: Disown removes the job from bash's job table, so it is skipped by the SIGHUP bash resends to its jobs on exit — it does survive, unlike a truly bare '&'. What it actually lacks is a live pane: no captured output, no way to type into it tomorrow, only 'ps' to confirm it is still running.
options: tmux new -d -s job './run.sh', then tmux attach -t job tomorrow
nohup ./run.sh & and tail nohup.out tomorrow
./run.sh & disown, then check ps tomorrow

L4.prompt_tpl: You open one tmux window (one pane) and run tmux split-window -h exactly {n} times in a row, each time splitting whichever pane is newest. How many panes does the window have now?
L4.answer: Every split-window call turns one pane into two, so it adds exactly one pane regardless of -h or -v. Starting from 1 pane, n splits give n+1 panes: n=3 gives 4, n=5 gives 6.
L4.explanation: Verified directly (tmux 3.4): starting one window and calling split-window -h n times for n=2..5 produced 3, 4, 5, 6 panes respectively (tmux list-panes | wc -l). The orientation of the split does not change the count, only the layout.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which single tmux new-session flag starts the session running but does not attach your current terminal to it?
L4.answer: -d
L4.explanation: tmux new-session -d -s job 'cmd' creates the session and returns you to your shell immediately; without -d, new-session attaches you to the session it just created. Confirmed against tmux(1) and by running both forms.

L4.prompt_tpl: Inside a shell running in a tmux pane, which environment variable is set (and is unset in a plain terminal) that scripts use to detect they are already inside tmux?
L4.answer: TMUX
L4.explanation: Verified with tmux send-keys and capture-pane: a pane's shell sees TMUX=/tmp/tmux-<uid>/default,<server-pid>,<session-id> and TMUX_PANE=%<n>. Nested tmux checks and prompt scripts key off TMUX being non-empty.

L4.prompt_tpl: You already have a session named deploy running. From a second terminal you accidentally type tmux new -s deploy again. What happens to the original session?
L4.answer: tmux refuses with "duplicate session: deploy" and exits 1; the original session is untouched
L4.explanation: Verified: running tmux new-session -d -s __dup twice printed "duplicate session: __dup" and exited 1 on the second call, and the first session kept running unmodified. new-session never merges into or attaches an existing name for you — that is what attach is for.
options: tmux refuses with "duplicate session: deploy" and exits 1; the original session is untouched
tmux silently attaches your second terminal to the existing deploy session instead
tmux creates a second, independent session also called deploy and both run side by side

L4.prompt_tpl: In a tmux session with exactly one window and one pane, typing exit at the prompt destroys the whole session, but closing the terminal emulator window your ssh connection was running in does not. Explain the difference.
L4.answer: exit terminates the shell, which was the only process attached to the only pane; when a pane's process exits tmux closes that pane, and closing the last pane of the last window destroys the session (and, with no sessions left, the server exits too, by default exit-empty behaviour). Closing the terminal emulator only drops the client-to-server socket connection — no process inside any pane is touched, so the session, its panes and their shells keep running exactly as before.
L4.explanation: Verified directly: sending 'exit' into the sole pane of a fresh session left "no server running" afterward (has-session then failed), while detaching or losing a client never affects has-session. The asymmetry is the whole reason tmux is used for long jobs.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a shared multi-user server (everyone logs in with their own account, not a container) you run tmux new -s work. A colleague with a different account on the same box runs ls /tmp and sees your socket directory, then tries tmux -S /tmp/tmux-<your-uid>/default attach. Can they get into your session? What actually stops or allows it?
L4.answer: No, by default: tmux creates its per-user socket directory as mode 0700 owned by the real uid that started the server (confirmed here: drwx------ on /tmp/tmux-<uid>, containing the srw-rw---- socket). /tmp itself is world-readable so the directory name is visible, but entering it or connecting to the socket inside it requires the owner's uid (or root) because of that 0700 bit — the colleague's attach fails with a permission error before tmux protocol even runs. This is an ordinary filesystem permission, not a tmux-specific safeguard, so it fails open if something (a misconfigured TMUX_TMPDIR, a shared /tmp with odd mount options, or root) changes those permissions.
L4.explanation: Verified: a fresh tmux server's socket directory was drwx------ owned by the starting user, with the socket file itself srw-rw---- inside it. The protection is entirely the directory's execute bit, which is why TMUX_TMPDIR pointing somewhere with looser permissions is a real way to weaken it.

prereqs: nohup, disown and what actually survives
