L0.body:
rsync -avzP src/ user@host:/dst/     # contents of src INTO dst
rsync -avzP src  user@host:/dst/     # creates /dst/src/ — the directory itself

#  -a  archive: recursive, preserve perms, times, symlinks, owner/group
#  -v  verbose   -z compress in transit   -P partial + progress (resumable)
#  --delete       remove files at the destination that are gone from the source
#  --dry-run / -n ALWAYS run this first when --delete is involved
#  -e 'ssh -p 2222'    choose the transport

rsync -avn --delete src/ dst/ | tail   # rehearse the deletions before doing them
L0.cloze:
rsync -avzP src{{c1::/}} host:/dst/     # this trailing slash means 'the CONTENTS of src'
rsync -avzP src  host:/dst/     # without it you get {{c2::/dst/src/}}
rsync {{c3::--delete}} ...              # make the destination match the source exactly
rsync {{c4::-n}} --delete ...           # rehearse it first — this flag changes nothing on disk

concepts.L1: `rsync -avzP --delete src/ dst/`. Delta transfer, resumable, preserves attributes. The trailing slash on the source controls whether the directory itself is copied.
concepts.L2: The trailing-slash semantics are the most common rsync mistake — `src` copies the directory, `src/` copies its contents. Getting it wrong nests a directory inside itself and the `--delete` flag then makes it destructive.
concepts.L3: The rsync algorithm is why the tool exists: the receiver splits its copy into fixed blocks and sends a rolling checksum plus a strong hash for each; the sender rolls the same weak checksum over its own version byte by byte and transmits only the literal bytes matching no known block, so a one-line change in a gigabyte file costs a few kilobytes. The trailing slash is the operational trap - `src/` means the contents of src, `src` means the directory - and getting it wrong with `--delete` first creates `/dst/src/` and then removes everything else under `/dst`. Rehearse with `-n` whenever `--delete` appears. Note `-a` implies neither `-H`, `-A` nor `-X`.

L4.prompt_tpl:
The directory {s} contains one file, data.txt. What path does the file end up at for each command? Answer in the form `A: <path> B: <path>`, using absolute paths.
  A: rsync -a {s}/ /backup/
  B: rsync -a {s} /backup/
L4.answer: A: /backup/data.txt B: /backup/{s}/data.txt
L4.explanation: Reading the trailing slash as 'the contents of' makes it memorable: `{s}/` copies data.txt straight into /backup/, while `{s}` with no slash copies the directory itself so it lands at /backup/{s}/data.txt. The mistake compounds: run B twice thinking it is A and you get /backup/{s}/{s}/, and adding --delete to 'fix' that then removes everything else under /backup.

L4.prompt_tpl: A nightly job runs `rsync -a --delete {s}/ /srv/data/`. One night {s} is empty because an earlier mount failed. What happens, and give two independent safeguards.
L4.answer: --delete makes the destination match the source, so an empty source deletes everything under /srv/data. Safeguards: (1) --max-delete=N so the run aborts rather than removing more than a plausible number of files; (2) verify the mount before running - mountpoint -q /mnt/source || exit 1 - and add set -euo pipefail so the check aborts the script. A third worth having is a dry run with -n whose output is diffed against expectations, and destination snapshots so the mistake is recoverable.
L4.explanation: This is one of the classic real-world data-loss incidents and it is not a bug in rsync: --delete did exactly what it was asked. The defence is to make the precondition explicit and to bound the blast radius.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which flag combination is `rsync -a` (archive mode) exactly equivalent to?
L4.answer: -rlptgoD
L4.explanation: -a expands to -rlptgoD: recursive, preserve symlinks, permissions, times, group and owner, and copy device/special files. It does NOT imply -H (hard links), -A (ACLs) or -X (extended attributes) - those cost extra time to preserve and must be requested explicitly.
options: -rlptgoD
-rlptgoDH
-rtgoD

L4.prompt_tpl: A source tree totals {total} MB. rsync's delta-transfer algorithm reports that {pct}% of that data matched blocks already present at the destination and so was not sent. How many MB of literal data were actually transmitted?
L4.answer: Bytes sent = total x (100 - matched%) / 100, since only the unmatched fraction has to cross the wire as literal data. total=500 MB, pct=90%: sent = 500 x 10 / 100 = 50 MB. total=4000 MB, pct=99%: sent = 4000 x 1 / 100 = 40 MB.
L4.explanation: This is the whole point of the rolling-checksum algorithm in L3: the receiver already holds most of the blocks, so only the fraction that failed to match anything - here (100-pct)% of the tree - needs to be transmitted as literal bytes.

L4.prompt_tpl: In `rsync -avzP`, the `-P` flag is shorthand for which two long flags, and which of them changes what happens to a transfer that gets interrupted partway through?
L4.answer: -P = --partial --progress; --partial keeps a partially-transferred file on the destination instead of deleting it, so it can be resumed from later.
L4.explanation: By default rsync deletes an interrupted transfer's partial file. --partial (bundled into -P along with --progress) keeps it instead, so a later rerun of the same command can treat it as a starting point and only the missing tail has to cross the wire again.
options: -P = --partial --progress; --partial keeps a partially-transferred file on the destination instead of deleting it, so it can be resumed from later.
-P = --partial --progress; --partial deletes any partial file immediately on interruption so the next run always starts from zero.
-P = --progress --stats; neither of these affects what happens to a partial file, since rsync always keeps it by default.

L4.prompt_tpl: A teammate runs `rsync -avzP src/ user@remote:/backup/` against a host whose sshd listens on port {port} instead of the default 22, and gets `ssh: connect to host remote port 22: Connection refused`. What is missing from the command, and what should it become?
L4.answer: rsync's own flags carry no notion of an SSH port; over ssh it just execs whatever command -e/--rsh names, defaulting to plain `ssh`. The fix is `rsync -avzP -e 'ssh -p {port}' src/ user@remote:/backup/`, exactly the -e 'ssh -p 2222' pattern this concept's L0 shows for choosing the transport.
L4.explanation: Because -e names the whole remote-shell command, any ssh option - a nonstandard port, an identity file, ProxyJump - has to be threaded through that string rather than given to rsync directly. Forgetting it produces an ordinary ssh connection failure, not an rsync error.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {size_gb} GB file gets a {edit_bytes}-byte insertion in the middle, shifting every following byte by that amount. Explain why rsync's rolling-checksum block matching still finds almost all of the unchanged data as already-present blocks, while comparing fixed byte-offset chunks - or comparing one whole-file content hash, the way git addresses a blob - would find almost none of it.
L4.answer: The receiver splits its (old, unedited) copy once into fixed, non-overlapping blocks and sends a rolling checksum plus a strong hash for each. The sender then rolls the same weak checksum in constant time at every byte offset as it scans its own edited copy, so even though the insertion pushed a given block's content forward by {edit_bytes} bytes, the sender's sliding window still hits that new offset and recognises it as matching a block the receiver already has; the paired strong hash then confirms the match. Only the inserted {edit_bytes} bytes plus roughly one block on either side fail to match anything. Fixed-offset chunking would instead compare corresponding positions in the two files directly, so every chunk after the insertion point is misaligned with its old content and reads as entirely different. A whole-file hash - what git stores as a blob's object id - answers a single yes/no question, are these two files byte-identical, with no notion of a partial or shifted match, so it cannot say which pieces changed at all.
L4.explanation: The defining property is that the weak checksum updates in O(1) per byte shift, so the search for a match is not tied to fixed block boundaries. Contrast this with 'Git plumbing': content-addressing by whole-object hash answers a global equality question and was never built to solve delta-transfer, which is exactly the problem rsync's algorithm exists for.

L0.body:
git reflog                     # every position HEAD has held, ~90 days
git reset --hard 'HEAD@{1}'    # undo the reset/rebase/merge you just regretted

git bisect start HEAD v1.2     # bad, then known-good
git bisect run ./test.sh       # automated binary search: log2(n) steps

git add -p                     # stage selected hunks, not whole files
git rebase -i HEAD~5           # reorder, squash, reword, drop
git worktree add ../hotfix main   # a second checkout sharing one .git

git cat-file -p HEAD           # the raw commit object: tree, parent, author
L0.cloze:
git {{c1::reflog}}                     # every position HEAD has held — the undo log
git reset --hard '{{c2::HEAD@{1}}}'    # go back to where HEAD was one move ago
git {{c3::bisect}} run ./test.sh       # automated binary search for the breaking commit
git {{c4::worktree}} add ../hotfix main   # a second working tree sharing one object database

concepts.L1: `reflog` to recover anything, `bisect` to find a breaking commit, `add -p` for partial staging, `rebase -i` to clean history, `worktree` for parallel checkouts.
concepts.L2: `git reflog` means almost nothing is truly lost — bad rebases, deleted branches, reset --hard are all recoverable for ~90 days. This single fact removes most of the fear people have about git operations.
concepts.L3: Git almost never deletes an object; it moves references. `reset --hard`, a bad rebase and a deleted branch all leave the commits in the object database, unreachable but present, until `git gc` prunes them. That grace period is only 30 days by default for a reflog entry pointing at a commit unreachable from any branch tip (`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`), versus 90 days while still reachable (`gc.reflogExpire`) - weeks, not months. The reflog is the index that makes them findable: it records every value HEAD and each branch has held, so `HEAD@{1}` is where you were one move ago, which is what makes most git operations reversible. `bisect run` turns a manual hunt into $\log_{2}(n)$ automated steps: exit 0 means good, 1-127 except 125 means bad, and 125 means 'cannot test this commit, skip it' rather than bad. `worktree add` beats stashing when you need another branch mid-task.

L4.prompt_tpl: A bug appeared somewhere in the last {n} commits and you have a script that exits 0 on good and 1 on bad. How many script runs does `git bisect run` need in the worst case?
L4.answer: $\lceil \log_{2}(n) \rceil$ runs: 6 for 64 commits, 7 for 128, 10 for 1000.
L4.explanation: Bisect is a binary search over the commit range, so each run halves the candidate set. That is why writing the test script is worth the effort even for a range of a thousand commits: ten builds instead of a linear hunt.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer ran `git reset --hard HEAD~{n}` on the wrong branch and lost {n} commits of unpushed work. What is the recovery, and what is the time limit?
L4.answer: git reflog to find the entry immediately before the reset, then git reset --hard 'HEAD@{1}' (or the SHA shown). The commits were never deleted - only the branch reference moved. The limit is git gc's expiry: unreachable objects that are still reflog-reachable are kept for 90 days by default (gc.reflogExpire), and reflog entries for unreachable commits for 30 days.
L4.explanation: The same recovery works for a botched rebase, a deleted branch (git reflog show <branch>, or git fsck --lost-found) and an amend that discarded work. What it does NOT cover is uncommitted changes in the working tree, which reset --hard genuinely destroys - that is what git stash and frequent WIP commits are for.

L4.prompt_tpl: Git commands split into two families: 'porcelain' (user-facing, output can change between versions) and 'plumbing' (low-level, stable, built to be scripted). Of `git log`, `git commit`, and `git cat-file`, which one is plumbing?
L4.answer: git cat-file
L4.explanation: cat-file reads a raw object (blob, tree, commit or tag) straight out of the object database with a stable, scriptable output format. log and commit are porcelain: their output is designed for a human terminal and is not guaranteed stable across git versions, which is why scripts prefer plumbing.
options: git log
git commit
git cat-file

L4.prompt_tpl: In any git repository, what single word does `git cat-file -t HEAD` print to stdout?
L4.answer: commit
L4.explanation: `cat-file -t` prints the type of the object a ref resolves to. HEAD always resolves to a commit object (verified: `git cat-file -t HEAD` prints `commit` in a fresh repo), whereas `git cat-file -t <tag>` on an annotated tag prints `tag`, and on a file's blob prints `blob`.

L4.prompt_tpl: You ran `git reset --hard` on the wrong branch a few weeks ago and only just noticed. By default, how many days does git keep the reflog entry for a commit that is not reachable from any branch tip, before `git reflog expire` removes it?
L4.answer: 30 days, controlled by gc.reflogExpireUnreachable. The commonly-quoted 90 days (gc.reflogExpire) only applies while the commit is still reachable from some branch - once reset --hard drops it, the shorter 30-day clock is the one running.
L4.explanation: This is the sign trap in the reflog safety net: the two expiry settings default to different values, and the one that governs the exact scenario people worry about (an orphaned commit from a bad reset) is the shorter one, 30 days, not 90.

L4.prompt_tpl: A `git bisect run ./test.sh` is aborting with 'bisect run failed' partway through, on a range where a few intermediate commits are known not to build at all. What exit code should test.sh use for 'this commit cannot be tested', and why can it not just reuse an ordinary failure code like 1?
L4.answer: Exit 125: it tells bisect to skip this revision without treating it as bad or aborting. Reusing 1 (an ordinary 'bad') would make bisect blame a commit only for being unbuildable, not for containing the real bug, corrupting the search; and codes 126/127 must be avoided too, since POSIX shells already use those for 'found but not executable' and 'command not found', and bisect aborts outright on any exit code above 127.
L4.explanation: This is the unfamiliar-instance version of the compute template on this concept: knowing that bisect run does a binary search is not enough to write a correct test.sh - you also need the exit-code contract (0 good, 125 skip, 1-127 except 125 bad, >127 aborts) or an unbuildable commit silently derails the bisect.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design a pipeline of exactly two commands - one plumbing, one from the find/xargs family - that prints `git show --stat` for every commit in the whole history that touched the path {file}. Which command lists just the matching commit SHAs, one per line, and why is that the right thing to hand to xargs rather than git log's default output?
L4.answer: git rev-list HEAD -- <path> | xargs -I{} git show --stat {}. `git rev-list` is the plumbing counterpart to `git log`: by design it prints nothing but the resolved commit SHAs, one per line, with no dates, authors or messages to trip up a line-oriented consumer. Verified: `git rev-list HEAD -- f.txt` in a two-commit test repo printed exactly the two touching SHAs, one per line, which xargs -I{} then substituted straight into git show --stat.
L4.explanation: This is the forward connection the concept's title promises: plumbing commands exist because porcelain output is for people and plumbing output is for pipes. rev-list feeding xargs is the same execution-engine pattern as 'find and xargs as an execution engine', just with git's own object graph as the source of names instead of a filesystem walk.

prereqs: literacy:The prompt, the command, the argument, and the Enter key

L0.body:
curl -sS https://api.example.com/health     # -s quiet, -S still show errors
curl -sSL https://x.test/redir              # -L follow redirects
curl -sSf https://x.test/missing            # -f: exit 22 on 4xx/5xx instead of 0
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"a":1}' https://x.test/
curl -d 'a=1&b=2' https://x.test/           # -d alone already implies POST

curl -o /dev/null -s -w \
  'dns=%{time_namelookup} conn=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} code=%{http_code}\n' \
  https://api.example.com/
L0.cloze:
curl {{c1::-sS}} URL          # quiet, but still print errors — the right pair for scripts
curl {{c2::-f}} URL           # make an HTTP 4xx/5xx a non-zero EXIT status
curl {{c3::-L}} URL           # follow redirects
curl -o /dev/null -s {{c4::-w}} 'ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}\n' URL   # per-phase timings

concepts.L1: `-s` silent, `-S` show errors, `-L` follow redirects, `-i` include headers, `-X` method, `-d` data, `-H` header, `-w` write-out format for timing.
concepts.L2: `curl -w '@format.txt' -o /dev/null -s` gives you DNS, connect, TLS and first-byte timing breakdowns per request. It's a complete latency diagnostic tool people mostly use as a fetch command.
concepts.L3: Two flags decide whether curl is safe in a script. Without `-f`, a 404 or a 500 is a perfectly successful transfer as far as curl is concerned - it exits 0 and writes the error page to stdout, so `curl -s $URL > config.json` cheerfully saves HTML. With `-f` the request fails with exit 22 and no body. And `-s` alone silences errors as well as progress, which is why `-sS` is the right pair: quiet on success, loud on failure. The `-w` variables make curl a latency profiler: `time_namelookup`, `time_connect`, `time_appconnect`, `time_starttransfer` and `time_total` are cumulative, so adjacent differences give the cost of each phase.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A server returns HTTP {code} for /missing. What is the exit status of each?
  A: curl -s -o /dev/null http://h/missing
  B: curl -sf -o /dev/null http://h/missing
L4.answer: A exits 0. B exits 22.
L4.explanation: curl considers the transfer successful whenever it completed, regardless of the HTTP status. -f (--fail) makes an HTTP error status a curl error, exit code 22, and suppresses the error body. Every script that fetches something and checks `$?` needs it.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bootstrap script runs:
  curl -s https://{host}/config.json > /etc/app/config.json
The endpoint returns a {code} HTML error page. What lands in the file, what is the exit status, and give the corrected command.
L4.answer: The HTML error page is written to config.json and curl exits 0, so the script continues and the application starts with a config file full of HTML. Corrected: curl -fsSL -o /tmp/config.json https://host/config.json && mv /tmp/config.json /etc/app/config.json - -f turns the HTTP error into a non-zero exit, -S reports why, -L follows a redirect, and writing to a temp file first means a failed fetch cannot leave a truncated or wrong file in place.
L4.explanation: The download-then-move pattern matters independently of curl: any fetch that writes directly to the destination path can leave a partial file if the transfer is interrupted. Fetch to a temp path in the same filesystem, then rename, which is atomic.

L4.prompt_tpl: curl {flag} https://example.com/report.csv against a server that has that file, run twice in a row from an empty directory. Where does the downloaded content end up each time, and does curl ask before the second run overwrites the first run's file?
L4.answer: With -o out.dat the file is always written to out.dat, whatever the URL's path is. With -O curl names the file after the URL itself -- the last path segment, so report.csv. Neither ever prompts: the second run silently overwrites whatever the first run wrote, which is why a script that must not clobber existing data downloads to a fresh temporary name first and renames afterward.
L4.explanation: -O only works when the URL ends in a real filename; a URL ending in / has nothing for curl to name the file after. -o takes an explicit name and is the more predictable choice inside a script for exactly that reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: curl {flag} https://example.com/ is run against an ordinary web server. Which HTTP method goes out on the wire, and does the response body get printed to the terminal?
L4.answer: -I and --head are the same flag: curl sends a HEAD request instead of GET, and a compliant server sends headers with no body, so there is nothing to print. -i keeps whatever method curl would otherwise use (GET here), and prints the response headers followed by the body.
L4.explanation: HEAD exists so a client can ask for metadata -- size, type, last-modified -- without paying for the body. A server that answers HEAD with a real body anyway can make curl -I hang waiting for bytes it told itself not to expect.

L4.prompt_tpl: curl -u {user}:{pw} https://api.example.com/ is run. What header does this put on the wire, and how does curl's behaviour differ between -u {user}: (colon present, password left empty) and -u {user} (no colon at all)?
L4.answer: curl base64-encodes user:password and sends it as an Authorization: Basic header -- an encoding, not encryption, so this is only safe over TLS. -u {user}: (colon present, nothing after it) sends that request right away with an explicit empty password -- the header is base64 of the literal string '{user}:'. Only when the colon is omitted entirely, -u {user} with no colon anywhere, does curl stop and prompt interactively for the password, which is the one way to supply it without it ever appearing in argv or shell history.
L4.explanation: curl treats the colon as the field separator between user and password: present-but-empty after it is still a real (empty) password, so the request goes out unchanged. Only the colon's total absence tells curl the password was never given at all, which is what triggers the interactive prompt -- curl's own answer to keeping secrets out of the process list.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A script runs:
  curl -X GET -d '{qs}' https://api.example.com/search
because someone wanted to be explicit that this is a read. Does curl actually send a bodyless GET? What goes wrong, and what is the fix if the goal is a real GET with these values as a query string?
L4.answer: No. -X only overwrites the verb word curl writes on the request line; it does not remove the payload -d attached or touch the Content-Length header. So this sends 'GET /search HTTP/1.1' carrying a request body -- a GET-with-body that plenty of servers, proxies and caches reject or silently drop. The fix is -G: curl -G -d '{qs}' https://api.example.com/search appends the -d data to the URL as a query string and sends a normal bodyless GET.
L4.explanation: curl's own manual is explicit that -X changes only the request-line word and nothing else about curl's behaviour -- it is documented, not a bug, which is why the fix is a different flag (-G) rather than removing -X.

L4.prompt_tpl: curl --connect-timeout {ct} --max-time {mt} https://slow.example.com/ is run against a server whose connection (TCP and TLS) completes immediately but which then sends nothing at all -- no headers, no body, forever. After how many seconds does curl give up, and which of the two timeout flags is the one that actually fires? Answer with the number of seconds.
L4.answer: --connect-timeout only bounds DNS plus the TCP/TLS handshake, and that part already succeeded, so it never triggers. --max-time bounds the whole operation from start to finish, so curl aborts after mt seconds: 10 for mt=10, 20 for mt=20, regardless of ct.
L4.explanation: A common mistake is setting only --connect-timeout and assuming it caps the whole request; with no --max-time the default is unlimited, so a server that connects but then stalls hangs curl forever.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A deploy script runs:
  curl -k -u admin:{pw} https://{host}/api/deploy -d @payload.json
Name every way this line weakens or leaks security, and rewrite it so the same deploy stays safe.
L4.answer: Two separate faults. First, -k (--insecure) turns off TLS certificate verification, so the https:// is decorative and a machine-in-the-middle can read or rewrite payload.json in transit. Second, -u admin:{pw} puts the password in argv, where it is written to the shell's history file and readable by any other local user via ps while curl runs. Fix: drop -k so the certificate is checked again, and move the credential into a file curl reads itself: curl -K creds.txt https://{host}/api/deploy -d @payload.json, where creds.txt (mode 600) holds a single line user = "admin:{pw}" -- curl reads that directly, and it never appears in argv or history.
L4.explanation: Command-line arguments are visible to every local user through ps and are written to shell history, the same exposure 'SSH keys, the agent, and forwarding risk' warns about for keys. curl's -K/--config file (or --config -, reading from stdin) is curl's own way to keep a secret out of argv.

L0.body:
ss -tulpn                 # TCP+UDP listening sockets with the owning process
ss -tan | awk 'NR>1 {c[$1]++} END {for (s in c) print c[s], s}'   # state histogram

dig +short api.example.com          # just the answer
dig +trace api.example.com          # follow delegation from the root

mtr -rwc 100 example.com            # per-hop loss and latency over 100 probes
tcpdump -i any -nn 'port 443' -w cap.pcap   # -nn: no name lookups
nc -vz host 5432                    # is the port open?
# in a script:  nc -z host "$port" && echo open
L0.cloze:
{{c1::ss}} -tulpn                 # listening sockets and the processes that own them
dig {{c2::+short}} api.example.com        # just the answer record
{{c3::mtr}} -rwc 100 example.com       # per-hop packet loss along the path
tcpdump -i any {{c4::-nn}} 'port 443'     # capture without resolving names or ports

concepts.L1: `ss -tulpn` for listening sockets, `dig +short`, `mtr` for path analysis, `tcpdump -i any -nn port 443 -w cap.pcap`, `nc` for raw connections.
concepts.L2: `ss` replaced `netstat` years ago and is faster and more informative, but every tutorial still teaches netstat, which isn't installed by default on modern distributions.
concepts.L3: The reason `ss` replaced `netstat` is architectural: netstat parses `/proc/net/tcp` as text, which is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ string formatting and re-parsing per socket, so on a host with tens of thousands of connections it takes seconds. `ss` queries the kernel over a netlink socket and filters server-side, answers instantly, and exposes state netstat cannot - congestion window, retransmit counts. It is usually the only one installed, since net-tools is not in a default modern image. `dig +short` is the scriptable form and `+trace` the diagnostic one. `mtr` shows sustained per-hop loss, and `tcpdump -nn` avoids reverse lookups that would pollute the capture.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service should be listening on port {port} but connections are refused. What is the single first command, and what do the possible outputs mean?
L4.answer: ss -tulpn | grep :{port}. If nothing is listed, the process is not running or failed to bind. If it is listed on 127.0.0.1:{port} rather than 0.0.0.0:{port} or [::]:{port}, it is bound to loopback only and no remote client can ever reach it - a configuration fix, not a firewall one. If it is listed on 0.0.0.0 and remote connections still fail, the problem is between you and the host: a firewall, a security group, or routing.
L4.explanation: The 127.0.0.1-versus-0.0.0.0 distinction is the highest-frequency answer here and ss shows it in one line. Reaching for firewall rules before checking the bind address wastes most of the time spent on this class of incident.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is `ss` preferred over `netstat` on a busy host, and why does `tcpdump -nn` matter?
L4.answer: ss talks to the kernel over netlink and can filter in-kernel, so listing sockets on a host with many thousands of connections is fast; netstat formats and re-parses /proc/net/tcp as text and becomes very slow at that scale. It also reports TCP internals netstat does not. tcpdump -nn disables both host and port name resolution: without it every captured packet can trigger a reverse DNS lookup, which adds latency and generates additional network traffic that pollutes the capture you are trying to read.
L4.explanation: There is a third practical reason for ss: net-tools is not installed by default on most current distributions, so netstat is often simply absent on the host you have just ssh'd into during an incident.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a host, the state column of `ss -tan` (skipping the header line) reads, top to bottom: LISTEN, LISTEN, ESTAB, ESTAB, TIME-WAIT. Piping that output through an awk script that, for every line after the header, increments a counter keyed by the first field (the state column), then at the end prints each state's count, how many times does ESTAB appear in that count?
L4.answer: 2. The awk script increments an array keyed by the first field (`$1`, the state column) once per line after the header; ESTAB is the first field on two of the five lines, so c["ESTAB"] ends at 2.
L4.explanation: This is the exact awk one-liner from this concept's L0; the only way to answer it is to trace, line by line, what the increment-and-count script actually does to the state field, which is the skill the concept is testing, not memorised ss output.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hostname resolves through a chain of {c} CNAME record(s) before reaching a name that has {a} A record(s). Because `dig +short` prints one line per record - every CNAME target in the chain, then every final address - how many lines total does `dig +short` print for this hostname?
L4.answer: One line per CNAME hop plus one line per final address record. For example, a single CNAME pointing at a host with one A record prints 2 lines: the CNAME target, then the address. In general it is (number of CNAMEs) + (number of A records) lines.
L4.explanation: dig +short strips everything except the record data, one record per line, and does not stop at the first CNAME - it keeps printing until it reaches the address records, which is exactly what makes it pipeable into other tools.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run `nc -z host {port}` in a script, and the target port is open and accepting connections. Checking `$?` immediately afterward, what integer does it equal?
L4.answer: 0. -z makes nc probe the port without sending data; when the TCP handshake on port {port} completes because something is listening, nc exits 0, the normal POSIX convention for success, which is exactly what `nc -z host "$port" && echo open` from this concept's L0 relies on.
L4.explanation: The whole point of -z in a script is that the exit status alone is the answer: 0 means the handshake completed, any nonzero value means it did not, so the caller never has to parse nc's text output at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Ignoring the handful of extra probes the first couple of discovery cycles need, `mtr -rwc {c} example.com` sends about {c} probe packets to each of the {h} hops on the path before printing its report. Approximately how many total probe packets does the whole run send?
L4.answer: About c times h. For c=100 and h=12 that is 1200 total probes: mtr's -c sets the number of cycles, and each cycle sends one probe per hop on the path so far, so a full run sends roughly cycles times hops packets in total (the true count is a little lower, since the first few cycles have not yet discovered the far hops).
L4.explanation: mtr's -c is per-hop, not per-run: the Snt column in its own report confirms each hop received close to c probes, so the total load a continuous mtr session puts on the path scales with both the cycle count and the path length, not just the cycle count.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to capture the traffic exchanged with {ip} on port 443 during a live incident on a busy production interface, including the TCP handshake and TLS ClientHello, write the capture to disk for later analysis in Wireshark, and avoid tcpdump generating any DNS lookups of its own while it runs. Write the exact tcpdump invocation, and say what each flag is for.
L4.answer: tcpdump -i any -nn -w handshake.pcap host {ip} and port 443. -i any captures on every interface so you do not have to know in advance which one carries the traffic; -nn turns off both host and port name resolution, so tcpdump itself never makes a reverse-DNS or /etc/services lookup while it runs; -w handshake.pcap writes raw packets to a file instead of formatting a line per packet, which keeps up with a busy interface and preserves the bytes Wireshark needs; host {ip} and port 443 is the BPF filter, evaluated in the kernel, that keeps the file to only the traffic in question instead of everything the interface sees.
L4.explanation: A busy interface is exactly where an unfiltered, unwritten, name-resolving capture falls over: printing and resolving every packet cannot keep pace, and a BPF filter evaluated by the kernel is far cheaper than capturing everything and filtering afterward in software.

L4.prompt_tpl: A public-facing host stops accepting new TCP connections even though `ss -tan` shows the listening socket present on 0.0.0.0:{port}. Running `ss -tan state syn-recv | wc -l` returns a number in the thousands, far above the double digits you would normally see. What does this indicate, and what would you check next to tell a SYN flood apart from ordinary backlog exhaustion under legitimate load?
L4.answer: A large syn-recv count means handshakes are stalling after the server's SYN-ACK: either an attacker is sending SYN packets and never completing the handshake (a SYN flood), or the accept backlog (net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog / net.core.somaxconn) is too small for genuinely simultaneous legitimate connections. Next: run dmesg | grep -i 'syn flood' for the kernel's own 'possible SYN flooding on port {port}' warning, which fires when the queue fills; look at source-address diversity in ss -tan state syn-recv - a flood shows many, often spoofed, sources hitting one port, while real load shows a normal, diverse client mix that eventually completes; and check whether net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is on, since that is the kernel's own automatic defence once the backlog fills.
L4.explanation: ss's state filter turns a vague symptom into a specific kernel-queue question; syn-recv sockets are connections stuck between SYN-ACK and the final ACK, and the kernel's own SYN-cookie mechanism and log line exist precisely to handle and report this state filling up.

concepts.t: SSH keys, the agent, and forwarding risk

L0.body:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'me@laptop'      # ed25519: small, fast, no parameter choices

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"; ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   # decrypt once, hold in memory
ssh-add -t 3600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519      # auto-expire after an hour

ssh -A host         # AGENT FORWARDING — root on `host` can now use your key
ssh -J bastion host # ProxyJump — forwards the CONNECTION, not the credential

# ~/.ssh/config
Host *
    ForwardAgent no          # the safe default
    IdentitiesOnly yes       # offer only the configured key
# before debugging auth, check what is loaded:  ssh-add -l; echo $?
L0.cloze:
ssh-keygen -t {{c1::ed25519}}          # the current default key type
{{c2::ssh-add}} -t 3600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   # load into the agent with an expiry
ssh {{c3::-A}} host                    # agent forwarding — grants USE of your key to that host
ssh {{c4::-J}} bastion host            # ProxyJump: forwards the connection instead

concepts.L1: The private key never leaves your machine; authentication is a challenge the client signs. `ssh-agent` holds the decrypted key in memory so you type the passphrase once, and exposes a Unix socket that clients ask to sign challenges.
concepts.L2: Agent forwarding (`-A`) puts that signing socket on the remote host. Anyone who can read it - root, or any process running as you - can sign challenges with your key for the life of the session. It delegates the key's authority, not just the connection.
concepts.L3: The concrete attack: you `ssh -A` into a shared or compromised host; a process there reads `$SSH_AUTH_SOCK` and uses your agent to authenticate to every other machine your key opens, including production. You never see it, the key file is never copied, and the audit log shows your username. `ProxyJump` solves the problem people actually use `-A` for - reaching a host behind a bastion - by tunnelling the TCP connection while the ssh session is negotiated end to end with the target, so the bastion sees only ciphertext. If you must forward, scope it to one `Host` block, set a short `ssh-add -t` expiry, and prefer a touch-required hardware key.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer runs `ssh -A {bastion}` and from there `ssh prod-db`. The bastion is shared with {n} other teams. State the exposure precisely and the correct alternative.
L4.answer: For the life of that session, a socket on the bastion lets any process running as that user - and root, always - ask the engineer's agent to sign authentication challenges. That is use of the key against every host it authorises, not just the bastion, without ever copying the key file and while appearing in logs as the engineer. Correct alternative: ssh -J bastion.example.com prod-db (ProxyJump), which forwards the TCP connection so the bastion only relays encrypted traffic and never receives the agent socket.
L4.explanation: The distinction to hold on to is credential delegation versus connection relaying. If ForwardAgent must be used at all, restrict it to a specific Host block, never Host *, and pair it with a short ssh-add -t lifetime or a touch-required hardware key.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which ssh_config block is the right default for a laptop that connects to {n} different hosts?
L4.answer: ForwardAgent no, IdentitiesOnly yes, AddKeysToAgent yes
L4.explanation: ForwardAgent yes globally is the dangerous default because it applies to hosts you have not thought about. IdentitiesOnly yes matters too: without it ssh offers every key in the agent to every server, which leaks which keys you hold and can lock you out after too many failed offers.
options: ForwardAgent no, IdentitiesOnly yes, AddKeysToAgent yes
ForwardAgent yes, so jumping through bastions always works
StrictHostKeyChecking no, to avoid host-key prompts

L4.prompt_tpl: You load a key with `ssh-add -t {mins}m ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, using the same time-format ssh-add shares with sshd_config. How many seconds will the agent hold the decrypted key before it expires? Answer with the number of seconds.
L4.answer: ssh-add -t takes a lifetime in the same time format as sshd_config: a bare number of seconds, or a number with an s/m/h/d/w suffix. For mins=30: 30*60 = 1800 seconds. For mins=90: 90*60 = 5400 seconds. After that many seconds the agent drops the key from memory and the next use prompts for the passphrase again.
L4.explanation: ssh-add -t sets a per-key lifetime, not a per-session one: each key you load can carry its own expiry, so a short-lived deploy key and a long-lived personal key sit in the same agent with different clocks running.

L4.prompt_tpl: You start a fresh ssh-agent, then immediately run `ssh-add -l` before loading any key with ssh-add. What does it print, and what exit status does it return?
L4.answer: Prints "The agent has no identities." and exits 1 - the agent is reachable but no key has been added yet
L4.explanation: Exit status distinguishes agent state precisely: 0 means at least one identity was listed, 1 means the agent answered but holds no keys, and 2 means ssh-add could not reach an agent at all - no SSH_AUTH_SOCK, or the agent process is gone. Checking `$?` after ssh-add -l tells 'agent up, empty' apart from 'no agent'.
options: Prints "The agent has no identities." and exits 1 - the agent is reachable but no key has been added yet
Prints "Could not open a connection to your authentication agent." and exits 2 - no agent is running
Prints the fingerprint of a default key and exits 0 - ssh-add auto-loads ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 on first call

L4.prompt_tpl: A deploy script runs `ssh-add -t {secs} ~/.ssh/id_deploy` once, then loops `ssh`/`scp` calls to {n} hosts, a few seconds apart. Calls that succeeded early in the run start failing partway through with `Permission denied (publickey)`, and the key file on disk is untouched. What is going on, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: ssh-add -t put a lifetime on the loaded key, not on the script: once that many seconds pass since it was added, ssh-agent drops it from memory while the key file on disk is untouched, so every ssh or scp call after that point is rejected with Permission denied (publickey) and no warning. Fix: give ssh-add a lifetime that comfortably outlasts the whole run, or drop -t here and instead limit exposure a different way, such as a dedicated key removed by the script when it finishes.
L4.explanation: The tell is that identical calls worked earlier in the same run and the key file has not moved, so nothing about the key changed - only the agent's clock did. `ssh-add -l` run right after the failure would show the key missing, confirming expiry rather than a permissions or network problem.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your agent holds {k} keys because IdentitiesOnly is not set anywhere in ~/.ssh/config. Logging into a server running the default `MaxAuthTries 6` starts failing with the connection dropped and `Too many authentication failures`, even though the right key is loaded. Explain why, and name the fix.
L4.answer: Without IdentitiesOnly yes, ssh offers every key in the agent to the server in turn, and each rejected offer counts as one of the server's MaxAuthTries attempts - six by default - not one attempt per connection. If the matching key is not among the first six offered, the server disconnects before ssh ever gets to try it. Fix: set IdentitiesOnly yes, globally or scoped to the Host block, so ssh offers only the key named by IdentityFile, or pass -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i path/to/key explicitly.
L4.explanation: This is the practical reason IdentitiesOnly yes belongs in a sane default Host * block: agents accumulate keys over a laptop's working life, and every extra one loaded is a wasted authentication attempt against a server that counts attempts, not correctness.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CI pipeline runs ssh and scp against {n} internal hosts reachable only through one bastion, once per run, and must never put the signing key at risk if the bastion is later compromised. Using ProxyJump, ControlMaster and a scoped agent lifetime, describe a configuration that reaches all {n} hosts without ever putting the agent socket on the bastion.
L4.answer: ssh_config on the runner: a Host bastion block with no ForwardAgent; a Host prod-* block with ProxyJump bastion, ControlMaster auto, ControlPath and ControlPersist 10m (from 'ssh beyond login'), and IdentitiesOnly yes pointing at a dedicated deploy key loaded into the agent with a short ssh-add -t lifetime for just the run. ProxyJump tunnels each connection's raw TCP through the bastion and negotiates SSH end to end with the target, so the bastion only ever relays ciphertext and never receives the signing socket; ControlMaster means only the first of the n connections pays the handshake; the short lifetime limits how long a stolen agent entry would even be useful, and it lives on the runner, never on the bastion.
L4.explanation: The design move is treating 'reach many hosts through one relay' and 'never hand out my signing key' as two separate problems with two separate mechanisms - ProxyJump for the first, no ForwardAgent plus a scoped key for the second - instead of collapsing both into ssh -A.

L0.body:
# main:  base - m1          topic (from base):  base - t1 - t2

git checkout topic && git rebase main
# result: base - m1 - t1' - t2'      NEW commits, NEW hashes

git log --oneline
#  4cbb83d t2      <- was 1c78b45
#  41f2553 t1      <- was 60b280d
#  1b8e2ec m1
#  452786a base

git reflog          # the ORIGINAL t1 and t2 are still there, reachable by SHA
git rebase --abort  # while a rebase is in progress
git push --force-with-lease   # never plain --force: this checks the remote first

git merge --no-ff topic       # the alternative: one merge commit, no rewriting
L0.cloze:
git rebase main     # replays each of topic's commits onto main, producing {{c1::new hashes}}
git {{c2::reflog}}          # the pre-rebase commits are still reachable here
git rebase {{c3::--abort}}  # back out of a rebase that is going badly
git push {{c4::--force-with-lease}}   # refuses if the remote moved since you last fetched

concepts.L1: Rebase does not move commits. It replays each commit's diff onto a new base and writes new commit objects, so every rebased commit gets a new SHA even when its content is identical - the parent is part of the hash.
concepts.L2: That is why rebasing a branch someone else has pulled is antisocial: their history now contains commits that no longer exist upstream, and merging the two produces duplicates. The rule is rebase private history, merge public history.
concepts.L3: Follow the mechanism and the rules fall out. A commit object holds a tree, a parent list, author and committer metadata and a message, and its hash covers all of that - change the parent and you have a different object. Rebase therefore walks the commits unique to your branch, applies each as a patch onto the new base, and writes fresh objects, which is also why conflicts can appear once per commit rather than once overall and why `--continue` and `--abort` exist. The originals stay in the object database and the reflog, so a rebase is recoverable. `--force-with-lease` refuses the push if the remote moved since your last fetch; plain `--force` does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: main is base then m1. topic branched from base and has {n} commits. After `git checkout topic && git rebase main`, how many commits does `git log --oneline` show on topic, and which of them have their original SHAs?
L4.answer: For n=2: 4 commits (base, m1, t1', t2'). Only base and m1 keep their original SHAs; every rebased commit gets a new one because its parent changed. In general the count is n + 2.
L4.explanation: The SHA covers the parent pointer, so replaying a commit onto a different parent necessarily produces a different object. The old objects are not deleted - they stay reachable through the reflog until gc expires them.

L4.prompt_tpl: You rebased a branch that {n} colleagues have already pulled, and now need to publish it. What do you do?
L4.answer: git push --force-with-lease, and tell colleagues to reset to the new tip
L4.explanation: Plain --force overwrites whatever is on the remote without checking, so it can silently discard a colleague's push made in the meantime. Merging main into the branch instead avoids rewriting but does not undo the rebase you already did; it just adds a merge on top of divergent history.
options: git push --force-with-lease, and tell colleagues to reset to the new tip
git push --force, since the rebase is already done
Merge main into the branch again and push normally

L4.prompt_tpl: topic and main share a common ancestor. Since then, topic has made {n} commits of its own, and main has gained {m} commits of its own that topic does not have. You run `git checkout topic && git rebase main`. How many commit objects does this rebase write?
L4.answer: Exactly n new commit objects are written, one per commit unique to topic - main's m commits already exist and are reused unchanged as the new base. For n=3, m=4: 3 new objects, regardless of m; for n=8, m=0: 8 new objects.
L4.explanation: Rebase only replays commits that are on topic but not on main; main's own commits are already in the object database and simply become the new parent unchanged, so the count depends on n alone and never on m.

L4.prompt_tpl: `git rebase main` is stopped on a conflict at the {i} commit of {n} being replayed. Which single command discards the whole rebase and returns topic to exactly the ref it pointed at before the rebase started?
L4.answer: git rebase --abort
L4.explanation: `--abort` walks back every partial rebase step and resets topic's ref to where it pointed before the rebase began, discarding any commits already replayed; `--continue` moves forward past a resolved conflict and `--skip` drops the current commit, neither of which undoes the rebase.

L4.prompt_tpl: topic has {n} commits, and every one of them touches a line that main also changed since the branch point. Roughly how many separate conflict-resolution steps might `git rebase main` demand compared to `git merge main`, and why do the counts differ?
L4.answer: Rebase can demand up to n separate resolutions - one each time a replayed commit's patch touches a line main already changed - because each commit is applied as an independent patch and you resolve then `--continue` after each one. `git merge` folds both histories into a single three-way diff and asks for at most one resolution per conflicting file, no matter how many commits caused the divergence.
L4.explanation: Rebase replays commits one at a time (apply, resolve, --continue), so a line touched by every one of topic's n commits can conflict up to n times; merge computes one diff over the whole branch, so the same divergence surfaces as a single conflict per file instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A chain of {n} commits has each commit's hash computed over its tree, message and its parent's hash - the same content-addressed chaining a Merkle tree uses. During an interactive rebase you edit the content of the {i} commit in the chain, counting from the base end, and leave the rest untouched. By the time the rebase finishes, how many of the n commits have a new hash?
L4.answer: For n=6, i=2: commits 2 through 6 all get new hashes, 5 commits - editing commit 2 changes its hash, which is embedded in commit 3's parent field, forcing commit 3 to be rewritten too, and so on to the tip. In general n - i + 1 commits change; commits 1..i-1 are never touched because the chain only propagates forward from the edit.
L4.explanation: Each commit's hash covers its parent's hash, exactly like a Merkle tree node's hash covers its children's - change one link and every hash from that point to the tip must be recomputed, which is why editing an early commit in a long interactive rebase rewrites everything after it, not just that one commit.

L4.prompt_tpl: A teammate runs `git rebase -i HEAD~{n}`, deletes the line for one commit to drop it, saves and quits. The very next commit after the dropped one now conflicts with main, though it never conflicted before. They conclude rebase is broken. What actually happened, and what should they check first?
L4.answer: Rebase is not broken: dropping a commit removes its diff from the sequence of patches being replayed, so the next commit's patch is now applied against a tree missing whatever the dropped commit changed. If that next commit's diff touched the same lines, the patch no longer applies cleanly and conflicts. They should check whether the dropped commit and the next one touched overlapping lines, and either re-add the needed change or fold it into the next commit rather than treating the conflict as a rebase bug.
L4.explanation: Each surviving commit replays as an independent patch onto whatever precedes it in the new sequence; removing a commit changes that context, so a later commit whose diff assumed the dropped change's lines were already edited can fail to apply - the fix is in the commit sequence, not in rebase itself.

concepts.t: find and xargs as an execution engine

L0.body:
find . -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -size +1M      # predicates AND together
find . -type f \( -name '*.tmp' -o -name '*.bak' \)      # explicit OR, escaped parens
find . -type f -exec grep -l TODO {} \;    # one grep process PER FILE
find . -type f -exec grep -l TODO {} +     # ONE grep, all filenames as arguments

find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l TODO   # same batching, via a pipe
find . -name '*.tmp' -delete               # no exec at all — fastest and safest
L0.cloze:
find ... -exec cmd {} {{c1::\;}}     # run the command once PER file
find ... -exec cmd {} {{c2::+}}      # run it ONCE with all the filenames as arguments
find . -print0 | xargs {{c3::-0}}    # the null-delimited pair, safe for any filename
xargs {{c4::-P4}} -n50 md5sum        # four parallel processes, fifty files each

concepts.L1: `find` evaluates a boolean expression of predicates against every path it walks and runs an action on the matches. `-exec cmd {} \;` runs one process per match; `-exec cmd {} +` appends as many filenames as fit and runs the command once per batch. `xargs` does the same batching from stdin.
concepts.L2: The difference between `\;` and `+` is one character and often two orders of magnitude in runtime, because process creation dominates when the command itself is cheap. Yet `\;` is what almost everyone types, because it is what the examples show.
concepts.L3: For 3 files the two forms cost 3 forks versus 1; for 200000 files they cost 200000 forks versus a handful, and at roughly a millisecond per fork-and-exec that is minutes against seconds. Use `\;` only when the command must see exactly one filename - it needs the name in the middle of its arguments, or it is a shell snippet doing per-file logic. `xargs` adds `-P` for parallelism and `-n` for chunk size, at the cost of needing `-print0` and `-0` to stay filename-safe. Two details worth carrying: GNU xargs runs the command once even on empty input unless given `-r`, and `-I{}` implies `-L1`, defeating batching entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: A directory tree has {n} matching files. Process creation costs about {ms} ms. Estimate the process-creation time for `find ... -exec cmd {{}} \;` versus `find ... -exec cmd {{}} +`, assuming the batched form needs about {b} invocations. Answer with the per-file form's process-creation time in milliseconds.
L4.answer: The per-file form costs $n \times ms$ milliseconds: 50000 ms (50 s) for n=50000 at 1 ms, or 400000 ms (400 s) for n=200000 at 2 ms. The batched form costs $b \times ms$: 4 ms or 32 ms. The ratio is $\tfrac{n}{b}$.
L4.explanation: The command's own work is identical in both cases; the entire difference is fork and exec overhead, which is why the gap widens with file count and is largest for cheap commands like grep or md5sum on small files.

L4.prompt_tpl:
find /var/log -name '*.{ext}' | xargs rm
On a tree containing a file named `app log.{ext}`, what happens, and give two correct rewrites.
L4.answer: xargs splits its input on whitespace, so `app log.old` becomes two arguments and rm attempts to delete `/var/log/app` and `log.old`, deleting the wrong things if they exist and erroring if they do not. Correct: find /var/log -name '*.old' -print0 | xargs -0 rm --, or simply find /var/log -name '*.old' -delete, which never leaves find's process at all.
L4.explanation: A third hazard in the original: with no matches, GNU xargs still runs rm once with no arguments unless -r is given. -delete avoids the whole class, and should be the first choice whenever the action is deletion.

L4.prompt_tpl: find's batched -exec form (the '+' variant) appends matched filenames into groups of at most {batch} names and runs cmd once per group. There are {n} matching files in total. How many times does cmd get invoked?
L4.answer: Invocations equal $\lceil n / batch \rceil$ (ceiling division): 1400 files at 200 per batch takes exactly 7 invocations; 1400 at 500 per batch takes $\lceil 2.8 \rceil = 3$; 5000 at 200 per batch takes exactly 25; 5000 at 500 per batch takes exactly 10.
L4.explanation: The + form keeps appending filenames to the current command line until the batch limit (bounded in practice by the kernel's ARG_MAX) is reached, then starts a fresh invocation; that ceiling division is the whole reason it costs a handful of forks instead of one per file.

L4.prompt_tpl:
GNU coreutils on Linux. Run: printf 'a
b
c
d
e
f
' | xargs -n{n} echo GOT   What are the resulting output lines, in order?
L4.answer: For -n2: three lines, GOT a b / GOT c d / GOT e f. For -n3: two lines, GOT a b c / GOT d e f. In general xargs -n{n} takes the words in the order they arrive and emits one line per group of {n}, each prefixed with GOT.
L4.explanation: xargs -n caps the number of arguments per invocation the same way find's -exec ... + caps filenames per batch; both trade invocation count against how much fits on one command line, and neither reorders the input.

L4.prompt_tpl: A directory contains exactly three files named a.{ext}, b.{ext} and c.{ext}. Using find's substitution placeholder for the matched filename, you want each file renamed with a .bak suffix appended. Which of these three commands actually does that?
L4.answer: find . -name '*.{ext}' -exec mv {{}} {{}}.bak \;
L4.explanation: GNU find refuses the second command outright: 'Only one instance of {} is supported with -exec ... +', because the batched form can only append the whole filename list once, at the very end. The third command hands mv three source paths and no destination directory, so mv errors with 'target ... Not a directory' instead of renaming anything; \; is the only form that puts one filename into two positions per invocation.
options: find . -name '*.{ext}' -exec mv {{}} {{}}.bak \;
find . -name '*.{ext}' -exec mv {{}} {{}}.bak +
find . -name '*.{ext}' -print0 | xargs -0 mv

L4.prompt_tpl: A tree under {dir} holds files matching *.tmp, and some of those names contain spaces, embedded newlines, or start with a dash (for example a file literally named -rf). Give a one-line find+xargs pipeline that deletes exactly those files safely, then say specifically what breaks with each of these two alternatives: (1) find {dir} -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm, and (2) rm $(find {dir} -name '*.tmp').
L4.answer: Safe form: find {dir} -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 rm --  . -print0/-0 delimit names with a NUL byte, which cannot appear in a filename, so embedded spaces and newlines survive intact; the -- stops rm from reading a name like -rf as an option. (1) plain xargs splits its input on IFS whitespace and newlines by default, so a name containing a space becomes two separate arguments and a name containing a newline is split into two rm targets -- and a name that starts with a dash is still parsed by rm as a flag, not a filename. (2) rm $(find ...) runs command substitution and then word-splits the result the same IFS-driven way, so it has the identical space/newline breakage, and the substituted name list is still parsed left to right by rm's own option handling, so a leading-dash name is again read as an option -- quoting the whole substitution does not fix this because it turns the entire list into one argument instead.
L4.explanation: NUL-delimiting is the only separator that cannot occur inside a filename, and -- is the independent, unrelated fix for names that look like options; a pipeline needs both, because IFS splitting and rm's option parser are two separate hazards. Compare the same NUL-delimiting rule used for safe read loops in Handling filenames safely.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to gzip {n} independent log files, each taking {t} ms of CPU-bound work, on a machine with {cores} cores. Running xargs -P{cores} -n1 gzip to parallelise them, and ignoring process-start overhead, how many milliseconds does the whole batch take in the best case?
L4.answer: The work fills $\lceil n / cores \rceil$ sequential rounds of t ms each, since at most cores files run in parallel per round: 17 files on 4 cores is 5 rounds of 400 ms = 2000 ms; 17 files on 8 cores is 3 rounds of 400 ms = 1200 ms; 100 files on 4 cores is 25 rounds of 400 ms = 10000 ms; 100 files on 8 cores is 13 rounds of 400 ms = 5200 ms.
L4.explanation: xargs -P gives the same overlap that manually backgrounding jobs and calling wait per batch would (see 'wait, `$!` and parallelism in bash'), without that bookkeeping -- but it still caps concurrency at -P workers, so total time tracks the number of rounds, not a flat n/cores speedup.

L0.body:
out.txt: a.txt b.txt         # target: prerequisites
	@cat a.txt b.txt > out.txt  # RECIPE — must begin with a TAB, not spaces

a.txt:
	@echo a > a.txt
b.txt:
	@echo b > b.txt

.PHONY: all clean
all: out.txt
clean:
	@rm -f a.txt b.txt out.txt

$ make          # BUILDING a.txt / BUILDING b.txt / BUILDING out.txt
$ make          # make: 'out.txt' is up to date.
$ touch a.txt; make   # BUILDING out.txt — only what is now stale
$ make -n       # print the commands without running them
$ make -j2      # build independent targets in parallel
# a make variable is $(VAR); a shell one in a recipe needs a doubled dollar
L0.cloze:
out.txt: a.txt b.txt        # {{c1::target}}: prerequisites
{{c2::<TAB>}}cat a.txt b.txt > out.txt   # a recipe line must start with this character
{{c3::.PHONY}}: all clean           # declare targets that are not real files
make {{c4::-n}}                     # show the commands without executing them

concepts.L1: make is a dependency engine, not a script runner. You declare targets, their prerequisites and the recipe that produces a target from them; make builds the graph, compares modification times, and runs only the recipes whose outputs are older than their inputs.
concepts.L2: It compares mtimes, not contents, so `touch` triggers a rebuild and a file restored with an older timestamp does not. And a recipe line must start with a literal tab: an editor that expands tabs produces `missing separator`, which names nothing useful.
concepts.L3: The mtime rule is the whole model and explains the usual confusions. A phony name like `test` has no file, so make would call it up to date if a file of that name ever appeared - which is what `.PHONY` prevents. A recipe runs each line in a separate shell, so `cd build` on one line does not affect the next; join them with `&&` or set `.ONESHELL`. `-j` parallelism is free precisely because the dependency graph is declared, so make knows which targets are independent. And because recipes run in a shell, a dollar sign must be doubled to reach the shell rather than make's own expansion. A good Makefile is self-documenting: its targets are the project's verbs.

L4.prompt_tpl: With the Makefile above, you run `make`, then `make` again, then `touch {f}` and `make` a third time. Which recipes execute on each of the three runs?
L4.answer: Run 1: a.txt, b.txt and out.txt are all built — make's default goal is out.txt, the first rule in the file. Run 2: nothing - make reports "'out.txt' is up to date." Run 3: only out.txt is rebuilt, because a.txt is now newer than out.txt while b.txt is unchanged and a.txt itself still exists.
L4.explanation: Note that touching a.txt does not rebuild a.txt: its own recipe only runs when the file is missing, since it has no prerequisites. Only targets whose prerequisites are newer than themselves are rebuilt, which is what makes incremental builds cheap.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Makefile target fails with `Makefile:{n}: *** missing separator.  Stop.` The line looks correct on screen. What is wrong and how do you confirm it?
L4.answer: The recipe line begins with spaces rather than a tab - an editor with expandtab set converted it. Confirm with `cat -A Makefile`, where a tab shows as ^I and spaces show as themselves, or `sed -n 'Np' Makefile | od -c`. Fix by restoring a literal tab, or configure the editor to preserve tabs in Makefiles.
L4.explanation: This is make's single most notorious papercut and its message names neither tabs nor the real problem. .RECIPEPREFIX can change the required character in GNU make, but every Makefile anyone else reads still uses a tab, so fixing the editor is the better answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Makefile builds {n} independent object files with no dependencies between them; each takes {s} seconds to compile. Running plain `make` builds them one at a time. Running `make -j{n}` on a machine with at least {n} free cores lets make build all of them at once, since the dependency graph already shows they don't depend on each other. Approximately how many seconds does the `-j{n}` build take, if recipe run time dominates and process start-up overhead is negligible? Answer with the number of seconds.
L4.answer: About {s} seconds. Because the {n} recipes share no prerequisites, make can hand all {n} to separate processes under -j{n}; wall-clock time approaches the slowest single recipe ({s} s), not the sum of all {n} of them run serially.
L4.explanation: Parallel builds are 'free' precisely because independence is declared in the graph, not discovered: make already knows these {n} targets don't depend on each other, so -j only needs cores, not extra bookkeeping from you.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which line correctly tells make that `{name}` is a phony target — one whose recipe should always run, never skipped just because a file named `{name}` happens to exist in the directory?
L4.answer: .PHONY: {name}
L4.explanation: Only listing {name} as a prerequisite of the special .PHONY target works: make checks that list and, if {name} is on it, always runs its recipe regardless of any real file called {name}. '{name}: .PHONY' instead declares a target named {name} that depends on a nonexistent file called .PHONY, and a '#' line is a comment make never reads.
options: .PHONY: {name}
{name}: .PHONY
# phony {name}

L4.prompt_tpl: A Makefile contains only `{target}: {dep}` followed by a recipe line `@echo done`. There is no rule for `{dep}` anywhere in the file, and no file named `{dep}` exists in the directory. What does running `make {target}` print to the terminal, and with what exit status does make itself exit?
L4.answer: make: *** No rule to make target '{dep}', needed by '{target}'.  Stop.  Exit status 2.
L4.explanation: make can't find a rule or an existing file for {dep}, so it can't decide whether {target} is stale; that is a fatal error, not a warning, so make prints the message, builds nothing, and exits with status 2 — the code the manual documents for 'make encountered errors'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Makefile contains `{var} := {val}` then a target `all:` with the single recipe line `@echo $({var}) $${var}`. There is no `export` line anywhere in the file, and `{var}` is not already set in the shell's environment before you run make. Exactly one line is printed. What is it?
L4.answer: {val}
L4.explanation: `$({var})` is a make variable: make substitutes {val} before the shell ever runs the line. `$${var}` is the doubled dollar reaching the shell as `${var}`, but {var} was never exported into the process environment, so the shell sees it as unset; an unquoted, empty expansion vanishes under word splitting instead of printing a blank field, so only one word appears, not two.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Makefile recipe reads: `{target}:` then `	{cmd} ; echo done`. `{cmd}` fails (nonzero exit) on roughly a third of runs, yet the CI job built from this Makefile always reports success, even on the runs where `{cmd}` failed. What is actually going on, and how does it follow from the shell's rule for the exit status of a `;`-joined command list?
L4.answer: The recipe line's exit status — the only thing make inspects to decide pass or fail — is the exit status of the LAST command in a ';'-joined list, here `echo done`, which always succeeds. {cmd}'s failure is discarded before make ever sees it, so the build is never marked as failed. Fix by joining with `&&` ({cmd} && echo done), which stops and propagates on the first nonzero exit, or capture `$?` after {cmd} and `exit 1` explicitly on failure.
L4.explanation: This is the general shell exit-status rule, not something special to make: ';' only sequences commands and keeps the last status, while '&&' stops at the first failure and propagates it. Make relies on a recipe line's own final status to know it failed, so a failure hidden behind ';' is invisible to it — see Exit codes.
